For many in the Boston area, the job hunt has become less of a process and more of a prolonged, disheartening battle.

We recently asked readers how long they’ve been looking for a job. Of the 115 respondents to our poll, 46 people (40%) said they’ve been job hunting for over a year — the largest group by far. Only two people (2%) reported being on the hunt for less than a month, whereas 45% combined said they’ve been looking for between one and 12 months. We also received a handful of e-mail submissions from readers who went in depth on their job hunt.

Some have endured the process for multiple years. Kristine A. from Dorchester said she has submitted her resume to over 600 organizations over the last three years and participated in roughly 60 interviews, with no luck.

“It’s simply grueling,” she said.

J.D. from Somerville, who has been searching for more than a year, said it’s been frustrating not even securing interviews for roles he’s successfully performed before — noting that age discrimination in the tech sector “is very real.”

Katie S. from Blackstone described the experience as eerily quiet. “The hardest part of job hunting right now is the silence,” she said. “The waiting has become the hardest work of all.”

“You put so much effort into customizing applications, but most companies never respond — not even to say no,” she added.

It’s not just that job hunting itself is tough, readers say, but that they’re juggling the slow job market on top of the state’s high cost of living and other expenses.

Jose G. from Amherst has been applying to jobs “all over New England” for more than a year. He landed a job for a few months, but then the business shuttered and he found himself “back at square one.”

“I have been turned down by many positions or in most cases have never heard back,” he said. “It’s been difficult for me and I assume so many others to afford to pay for student loans, rent, and everything else.”

Below, readers shared what it’s like navigating the job market now – confronting AI’s impact in the job hunt, ageism, intense competition, and more.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

What’s the job search like right now?

‘This whole process is a giant black hole’

“The most challenging part is simply that this whole process is a giant black hole. You take time to tweak resumes and craft compelling cover letters just to hear silence in return. The competition is crazy – especially if you are looking for a fully remote role or hybrid role, like myself. On top of all of that, before AI it was all about getting yourself to the top of the resume pile. Now, you still need to get to the top but you also need to make sure your resume has the right keywords to make sure AI picks you out of the bunch as a potentially ‘good’ candidate.” – Amanda D., Canton (job hunting for 5-8 months)

“Fortunately I still have a job, but I have been looking for a new opportunity, but have not had any luck. I feel that resumes fall into a black hole and seldom do you hear back.” – Joe, Southborough (job hunting for 5-8 months)

“From getting outright ghosted after speaking with hiring managers to getting auto-rejected by ATS systems and so much more, I’ve seen a lot during my job search. The most challenging part has easily been putting in so much time and effort and seeing very little return on investment. I’ve actually had some success in side hustle pursuits but that pales in comparison to the comp package I was getting in Big Pharma just a couple years ago before I got laid off.” – Max, Cambridge (job hunting for more than a year)

‘You start to question yourself, wondering if you’ve lost your value’

“It has been almost a year since I started looking for a job, and this journey has been one of the hardest experiences of my life.

I apply to jobs every week — hundreds of them by now. Most of the time, I don’t hear anything back. Some applications are met with automated rejections, others with complete silence. I follow up, I network, I rewrite my resume, and still, nothing moves. Out of all those applications, I’ve had only two interviews — both of which I had to chase for months just to get a chance to speak. One ended in rejection, and I’m still waiting for news on the second.

Along the way, I’ve encountered scammers who pretend to be recruiters or hiring managers. They sound convincing, they ask for personal information or money, and they prey on people’s hope and desperation. I’m an experienced professional, and even I almost got trapped. That’s how sophisticated these scams have become.

I have a master’s degree and over fifteen years of solid experience in financial services. I’ve worked since I was fourteen years old and have always taken pride in my work ethic. Until now, I’ve never had a problem finding a job. But this economy — this job market — has been brutal. You start to question yourself, wondering if you’ve lost your value, if something is wrong with you. It truly messes with your confidence and sense of self-worth.

What hurts the most is that I’ve applied for roles I’m overqualified for, jobs I would gladly accept just for the opportunity to work, to contribute, to feel useful again. I’ve also applied for positions at my level — roles I know I could do exceptionally well — and yet, nobody gives me a chance.

I’m sharing this story not out of self-pity, but because I know I’m not alone. There are so many capable, hard-working people out there facing the same silence, the same discouragement, the same invisible wall. I just hope by speaking up, we can bring more attention to how broken this system feels right now — and maybe restore some humanity and fairness to the hiring process.” – My N., Boston (job hunting for almost 1 year)

‘It’s jarring to feel this invisible in the job market’

“I’ve been looking for work since the end of January, after being laid off from a large real estate company where I worked for almost 20 years. I was part of their in-house creative marketing team, handling video and animation. I really liked the stability and the work itself, but my role was eliminated during a restructuring.

Since then, I’ve been applying to three to five jobs a week, mostly in marketing, multimedia, or creative production. I’ve only had a couple of interviews the whole time. Most postings have well over a hundred applicants, and 98% of the time I just get an automated rejection. Sometimes I’m not even sure all the listings are real openings.

I’m halfway through my unemployment benefits now. I’ve been able to stay afloat, but I haven’t been able to afford health insurance. Even with ACA subsidies, it’s too expensive when I still have to cover food and my mortgage. I’ll still be penalized at tax time for not having coverage, which makes it even harder.

It’s been frustrating. After nearly two decades of steady work, it’s jarring to feel this invisible in the job market. I know a lot of people are in the same position, but it helps to see this issue being talked about.” – Anonymous reader

‘Getting screened out by AI before the process can even begin’

“The incursion of AI in Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) erects yet another layer between candidates and a human being. It remains to be seen whether there is any advantage to machine screening of resumes or whether better candidates may be found by having an intelligent human being read resumes.” – Sam L., Worcester (job hunting for 1-4 months)

“Applying to open positions and getting ghosted because each role has thousands and thousands of applicants, which leads to recruiters using AI to sort through applications and leaving the vast majority of applicants with no response. It would be easier on the average job-seeker if real people were looking at resumes, even briefly, and using stock rejection emails for all the unqualified candidates.” – Rebecca M., Andover (job hunting for 5-8 months)

“Getting screened out by AI before the process can even begin – immediate rejections despite perfect role alignment. Sifting through hundreds of fake job listings.” – Lauren N., Amesbury (job hunting for 9-12 months)

‘Graduated college in 2023, ‘overqualified’ for a lot of entry level positions’

“Getting an interview for a job with a decent salary. I am currently employed, but am making 50% of what I was making previously. I am going into a lot of debt. The job market is a confidence killer.” – Katelyn, Duxbury (job hunting for more than a year)

“Salaries just seem much lower than before. Really shocking to see the pay cut I may need to take if I do find something.” – Len M., Framingham (job hunting for 1-4 months)

“Graduated college in 2023, ‘overqualified’ for a lot of entry level positions and did not hear back from more mid-level positions. Currently resorted back to hospitality full time.” – Tyler F., Quincy (job hunting for 5-8 months)

“Knowing that I’m often overqualified because I’m having to apply to positions that I cleared decades ago and still getting rejected.” – John, Worcester (job hunting for 9-12 months)

‘I am thankful to have an offer, but it pays me 20% less than what I’m making’

“Getting the offer. I was laid off in mid-July. Dozens of interviews since then, half a dozen final rounds, where I just lost out to another candidate. I am thankful to have an offer, but it pays me 20% less than what I’m making, and less PTO. So, I’m still looking for other opportunities, and struggling to get other offers. For context, I used to have multiple offers to choose from, as recently as mid-2023, where it took me less than a month to land a new role! Competition is insane now, employers hold all the cards, and I have an MBA and am in my 30s. If I’m struggling, how are others surviving?” – Anonymous reader, Greater Boston (job hunting for 1-4 months)

“The competition. I’m applying for things for which I meet or exceed every qualification, and am not even getting phone screens, let alone interviews. The only interviews/FaceTime I seem to be getting are with LinkedIn connections and/or people who know me from the industry, and even then I’m beaten by colleagues using the same or similar tactics.” – Adam, Needham (job hunting for 5-8 months)

‘Rampant ageism’

“The most challenging part is that absolutely no one will hire someone over 50, regardless of professional experience or being a perfect fit. At 55 I have to work for at least ten more years and put money away, but cannot get hired for a professional job.” – J.M., Watertown (job hunting for more than a year)

We just want (and need to) make more than $15 an hour to survive, especially professional workers … Getting back into the workforce during or after this time is becoming nearly impossible unless you want to do minimum wage jobs.” – Amanda, Stoneham (job hunting for more than a year)

“My issue is my age, 68 years old. I still enjoy work and contribute immensely. I consult, but I feel isolated, not working in a team” – Kevin S., Newburyport (job hunting for more than a year)

Housing affordability once again ranked high on the list of priorities, with many residents describing a city that feels increasingly out of reach for working- and middle-class Bostonians.

Immigration policy continues to spark sharp divisions among readers, with some calling for more support and compassion for new arrivals and others urging city leaders to redirect resources elsewhere.

As Mayor Michelle Wu prepares to begin her second term leading the city of Boston, readers have made it clear what they hope she’ll focus on first: making the city more affordable and keeping its residents safe.

In an informal Boston.com poll asking readers what issues they want the mayor to prioritize, nearly 80 people responded. Housing affordability and public safety emerged as the top concerns, capturing a combined 49% of responses. Over a quarter of readers who voted “Other” shared woes that ran the gamut from stopping police corruption to getting rid of bike lanes and reversing academic decline.

Many readers expressed frustration about the cost of living in Boston, urging Wu to focus on immediate, tangible solutions.

As housing, utilities, and everyday costs of living continue to climb, a growing share of Massachusetts residents say the math of staying in the Bay State no longer works. In a recent Boston Globe/Suffolk University poll and an informal survey of Boston.com readers, residents said Massachusetts is just too expensive to get by.

The Globe/Suffolk survey found that about one-third of Massachusetts voters have seriously considered leaving the state in the past year because of affordability pressures, even as a majority still believe the state is generally moving in the right direction. Inflation, health care costs, housing, taxes, and soaring utility bills topped the list of financial stressors.

Against that backdrop, we asked Boston.com readers a more pointed question: Are you planning to leave the Commonwealth in 2026 because of affordability concerns?

More than 300 people responded, and the results were stark. Nearly two-thirds said they are planning to leave the state, while another 21% said they are thinking about it. Just 17% said they plan to stay.

Many readers described feeling priced out despite working full time, earning solid incomes, or having deep roots in Massachusetts.

“I have to work two jobs full and part time to make ends meet, and I can’t. I’m moving to Rhode Island,” Hakeem from Cambridge said.

Others pointed to rising rents, childcare costs, property taxes, and utilities as breaking points — while a smaller but vocal group said the state’s schools, hospitals, jobs, and values still make the high cost of living worth it.

Below, readers share how affordability is impacting their decision to stay in or leave the Bay State.

Boston’s Major League Soccer team New England Revolution is slated to receive a new stadium and other improvements per a deal struck last week between its owner, the Kraft Group, and the cities of Everett and Boston — a move Boston.com readers largely support, albeit with some concerns.

A majority of readers who responded to the poll — 59% of the more than 100 respondents — support the deal, often citing the need to revitalize the surrounding neighborhood and improve the environmental conditions at the shuttered power plant site. Others expressed concern about traffic and transit impacts (17%), while another 16% said they opposed the stadium altogether. Another 8% need more details before forming an opinion.

On Dec. 31, the Kraft Group announced it had struck two separate but similar deals — Everett officials valued the agreement “at more than $90 million over a 20-year period,” and Boston at “nearly $48 million” over 15 years.

The Boston funds will go toward improving infrastructure around the Charlestown neighborhood, particularly the Sullivan Square area, while the Everett funds will be used for other infrastructure investments and community benefits.

Reader Jay K., formerly of Brookline, said Sullivan Square “has been a disaster for years” and could use the cash infusion from the deal — not to mention “the money the spectators will bring in,” he added.

Mike B. from Boxford was equally enthusiastic about the new stadium: “It’s about time! While there are challenges, especially due to the lack of parking, this is a win for Everett, Boston, and New England sports.”

Others, however, weren’t so optimistic.

“It’s already nightmare traffic for any day of the week,” Vis P., Malden lamented. “It will be a commuters’ nightmare,” he added.

Below, readers share their reactions to the Kraft Group’s deals for the Revolution stadium in Everett.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

As long as they actually build the proposed bridge it shouldn’t be a problem getting there from the Orange Line.” — Michael, Roxbury

“You’ve got someone who wants to take a blighted, contaminated, former industrial zone and turn it into something beautiful with public access to the waterfront at no cost to the taxpayers.” – J.D., Easton Boston

Boston.com readers are overwhelmingly confident the Patriots are bound for the Super Bowl, with trust in both their matchup against the Denver Broncos on Sunday and a growing belief in the team’s identity under first-year coach Mike Vrabel and quarterback Drake Maye.

In an informal poll of over 1,000 readers, an emphatic 88% said “yes,” the Patriots will reach the Super Bowl, while 8% expressed uncertainty, and just 4% said “no way.”

Much of the optimism centered on New England’s stellar defense and Broncos’ quarterback Bo Nix suffering a broken ankle during their 33-30 win against the Buffalo Bills on Saturday. Jarrett Stidham is stepping in to replace Nix during the AFC Championship game on Sunday, Jan. 25.

Several readers pointed to the challenge facing a Denver team expected to start an inexperienced quarterback, a scenario many believe plays directly into the hands of a Patriots defense.

“With Denver’s lead QB out, I feel that opens a good chance for the Patriots to advance to the big game,” said reader Wayne from Tewksbury.

Readers also highlighted the culture Vrabel has instilled in his first season on the sideline. Fans repeatedly cited the team’s determination and resilience as its winning combo.

“The Patriots play with joy, tenacity, a love of the game, and a brotherhood of men that is a recipe for success! Coach Vrabel is a true leader and motivator of men,” said Doug L. from Beverly.

Still, not everyone was ready to jump to conclusions about New England in the Super Bowl. A smaller but vocal group of readers urged caution, pointing to the difficulty of playing in Denver given the high altitude and the Patriots’ historical struggles there.

Here’s what readers had to say when we asked them to weigh in on the Patriots’ Super Bowl prospects against the Denver Broncos.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Do you think the Patriots will make it to the Super Bowl?

Yes!

What a season!” — Sue B., Brighton

Gov. Maura Healey is set to address the Commonwealth Thursday evening, delivering a speech to tout her achievements from the past year and to likely promote her reelection bid this fall.

Healey officially launched her gubernatorial reelection campaign on Tuesday with promises to address affordability concerns and to continue resisting president Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

During her address, Healey is expected to reflect on the past year and outline her policy priorities for 2026. This includes specific plans to reduce residential gas and electric bills, as well as “several new initiatives to lower costs,” according to a release.

Healey is one of seven candidates running in the 2026 gubernatorial race. The primary is slated for Sept. 1, followed by the general election on Nov. 3.

Unlike her republican challengers, Healey has not self-funded her campaign.

GOP prospect Michael Minogue leads the pack with $5.5 million of his own funds poured into his campaign, followed by Mike Kennealy with $1.8 million, and Brian Shortsleeve with $200,000.

When we asked readers if they agree with Mass. GOP candidates bankrolling their own campaigns, we heard from just over two dozen respondents. Among them, a majority (78%) supported self-funding, arguing candidates can spend their money as they like — plus, it gives them a boost against more well known incumbents, readers said.

“If they struggle with finding fundraising elsewhere, what else are they supposed to do — give up?” Michael from the West End said. “This seems like a non-issue turning into an issue to stifle competition, egregious at best.”

There is no limit to the amount of money candidates can contribute to their own campaigns, according to the Office of Campaign and Political Finance. There are, however, limitations on the amount individuals, lobbyists, political action committees, and other political groups can contribute.

Below, readers share why they support Massachusetts Republican gubernatorial candidates self-funding their campaigns.

For many New England Patriots fans, Tom Brady’s neutral stance ahead of Super Bowl LX landed harder than expected.

“I don’t have a dog in the fight in this one,” Brady told Jim Gray on the “Let’s Go!” podcast, speaking about the Patriots-Seahawks matchup. “May the best team win. And in terms of the Patriots, this is a new chapter in New England, and I’m glad everyone’s embraced the Mike Vrabel regime, all the amazing players that have worked so hard to get their club to this position.”

While Brady framed his comments as part of a new chapter — one shaped by broadcasting and minority ownership with the Raiders — a large majority of readers told us it didn’t sit right.

When we asked Boston.com readers to weigh in, nearly 700 respondents voted, revealing a fan base split between disappointment, understanding, and indifference — all tied to the complicated reality of seeing a Patriots icon speak like an outsider during the franchise’s biggest moment in years.

“Tom prob should be speaking a little warmer toward the fan base that supports him no matter what for 20+ years,” wrote Keith from Medford.

Sean R. of Chelmsford echoed that sentiment more bluntly: “His biggest fans are New Englanders. This was a slap in the face to his biggest fans.”

Still, not everyone was upset. Some readers emphasized perspective, pointing to everything Brady already gave the franchise.

“He helped us win 6 Super Bowls and stayed loyal throughout all those years, despite Bill. He doesn’t owe anything,” Roberto V. of Haverhill wrote.

Others landed somewhere in the middle, wishing Brady would acknowledge his legacy without demanding full-throated fandom. “He’s entitled to his opinions, but loyalty to the legacy would be nice,” said Chris.

A viral workplace question has been circulating online: Would you rather take a $240,000 in-person job or $120,000 remote one?

That got us thinking — what if the in-office job is located in Boston, where commuting time and cost of living can be significant?

So we asked readers to weigh in on the modern workplace dilemma: higher pay in the office, or lower pay with the flexibility of working from home?

More than 400 readers responded to our informal poll. While the higher paycheck came out ahead, the results show a workforce still split on what matters most.

In total, 56% of readers said they would take the $240,000 in-person Boston job, compared to 40% who chose the $120,000 remote role. Another 4% said neither option worked for them, with many in that group saying a hybrid setup would be their ideal scenario.

Why some chose the $120K remote job

Readers who chose the lower-paying remote role mostly cited time and flexibility — especially parents and longtime commuters.

“3 kids under 8 — commuting plus the cost of it is horrible. You can’t get the time back,” one anonymous reader wrote.

Erica from West Roxbury said working from home allows them to juggle school schedules and appointments “without hiring additional childcare or paying for before or after-school programs.”

For many, the commute was the deal breaker.

“An in-person job adds at minimum two hours to my work day,” RM from Arlington wrote, saying their mental and physical health is “so much better without the hassle of a commute.”

Others argued that once you factor in commuting costs and higher expenses living near the city, the salary gap shrinks — even feeling “close to the same.”

Why others picked the $240K in-office Boston job

Readers who chose the $240,000 in-person job largely pointed to the salary — and, for some, a desire to get back to pre-pandemic norms.

“$120K isn’t much these days. Especially around Boston,” Dan from Winchester wrote.

Others said the pay gap made it simple: “The extra $120K is life changing,” wrote Michael from Arlington, citing housing costs, retirement savings, and childcare.

Several also said they prefer being around colleagues.

“I like working in an office environment and having interactions with other humans. Remote work is isolating,” Douglas from Dorchester wrote.

“I worked 5 days a week for 30 years — remote work only started in the last five,” said Shaun from Weymouth, while another added, “People need to get out of the house and get used to in-person interactions again.”

The split underscores an ongoing tension in today’s job market: Is doubling your salary worth giving up remote flexibility — especially in a city like Boston?

Boston.com readers are weighing in on the future of parcel P-3 in Roxbury — and many say the long-vacant site represents an opportunity the city can’t afford to miss.

Last week, we asked readers what should happen to the 7.7-acre, publicly owned Tremont Street parcel after the expiration of a mixed-use development plan and the city’s pivot toward potentially rebuilding Madison Park Technical Vocational High School there.

More than a dozen readers responded to our poll, with the majority in agreement: support for investing in vocational education triumphed over the parcel’s initial mixed-use development.

Several readers said a new Madison Park high school would be a concrete public benefit on land that has sat idle for decades.

“It’s a real win for Boston’s youth for Madison Park to be built on the P-3 Parcel,” Pip L. from Jamaica Plain said.

“The new Madison Park School will be a state-of-the-art career tech school that will have the important role of giving PBS students many paths to rewarding, well-paying careers in the trades (electricians, plumbers, auto mechanics, hair dressers, etc.) without the burden of the need to attend college. Many of our students will not be in a position to take on the debt and time of a college education. Very important for Boston to get this done,” he added.

Others echoed the call to update school infrastructure across Boston Public Schools more broadly.

“BPS buildings are old and inadequate to deliver a 21st century educational experience,” David H. from Dorchester argued. “Indeed, this is part of the reason young families move out of the city. It’s time to prioritize the implementation of a comprehensive school building plan.”

The emphasis on trades and workforce development came up repeatedly among readers. Collette of Brighton pointed out that Madison Park is the city’s only vocational high school and suggested students should have a clearer pathway into union jobs after graduation.

John S., a Dorchester youth coach of more than 30 years, argued that strengthening vocational education is critical and expressed frustration that promised affordable housing “consistently falls through the loopholes of this city’s rules and regulations.”

Still, even among those who acknowledged the need for housing, there was recognition that the original plan’s reliance on life sciences funding may no longer be viable in today’s market.

As debate continues at City Hall and in Roxbury, readers made one thing clear: whatever happens on parcel P-3, they want the decision to reflect both the city’s fiscal realities and its commitment to the next generation of Boston’s students.

Massachusetts lawmakers are once again weighing whether to stop the twice-a-year clock change — and most Boston.com readers who responded to our informal poll say it’s time to end the practice.

Earlier this month, Senate President Karen E. Spilka announced her support for legislation filed by State Sen. John F. Keenan that would eliminate the biannual switch between standard time and daylight saving time.

The bill (S.2157) proposes moving the state to a permanent Atlantic standard time system instead, but only if two or more New England states adopt the same time system.

Supporters of the proposal say the clock change disrupts daily routines and sleep schedules, while research has linked the shift to short-term spikes in heart attacks, strokes, and other health issues. The bill is currently being reviewed in the state Senate after being moved to the chamber’s rules committee.

We asked readers whether Massachusetts should stop changing its clocks. More than 470 readers responded, with a majority (83%) voting “yes” and just 17% voting “no.” Though most were in favor of ending the practice, many readers differed on which time system the state should adopt permanently.

Several readers said the clock change itself — rather than the specific time zone — is the real problem.

“It’s a relic of a bygone era that does more harm than good. We mustn’t be afraid to move on just because it’s always been that way,” Brian R. from Norwell said.

Others like Lana C. from Dorchester described the adjustment as disruptive to sleep and daily routines.

“Twice a year my sleep/wake cycle is disrupted for no apparent good reason,” she said.

Some readers said their preference is simply to keep the later daylight hours that come with Daylight Saving Time.

“I love daylight after work. From early March through October I think we’re in the right time zone (and in June the sun gets me up so early I can’t imagine being on Eastern standard time). Winters are dark and winter mornings are not great for getting to work and school in the dark, but school schedules can be tweaked, can’t they? And it wouldn’t be changing the clocks, which is terrible for people,” argued Tom D. from Malden.

But readers who opposed ending the clock change said the proposal could create new problems — particularly darker winter mornings.

“It would be way too dark for the school buses in the winter if the clocks were on Atlantic time (effectively Daylight Savings time schedule in the winter). Safety for the kids is key,” K.G. from Billerica said.

Others raised concerns about coordination with neighboring states and the rest of the region.

“It would make no sense for Massachusetts to change to Atlantic Standard Time (i.e., Eastern Daylight Time year-round) unless the other New England states — at least, those north and east of us, New Hampshire and Maine — did as well,” said Ken P. of Lexington.

Still, for many readers who responded, the inconvenience of changing clocks twice a year outweighed those concerns.

The Lexus SUV at the center of the Karen Read murder trial is going up for auction Thursday in Woburn, and if you ask Boston.com readers, the bids could go anywhere from a lowball flip to well past half a million dollars.

The 2021 Lexus LX 570 — which prosecutors alleged Read used to fatally strike John O’Keefe in Canton in January 2022 — will be auctioned at Manzi Appraisers on May 14. A jury last year acquitted Read of murder and manslaughter charges, convicting her only on a drunk driving misdemeanor. She still faces a wrongful death lawsuit from O’Keefe’s family.

The SUV had a rough few years sitting in storage, according to the Boston Herald: a dead battery, a mouse nest, a dismantled dashboard, and a missing right taillight — the same taillight prosecutors argued shattered when Read backed into O’Keefe. A mechanic hired by Read’s attorney’s spruced it up before the sale, the Herald reported. JJManning Auctioneers is handling the auction. According to Kelley Blue Book, a Lexus LX SUV in similar condition could go for anywhere between $55,180 to $63,880.

We asked Boston.com readers how much they think the SUV will sell for and received more than 200 responses spanning the full spectrum of cynicism, true-crime enthusiasm, and practicality.

The majority vote — about 35% of readers — said the SUV would be sold for less than $70,000, with several readers arguing the SUV’s troubled history would hurt rather than help its value. Just 6% said it would sell for around $70,000.

“It’s a used Lexus with a bad Carfax and worse karma,” wrote Mike H. of Revere.

Over a quarter of readers predicted the car would clear $100,000. And 20% of readers went further still, betting on $200,000 or more; one Colorado commenter predicted it would top $500,000, calling it “iconic.”

A handful of readers noted that the LX 570 has genuine collector appeal beyond the courtroom drama. Plus, at just over 12,000 miles, the car has relatively low mileage.

The auction is live and in-person only. Bidders must register with a valid ID and $20,000 in bank funds. A 10% buyer’s premium will be added to the final bid.

A large portion of Massachusetts residents say their quality of life is declining, a MassINC poll found – and Boston.com readers say they are feeling the pinch.

Of the 854 Massachusetts residents MassINC polled, 42% reported being worse off financially than one year ago, the organization said in a news release. Over half of respondents said housing is unaffordable, according to the poll. Many residents also cite healthcare, higher education, child care, and taxes as some of their biggest economic concerns.

Only 27% expect their finances to improve in the coming year. Respondents estimated that being middle class would require a household income of between $97,000 and $112,000 just to be maintained.

Massachusetts has the highest threshold to break out of the middle class in the country, according to a recent study by financial technology company SmartAsset. A household in Massachusetts needed income between $69,885 and $209,656 to be considered middle class, the study found.

When we asked Boston.com readers for their biggest financial challenges, we heard from 70 respondents. Among the chief complaints were taxes that overwhelm budgets, housing that has become increasingly unaffordable, and healthcare costs that have skyrocketed.

“Quality of life isn’t slipping – it’s plummeting,” reader Gwen G. from Brookline said.

Boston is a finalist to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention, but many Boston.com readers are skeptical about whether the city should take on the event.

Boston is one of five finalist cities alongside Atlanta, Chicago, Denver, and Philadelphia under consideration to host the convention.

State and city leaders, convention organizers, and business advocates gathered Monday at Big Night Live for the Democratic National Committee’s final site visit in its five-city tour.

Supporters pitched Boston as a walkable, transit-friendly city capable of hosting tens of thousands of delegates, media members, and visitors.

DNC chair Ken Martin called the convention “a great economic boon for any city,” noting it could bring “close to 50,000 delegates, guests, and members of the press” to Boston.

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu pointed to the city’s infrastructure and accessibility as major selling points.

“Logistically, our city’s walkability, easy public transit, and excellent public safety infrastructure have made us the go-to hub for major events and gatherings all year round,” Wu said.

Even Amy Carnevale, chairwoman of the Massachusetts Republican Party, voiced support for Boston’s bid, citing the possible financial benefits for the city and state.

“With 24% of Boston’s office space vacant and the cost of doing business 49th highest in the country, Massachusetts can’t afford to turn away any business, even from our Democrat friends,” Carnevale said in a statement. “At a time when businesses are leaving Massachusetts in droves, we welcome contrasting the economic policies driven by the Governor of Massachusetts to the policies of Governors of the most competitive economic states led by Republicans.”

Supporters of the bid also argued that Boston’s deep Democratic roots make it a politically safe choice for the party.

“There’s always a conversation about site selection and putting in a swing state or putting in a place that sends a message about electability,” Steve Kerrigan, president of Boston 2028, the host committee assembled to lead the city’s bid, said Monday. “We are the most reliably Democratic part of this great country of ours and we can pull this off with great fervor and great success.”

Kerrigan also said Boston’s layout would improve the delegate experience compared to the city’s previous turn hosting the convention in 2004.

“This allows our delegates and guests — the vast majority of whom will be able to walk to this arena or take a secured T line — [to] get here early and then pop out and go into the Bulfinch Triangle for dinner,” he said. “The proximity to things make the delegate and guest experience far more enriched in a community and a place like this than if you just had a facility in the middle of parking lots.”

Gov. Maura Healey highlighted Boston’s historical significance as another advantage.

“What better way to honor the history of our country than a celebration of our democratic process and civic engagement in the place where it all began?” she said.

Still, memories of the city’s last time hosting the Democratic convention in 2004 remain fresh for some critics.

“It’s only been 22 years since the Democratic Convention last invaded North Station, not long enough to erase the memory of what a waste of time it was,” Jon Keller, WBZ’s political analyst, wrote in his MASSterList column.

“The Menino administration predicted the thing would generate $154 million in economic benefits to the metro area; a follow-up study by a local think-tank pegged the actual number at less than ten percent of that,” he added.

When we asked readers whether Boston should host the DNC, most respondents said no. Of the 53 readers who responded, 62% opposed the idea, while 38% supported it.

Some readers argued the convention would create more disruption than benefit.

“It will cost much more than it will generate. Furthermore, it will make Boston a hotbed of protest and demonstrations. Not in favor,” said an anonymous reader from Roslindale

Others said the Democratic Party would be better served holding the convention in a battleground state.

“I don’t think it’s the best location. Strategically speaking, we’ve got to invest in cities/states that are actually in play for 2028: Texas, Georgia, North Carolina,” Bryan from Boston said.

Supporters, meanwhile, said Boston’s strong Democratic identity makes it a natural fit.

“Massachusetts is a very blue state. The Democratic Party is polling low among their voter base. They need to focus on convincing those voters to stick with them with the same energy the party has tried to win over independent and Republican voters. Boston is friendly ground and a great location to do just that,” Adam B. from Salem said.

Brown, who arrived in Boston as the No. 3 pick in the 2016 NBA Draft, established himself as a key player in the Celtics’ storied history. Red Line riders are a week into a 10-day shutdown between Alewife and Park Street, and the picture readers are painting isn’t pretty: shuttle buses stuck in traffic, hourlong waits in the rain, and commutes that have doubled or tripled in length.

The shutdown, running July 21-30, allows MBTA crews to replace 18 primary and six secondary floating slabs, replace rail throughout the closure zone, and complete full-depth track work at Central Station.

We asked readers how they’ve been getting around it. And of the 30 who responded, shuttle buses were the most common answer, with 13 people saying that’s how they’re commuting. Nine said they’re using some other mode entirely, four are avoiding commuting during the shutdown altogether, two are taking a city bus, one is walking or biking, and one is relying on the Green Line Extension.

The shuttle bus experience

For the majority riding shuttles, the story has been one of gridlock.

Daniel D. of Quincy called his door-to-door commute from Quincy to Kendall Square “completely unacceptable and outrageous,” stretching to two hours each way — four hours total. He described waiting more than 30 minutes in the rain at Kendall Square because arriving buses were already full.

“I have completely given up hope on the MBTA,” he said, adding that he wished agency leadership would experience the shuttle lines themselves.

Erin of Woburn had a similarly rough go of it. She said her commute has increased from an “already excessive 90 minutes (taking the bus then the Red Line to Kendall) to a crazy commute of almost three hours!” and described watching her bus pull away at Alewife on back-to-back days after a shuttle ride that crept through Cambridge for roughly 90 minutes.

“I don’t have much hope for the rest of this,” she said.

Chris of Belmont called an evening commute “awful,” saying a normal 45-minute trip took more than two hours on July 22.

Not every account was pure frustration. Pat of Watertown credited an express shuttle connecting Harvard to South Station with keeping their commute to a comparatively manageable hour and 45 minutes, though she argued the MBTA should have given riders more than a month’s notice.

“It’s awful, but it would have been so much worse if they didn’t offer this express bus,” she added.

Others found that walking matched or beat the shuttle. Mitzi of Quincy said a normally 45-minute Wollaston-to-Harvard trip took an hour and a half, while Paul, who commutes through Kendall, gave up on a shuttle from Charles/MGH to Kendall after finding it was no faster than walking across the Longfellow Bridge, and later abandoned an evening shuttle to walk home.

“The traffic was so gridlocked that I walked from Kendall to Bowdoin in the rain rather than wait. The shuttle queue was disorganized, with no clear system for boarding, and T personnel, though friendly and well-meaning, had no real answer for the inevitable chaos that erupts every time a bus pulls up,” he said.

Paul argued that without dedicated bus-only corridors, and redirecting personal cars and rideshares away from the bus routes, adding more shuttles will only worsen congestion rather than solve it.

Finding other ways around

Riders who ditched the shuttles altogether described mixed results.

Lauren M. of Central Square said taking the Quincy ferry to the Aquarium T stop and walking the rest of the way was “still 30 minutes faster and more pleasant than the shuttle situation.”

Evan of Dorchester decided the aggravation wasn’t worth it and started driving and paying for parking instead.

Nate K. of Brighton said a normally 15-to-20-minute Red Line trip to Central Square to go to his gym took over an hour and that he’s considering rearranging his gym schedule to avoid the trip entirely.

“The workarounds for the shut down are pretty lousy,” he said.

Not everyone has been negatively affected, however.

Lucien of East Cambridge, who lives roughly equidistant from Kendall and Lechmere, said switching to the Green Line Extension has kept his commute painless.

The shutdown continues through July 30.

With less than two weeks until World Cup kickoff, fans across New England are buzzing with anticipation as their favorite teams prepare to take the global stage. But alongside the excitement comes a hefty price tag.

Attending the World Cup was never going to be cheap. Still, many fans say the final cost — once tickets, hotels, transportation, parking, and food are factored in — has been enough to induce serious sticker shock.

We asked Boston.com readers to share how much they’ve paid to attend World Cup matches, and the totals ranged from around $1,000 for local fans attending a single game to well over $3,000 for out-of-state travel and larger groups.

A ticket for Gillette Stadium’s opening match between Scotland and Haiti on June 13 starts at $657, with the priciest seats exceeding $15,000 as of Thursday afternoon.

For some fans, the expenses begin long before kickoff.

Sara of Malden said she and a friend are traveling to Kansas City, Mo. for a match, spending roughly $800 on two tickets, $1,100 on flights total, and $350 a night for a three-night hotel stay. Add another $60 for stadium transportation, and the trip quickly climbs past $3,000.

Others are trying to spread out costs where they can. Chris of Marlborough said he spent $2,200 on six tickets across three games at Gillette Stadium, plus another $231 for prepaid parking at an unofficial Route 1 lot via ParkWhiz.

Even local fans attending a single match say the costs add up fast.

Stachia S., of Dorchester, said she and another attendee paid $500 each for Category 1 tickets. By carpooling and parking off-site, they managed to keep transportation costs relatively low — $60 for parking split between them — bringing the total to just over $1,000 for two people.

For families or larger groups, the total can soar.

Saad H. of Cambridge estimated his household of three will spend thousands of dollars. He said tickets and parking totaled $3,200 for three people, not including other game day festivities.

“The rest will be refreshments on the day and jerseys for three, which are not cheap,” he said.

Hotels and accommodations are also expected to put pressure on fans’ budgets during the tournament. New Airbnb data released in early May found that 77% of entire-home listings still available for tournament-time stays were priced below $500 per night.

Then there’s simply getting to the stadium.

Commuter Rail tickets cost $80 roundtrip, official buses are priced at $95, and parking at one of Gillette Stadium’s roughly 5,000 spaces runs $175 per spot. Foxborough police did not respond to requests for comment on whether parking along Route 1 or on homeowners’ property will be permitted during the World Cup.

Still, despite the mounting costs, many fans appear willing to pay a premium for what could be a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

Boston.com readers overwhelmingly support a proposal to cap resale ticket prices in Massachusetts – a measure that has been taken up by lawmakers and New England musicians alike.

The amendment, No. 20, titled “To make music affordable by reining in predatory ticket scalping,” was filed by Sen. Dylan Fernandes, a Falmouth Democrat representing Plymouth and Barnstable. It was one of 595 amendments attached to the Senate’s $325 million economic development bill (S. 3187), which senators passed on Thursday.

The amendment, based on “Noah Kahan” legislation he filed in June, would cap the resale price of concert tickets at 110% of the original ticket’s face value, and limit service fees charged by resale platforms to no more than 10% of the total price. It would also ban the sale of “speculative tickets,” tickets a reseller lists or advertises without actually possessing, and prohibit resale websites from deceptively marketing themselves as official or affiliated with a venue, team, or artist. The attorney general’s office would be authorized to bring enforcement actions against violators.

The push to rein in resale prices gained momentum last week when Gov. Maura Healey picked up the legislation, dubbing it “The Great Divide Act.” Announcing the bill, Healey said she wanted to make sure “Massachusetts fans can better afford to see their favorite performer or team.”

Noah Kahan, who made history this summer as the first artist to headline four consecutive sold-out shows at Fenway Park, joined Healey’s announcement virtually and endorsed the measure, saying “I love my fans and want to protect them however I can.”

Over 40 New England-based artists, including the Dropkick Murphys, the Pixies, and MGMT, joined the Vermont-native in signing a letter Thursday throwing their support behind the amendment.

“Live performance should not be a luxury. Our art is not a commodity to be bought and resold at extreme markups against our wishes,” the letter read.

Ahead of the Senate’s session, Fernandes told Boston.com his amendment is simply about “making music more affordable for people.”

“[This is about] making sure the money stays in the pocket of Massachusetts residents and doesn’t just go to these massive private equity-backed ticket scalping software companies,” he said. “We need to take art back and give it back to artists, give it back to fans, and rein in this multi-billion-dollar ticket scalping marketplace in the United States,” he added.

We asked Boston.com readers where they stood on the issue and if they would support capping resale ticket prices in Massachusetts. Of the 165 readers who responded to our poll, 85% said yes, while 15% said no.

Many readers who supported a cap said they’ve been priced out of shows entirely.

“Concert tickets have become cost prohibitive. I’ve been a life long concert goer and I rarely can afford to go anymore,” said Michelle of Needham.

Other readers chimed in with personal experiences of losing out on the opportunity to go to concerts because of sky-high ticket costs.

“I wanted to take my daughter to see Noah Kahan for her 13th birthday,” Michelle H. of Norfolk explained. “I got a presale code but didn’t have any luck getting tix to any of the four Fenway shows. I can’t afford the $600 resale tix so now we aren’t going. That was the only thing on her birthday list.”

Readers opposed to a cap generally argued the market should be left alone.

“I believe in a supply and demand driven market. Yes, some tickets have high resale prices, but I’ve also gone to a lot of shows for cheap,” argued Ric M. of Winchester.

Dave K. from Cambridge agreed, saying “high ticket prices are a function of economic reality here,” and that “the high prices are not a ‘problem,’ they are a functioning market signal of this reality.”

A Reddit post making the rounds in a local subreddit recently set out to solve a very Boston problem: how to talk about the region’s roads without immediately outing yourself as an out-of-towner.

The guide laid down some rules: Drop “the” before highway numbers unless you’re talking about an interstate, and use “route” if it’s not. It’s apparently always “the Pike,” not I-90, and I-93 is also supposedly always “the Expressway.” Skip “Route” for three-digit highways, and use “the Sumner,” “the Callahan,” “the Ted Williams,” and “the Expressway,” for tunnels, never just “the tunnel.”

We asked readers whether the guide got it right. Over 40 readers voted, and the results suggest most think the guide is mostly correct but missing some local nuance: 57% of respondents said they agreed with some points, 30% agreed with the guide outright, and just 6 said it got it wrong.

Among respondents, disagreements weren’t necessarily about the rules themselves, but about geography.

Several readers pointed out that “the Expressway” isn’t a blanket nickname for I-93; it specifically refers to the stretch of highway south of the city.

North of Boston, some readers said, locals just call it “93.” As one East Boston reader put it, “‘Expressway’ is only used when you are south of Boston; north it’s just ‘93.’” A Dorchester reader made a similar case, describing the road heading south from Chinatown as “the Southeast expressway.”

The tunnels sparked their own mini-debate. While the original guide insisted on “the Ted Williams,” several readers said true locals shorten it further to just “the Ted,” and pointed out the guide left out a few tunnels and bridges of its own, like the Zakim and the Tobin.

“It’s ‘The Ted’ and ‘The Zakim,’ not ‘Ted Williams Tunnel’ and ‘Leonard P. Zakim Bunker Hill Memorial Bridge,'” Heather of Tewksbury wrote, adding that a proper local guide should also cover the “the obvious U-TURN = you-eee!”

Others pushed back on the guide’s central premise. A few readers said they use “the I” before highway numbers regularly, contrary to the post’s advice, and a Watertown reader summed up the mood over the tunnel debate: “The tunnel, based on where you’re coming from, has no name given.”

From fleeting glimpses of dorsal fins slicing through the waves to near-miss moments that left hearts racing, readers’ stories reveal a surprising mix of fear, fascination, and even humor.

Not every Democratic incumbent is dodging debates, though. Gov. Maura Healey has locked in two October debates against Republican Mike Minogue. It is not clear when those debates will be held. Boston.com reached out to Healey and Minogue’s campaigns, but did not hear back in time for publication.

Electric rates jumped for Massachusetts customers on Aug. 1, and while the increase should only directly hit a portion of the state’s residents, many Boston.com readers say they’re already feeling squeezed by their summer electric bills.

Ahead of the rate change, we asked readers whether they were worried about the hike and asked them to share what they’ve actually been paying each month this summer. The response was clear: Readers are concerned, and many say their bills already feel unaffordable.

Of 103 people who answered Boston.com’s poll question, “Are you concerned about the Aug. 1 electric rate increase?,” 88% of respondents said yes, they were concerned. Eleven said they weren’t, and one reader said they weren’t sure.

The rate change applies to “basic service” customers, who buy their electricity supply directly from their utility rather than through an alternative arrangement. According to the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities, roughly 27% of customers served by Eversource, National Grid and Unitil were on basic service as of April 1. The remaining 73% get their power either through a municipal aggregation plan, in which a city or town negotiates supply rates on residents’ behalf, or through a contract with a competitive supplier selected on their own.

Basic service prices are set through a competitive bidding process and, by state law, are required to change at least twice a year. For Eversource East customers on basic service, bills are projected to rise by about 4.75%; Eversource West customers could see an increase of about 6.68%. National Grid customers on basic service face an estimated 3.08% increase, while Unitil customers could see bills rise by about 5.88%.

By contrast, municipal aggregation plans — now offered in more than 240 Massachusetts cities and towns — tend to lock in supply prices for longer stretches, sometimes multiple years, giving residents more pricing stability than basic service typically offers.

Some readers pointed to their own experience with local power arrangements.

Matt of Winthrop said the promise that most bills won’t change doesn’t match what he’s already paying: “[I pay] 550-600 a month already … Utilities here in MA are already way too high and above the national average.”

Michael W. of Mansfield noted that his town isn’t on municipal aggregation at all — it has its own municipal light plant, a separate arrangement in which the town itself owns and runs the local utility.

“I am on a muni – Mansfield Municipal Electric Department. Why are people not signing on to community solar?” he asked.

Massachusetts Democrats are at the polls Tuesday deciding one of the most closely watched races in this cycle — whether Sen. Ed Markey earns another six-year term as U.S. Senator in Congress, or U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton unseats him. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Markey, 80, is leaning on nearly five decades in Congress and a long history of progressive politics to hold on to his seat. Cambridge has been grappling with renewed scrutiny of its decision to drop ShotSpotter after the July 4 killing of city worker Xavier Bautista.

Authorities say Bautista, 32, was shot during an early-morning overtime shift and that his body wasn’t found for more than an hour. Prosecutors have charged one man, Rayquon R. Brown, 29, of Canton, in connection with the killing and said the attack appears to have been random, carried out by a group who allegedly set out looking for someone to shoot. Brown was charged on Monday and pleaded not guilty to murder, illegal gun possession, and being an armed career criminal. He was ordered held without bail.

Police unions have argued that the absence of the gunshot-detection system, which the City Council voted to discontinue in May, delayed the discovery of Bautista and the response to the scene.

“It is plausible that an active ShotSpotter system could have resulted in first responders arriving on-scene to render aid to the victim more quickly, particularly in this case when the shooting was not reported via 9-1-1,” Cambridge Police Department spokesperson Sgt. Robert Reardon told CambridgeDay.

The case has reignited a debate that split the council earlier this year, and Boston.com wanted to know where readers stood. We asked if Cambridge City Council should bring back the use of the technology. Of 117 readers who weighed in, the response was overwhelmingly in favor (91%) of bringing back ShotSpotter. Nine percent said no, and just one reader was unsure.

Many who favor bringing the technology back pointed directly to Bautista’s death as proof of what’s lost without it, arguing that faster detection could have meant a faster response.

As one reader, Alex of Roxbury, put it, “It is not perfect, but this technology is useful in quickly identifying very serious and time sensitive incidents.”

Another reader, A.A. of Cambridge, was more blunt: “Common sense to use such technology to safeguard the residents. Foolish not to use it.”

A smaller group of readers pushed back, questioning whether the system actually improves outcomes and whether its cost – $50,000 per year, covered by a federal grant, according to GBH – is justified, given that it may flag gunfire that doesn’t correspond to any reported crime.

The debate over Massachusetts’ nightlife just got a fresh jolt from the State House.

Late Thursday, the Massachusetts Senate passed a $575.4 million economic development bond bill that, among its many provisions to boost small businesses and fund housing and research, includes a slate of measures its sponsors have dubbed the “fun agenda.”

Included in the agenda was an amendment letting cities and towns opt-in to bring back “happy hour” discounted drink specials for the first time since the 1980s, and a separate provision permanently allowing municipalities to designate “Conviviality Districts” where the public can drink outdoors in specified areas. Both amendments were adopted, and the bill now heads back to the House for further consideration.

The Senate’s vote lands just as the clock is running out on a related, more immediate question: whether Massachusetts should keep bars and restaurants open later.

Back in June, lawmakers approved a temporary pilot letting participating cities and towns push last call to 3 a.m. through the end of July, timed to a summer packed with World Cup matches in Foxborough, 250th anniversary celebrations, and Sail Boston. With that pilot set to expire in less than two weeks, Healey has made clear she wants the later hours to stick around.

In a WEEI radio interview last week, the governor said of the extended last call, “I’d like that to continue,” describing the push as “about vibe and energy.” She’s also said she expects the summer to have “a lasting positive economic impact” on Massachusetts.

We asked Boston.com readers whether they’d support making later bar and restaurant hours permanent, and the responses were clear: no later last call, no party.

Of the 233 respondents to our poll, a whopping 70% said they would support keeping bars and restaurants open later, while just over a quarter were against it. Just 4% were unsure.

Many readers who favored keeping the later hours pointed to what other major cities offer and argued Massachusetts’ current rules feel outdated.

“Every other major city does this and the nightlife and culture are better for it. Being so puritanical is just shooting ourselves in the foot,” reader A.N.C. said.

Craig of Middleton said he remembers having access to late-night bars and restaurants when he was younger and doesn’t understand why his own kids don’t have that “privilege” now.

“Personally, I think it is lame our bars aren’t open until 2-3 am,” he said.

But not every reader was on board. Kristen of Melrose said the risks outweigh the benefits, warning that later hours could mean “too many additional drunk drivers on the roads later into the night, more fights, more assaults, and not enough police resources.”

As the country hurtles toward its 250th anniversary on Saturday, Boston.com asked readers a simple but loaded question: Is the United States the greatest country in the world? More than 150 answered, and the results reveal a readership — and by extension, perhaps, a country — deeply divided.

Of the 159 respondents, 41% said yes, the U.S. remains the greatest country on Earth. Just under a quarter (23%) landed in the middle, arguing the country is not the greatest, but is still pretty good. And 36% said the U.S. is not the greatest country at all.

“America has been and still is the land of opportunity. No other country can compare,” wrote Robert P. Durham of Connecticut, echoing the sentiment of many “yes” voters who pointed to opportunity, freedom, and the enduring pull the U.S. has on people around the world.

Others weren’t ready to go that far, but weren’t ready to give up on the country either.

“A bad day in the US can still be a good day in a lot of places. But compared to our similar counterpart countries and who we used to be we have fallen far off the pedestal,” wrote Beth of Ayer.

But for many respondents, the answer was a hard “no.”

“America is number one at infant mortality, child obesity, arms sales, pollution, and medical bankruptcy. It remains the greatest country in its widespread military bases. Its remaining exports are social discord, avarice, and gratuitous violence,” wrote Cam B. of Worcester.

The mixed verdict comes at a strange moment for national pride. This summer, the World Cup has brought millions of visitors streaming into U.S. cities — including Boston, where kilted Scotland supporters have been a fixture downtown — for a monthlong celebration that’s injected a burst of community and goodwill into the country.

But scratch the surface of readers’ responses, and that goodwill runs up against deeper, more entrenched anxieties about democracy, inequality, and, for many respondents, about the direction the country has taken under the Trump administration.

Reader after reader cited the current political climate as the reason their faith in American exceptionalism has cracked, even as many of the same respondents said they still believe in the country’s underlying promise of freedom and equality formed 250 years ago.

For nearly four decades, Michelle Hassler has spent her career caring for some of Brigham and Women’s Hospital’s sickest patients.

The oncology nurse never imagined she’d be spending Wednesday on a picket line instead of at a patient’s bedside.

But after months of contract negotiations that she says have stalled over wages, health insurance costs, and other workplace issues, Hassler, 59, said she and thousands of her colleagues felt they had reached a breaking point.

“We just want to be respected for what we do, and we’re just really not feeling that,” she said. “For me, after 37 years, this is the least amount of respect I think I’ve ever felt.”

More than 4,000 union nurses at Brigham and Women’s walked off the job Wednesday in a one-day strike after negotiations between the Massachusetts Nurses Association and Mass General Brigham failed to produce a new contract. The striking nurses will be locked out through July 13.

The two sides remain divided largely over pay and benefits. The union is seeking cost-of-living wage increases in addition to the hospital’s existing annual step increases, along with affordable health insurance, limits on the use of travel nurses, and contract provisions it says will help recruit and retain permanent nursing staff while protecting patient care.

Hospital leaders say Brigham nurses are among the highest-paid in the market and that their proposal preserves the annual 5% step increases nurses receive as they move through the wage scale, while maintaining competitive health, retirement, paid time off, and other benefits. Mass General Brigham has also said the hospital remains fully operational during the strike and that qualified agency nurses have been brought in to ensure patients continue receiving safe, high-quality care.

“Our proposal ensures every nurse receives a raise through annual step increases or a top-of-scale increase while also preserving competitive health benefits, retirement support, paid time off, shift differential payments, and professional development opportunities as part of our overall compensation package. We respect and value our nurses and remain committed to reaching a fair agreement,” Brigham and Women’s Hospital said in a statement.

The strike has sparked strong opinions among Boston.com readers, too.

We asked readers whether they agreed with the nurses’ decision to strike, and nearly three-quarters of respondents sided with the union. Of the 382 people who responded to our poll, 71% said they supported the strike, just over a quarter (27%) opposed it, and just 3% said they were unsure.

Many readers argued nurses deserve higher pay, better benefits, and more support after years of caring for patients through the COVID-19 pandemic and beyond.

“Would rather line the pockets of the healthcare workers that actually care for the public rather than the c-suite executives,” Ryan of Dorchester wrote.

Others pointed to their own experiences receiving care at the hospital.

“I’ve been a patient and they do not have enough help! My nurses are always apologizing to me for having to wait. They have too much to do,” Janice of Reading wrote.

Kyle of Scituate called nurses “the backbone of our health care system,” and said “it’s time they receive the compensation they deserve!”

Readers who opposed the strike said they believe Brigham nurses are already well compensated or worried the work stoppage could affect patient care.

“BWH nurses are already the highest paid nurses in Boston,” Rob of Quincy wrote.

New graduates working 40-hour weeks at Brigham earn $86,700, according to documents the hospital shared with Boston.com. Nationally, registered nurses earn $93,600 in median pay as of May 2024, according to the latest census data.

A proposal to tax million-dollar vacation homes on Cape Cod and use the money to help year-round residents afford housing has struck a nerve with Boston.com readers, who were largely against the idea.

The plan, known as Home Rule Petition 26-02, comes from Dan Gessen, a 26-year-old Falmouth native and Barnstable County Assembly delegate. It would let individual Cape towns opt in, through a Town Meeting vote, to an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value on residential properties worth more than $1 million that aren’t occupied as a primary home. Towns could also set their own, higher thresholds. Barnstable County would collect the money and funnel it into a new Cape Cod Year-Round Housing Fund, which participating towns could tap for mortgage assistance programs for year-round residents.

Gessen said the surcharge addresses a problem that’s become impossible to ignore: when he was born, the median Cape home cost about $195,000. Today it’s nearly $800,000, pricing out the teachers, firefighters, and health care workers who keep the region running.

The petition follows the state’s 2024 Seasonal Communities Act, which gave towns new tools to tackle seasonal housing pressure but no dedicated funding, Gessen said. It’s his second attempt at raising money for the issue; an earlier petition seeking a transfer fee on high-value home sales cleared the county assembly in February and awaits action in the Legislature. For his newest proposal, Gessen said he was partly inspired by Rhode Island’s “Taylor Swift Tax” on high-value, non-owner-occupied homes, though he said he built local control into the Cape version.

We asked readers if million-dollar vacation homes should face an extra tax to help year-round residents afford housing. Of 330 respondents polled, 77% said “no,” 22% said “yes,” and just 5 respondents said “it depends.”

Opponents were the clear majority, and their objections tended to cluster around fairness and simple math. Many argued that a $1 million threshold is no longer a meaningful marker of wealth on the Cape, where the median luxury home sale price was $1.35 million, according to the Institute for Luxury Home Marketing’s July 2026 report.

“The million dollar threshold is too low. On my street in Falmouth a simple unimproved Cape is valued well over a million. Perhaps a $2 million threshold,” wrote Bob, of Falmouth.

Others said seasonal homeowners already pay significant property taxes without using year-round services like schools, and worried the surcharge would push out the very people who help sustain the local economy through the off-season.

“You’re pushing people out that support the Cape in the summer, money that carries the Cape through the winter,” wrote Mark P., of Eastham.

Supporters, though fewer, argued the math cuts the other way: if someone can afford a $1 million vacation home, they can afford to help those who can’t.

“If you are able to afford a million dollar vacation home you will be able to afford the extra tax,” wrote John, of Woburn.

Others tied the surcharge directly to the housing shortage itself: “Vacation homes reduce the housing stock,” wrote Charlie of the North Shore. Emera of Quincy, put it more bluntly: “Locals can’t afford to live and work there anymore.”

Massachusetts lawmakers are weighing a proposal that would allow cities and towns to install automated cameras to ticket drivers for speeding, running red lights, blocking intersections, and other traffic violations. But Boston.com readers largely oppose the measure.

Asked whether they would support the bill, most respondents said they would not. Of the 633 readers who responded to our poll, 74% said they oppose the proposal, 24% said they support it, and just 2% said they were unsure.

Readers who opposed the legislation frequently described it as an invasion of privacy and questioned whether automated cameras should replace police officers in enforcing traffic laws.

“It’s dystopian. A person should be ‘ticketed’ by a human not a machine,” argued Coach from Norwood.

A new ballot initiative could change how Massachusetts data centers get approved. The measure, filed by West Springfield resident Jim Fleming after residents near Holyoke and Westfield raised concerns about nearby projects, would bar local permitting boards from signing off on a data center until developers meet several conditions. Among them would be a plan to protect ratepayers from higher electric bills and proof that water needs can be met during a drought. Even then, the project would still need approval from two-thirds of local voters to be green-lit.

The proposal is one of several responses to a wave of data center development moving through cities and towns statewide, some of which have already passed their own limits on size or power use. It also arrives alongside two bills in the Legislature addressing electricity costs and environmental requirements tied to the facilities. Fleming’s petition is now awaiting review by the attorney general, who is expected to rule by Sept. 2 on whether it can move forward toward the 2028 ballot.

We asked readers where they stood, and most were in favor. Of 57 people who responded to our informal poll, 46 said they’d support the measure, while 10 said they would not.

Many “yes” respondents framed the initiative as a matter of local control and fairness, arguing that residents — not developers — should bear the final say over projects that could strain infrastructure.

“It’s common sense,” Ted of Belmont said. “Residents’ energy costs shouldn’t have to subsidize data centers, and we need to know the impact on our neighborhoods and environments before more data centers can be built,” he added.

Others pointed to specific concerns close to home. “I live in Lowell and do not like the way the data center here has affected the community,” wrote Joseph S. In April, a group of Lowell residents sued the city’s data center and the state’s environmental regulation agency over concerns about negative impacts to the community.

Jim of Somerville added that any new facility “should not be allowed until they prove they can acquire their own power and soundproof the location so existing neighborhoods are not adversely impacted.”

Readers who opposed the measure mostly zeroed in on the two-thirds voter threshold, calling it too high and not a feasible path to approval.

“The killer is the 2/3 threshold. That will never be met, so it’s effectively a ban,” wrote Jake, of Boston.

Massachusetts remains a draw for many residents because of its schools, health care, and quality of life. But for many Boston.com readers, the state’s rising costs have prompted serious thoughts about moving elsewhere.

In a recent Boston.com poll, we asked readers if the state’s taxes and/or high cost of living made them consider leaving. Sixty-six percent of 512 respondents said taxes and/or the cost of living in Massachusetts had made them consider leaving the state. Another 22% of respondents said they had already left, while 12% said they had not considered leaving.

The poll came as a new survey from the Mass Opportunity Alliance (MOA) examined why some former Massachusetts residents have relocated elsewhere. MOA, a pro-business nonprofit formed in 2024, surveyed 1,151 people who voted in Massachusetts in the 2024 election but have since moved to New Hampshire, Florida, or North Carolina. The survey found that taxes and housing costs were among the most frequently cited reasons respondents gave for leaving.

Among Boston.com readers who said they had considered leaving, taxes were one of the most common concerns. Some readers pointed to rising property taxes, utility costs, and what they described as an increasing overall financial burden.

“Our taxes keep going up and keep getting increases in fees and monthly costs. The cost of living is just too high in this state,” said MaryAnn M. of Amesbury.

Nationally, Massachusetts ranks among the top 10 states with the highest income tax, according to TurboTax. The state has a 5% tax on both earned and unearned incomes, as well as an 8.5% tax on certain capital gains. Plus, individuals who make over $1 million pay a 4% surtax on their income.

Others said the cost of remaining in Massachusetts — particularly the price of either buying a home and/or paying real estate taxes — had become a deciding factor. Several readers said they planned to stay while their children were in school but expected to move afterward.

“I am here for the schools. Once my kids are out of school, I intend to move so I have less of a tax burden,” said Deb D. of Wayland.

According to Rocket Mortgage, Massachusetts narrowly missed the top 15 ranking of states’ property taxes. The Comonwealth took the No. 16 spot, with a property tax rate of $6,352.52, based on the state’s median home value ($635,252).

For some retirees and empty nesters, the combination of taxes, housing costs, and fixed incomes has made other states more appealing.

“I don’t plan to stay here in retirement. Taxes, especially property taxes (which have doubled on my home since the start of the pandemic), are way too high to survive on a fixed income,” said Alex of Roxbury.

Among readers who had already left Massachusetts, many said lower taxes and a reduced cost of living influenced their decisions. Some cited moves to states including Florida, New Hampshire, North Carolina, and South Carolina.

“I left for Florida for better taxes. No property tax and lower cost of living even near the water is so much nicer,” said Mark of Naples, Florida.

But not all readers viewed Massachusetts’ taxes as a reason to leave. Some said they were willing to pay more because they believed the state’s public services, including education and health care, were worth the cost.

“Massachusetts excels in a high standard of living: education, and health care, to name a few, these are worth paying more in taxes,” said Cynthia K. of Amherst.

Others said the state’s investments in public services were exactly why they planned to stay.

“Quality education, health care, safety, and worker rights protected in a blue state as an island against Trump era policies and overreach make it worth it,” said Joe of Millis.

A long-debated plan to redevelop a 7.7-acre vacant parcel in Roxbury is once again in flux — and city leaders, developers, and community members are divided over what should happen next.

The publicly-owned Tremont Street site, known as parcel P-3, has sat empty for decades. Several redevelopment efforts have fallen through, including a large retail and residential complex in 2019.

In 2023, the Boston Planning & Development Agency designated HYM Investment Group and My City at Peace to lead a mixed-use project with housing, commercial, and a life-sciences lab space. But shifting market conditions — particularly a steep drop in demand for lab space — stalled the project. The tentative designation expired Jan. 31 and is no longer active, according to the Boston Planning Department.

Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration is now considering a different path: rebuild Madison Park Technical Vocational High School — Boston’s only vocational high school, which serves about 1,000 students — on the site. In December, the school was selected for the Massachusetts School Building Authority’s Core Program Eligibility Period, the first step toward securing state funding for a major rebuild.

On “Boston Public Radio” last month, Mayor Wu said the original redevelopment struggled to move forward because of the economics, not the Madison Park proposal, calling the idea of subsidizing affordable housing with lab space as a “pipe dream” in today’s market.

“The economics do not work. Lab spaces are at 30% vacancy and this project for multiple years now was not able to advance or make meaningful progress towards a groundbreaking,” she said.

The shift has divided the development team.

OnyxGroup Realty & Development said it is stepping back from the original plan, writing in an open letter that “the economic landscape has changed” and that “the life sciences investment is not coming,” according to the Boston Herald.

HYM and other development partners, however, are pushing to keep their mixed-use vision alive. At a Roxbury community meeting Monday, HYM’s Thomas O’Brien said he remains committed to the project.

“While we care deeply about the high school, we care deeply about the Boston Public School system, we also care deeply about this community, and we’ll continue to care about this mission and this potential opportunity,” he said.
