BOSTON, Mass. — Roughly a month into the school year, families of students and local leaders are sounding the alarm about “unreliable” school buses.

Data obtained by Boston 25 News shows that during the first seven days of the 2026-27 school year, Boston school buses were on time for morning drop-off an average of 80% of the time. During the same period last year, the average was 83%.

Carol Benjamin is the grandmother and caretaker of three children who attend three different district schools. Two of her students have special needs, but all three reportedly dealt with unreliable buses to and from their Dorchester home.

“If you don’t do a regiment and a routine, it does destroy them,” Benjamin said Tuesday.

Her 9-year-old granddaughter Erin, who is deaf and nonverbal, attends Horace Mann School for the Deaf in Charlestown.

Benjamin said Erin wakes up at 4:30 a.m. for a bus scheduled around 6:10 a.m. That ride can take more than an hour, and Benjamin said the bus is regularly late or sometimes does not show up.

“In the morning it is horrid,” Benjamin said.

Benjamin first reached out to Boston 25 in January, but the transportation problems have only gotten worse, she said.

During an interview Tuesday, her oldest grandchild, Jeremiah, arrived home from Boston Prep around 5:15 p.m. Benjamin said Jeremiah had been dismissed at 3:15 p.m., making the trip home about two hours.

Boston City Councilor At-Large Erin Murphy, who has been in contact with Benjamin, called the delays a “huge disruption” and said the city needs to step up.

“When we have a close to $200 million bus system, we need to do better than 80%,” Murphy said.

Fellow Boston city councilor Julia Mejia echoed Murphy, writing in part:

“This disconnect is exactly what we need to address. We are investing significant public dollars into BPS transportation, including tools like the Zum app, and we need to make sure families are actually seeing a return on those investments. We also need to holding Transdev to meaningful account when they continue to fall short of getting our students to school safely and on time.”

Boston Public Schools told Boston 25 in a statement Tuesday:

“We recognize that any delays are frustrating for affected families, and we strive to remain in communication with families to address any concerns. BPS is taking steps to ensure consistent service and prevent disruptions for our students across the district.

There are many factors that can impact on-time performance (OTP) as the school year begins, including traffic conditions, drivers familiarizing themselves with new routes, students and families adjusting to new schedules, amongst others. The OTP achieved so far this school year reflects a strong start to the year and one of the strongest school starts on record. We will continue to closely monitor OTP and push for continuous improvement, as we strive to provide every student with safe, reliable, and on-time transportation to and from school everyday."

Benjamin said the impact can be especially difficult for children who already feel different from their peers.

“You’re already told you’re different, but when a bus doesn’t show up, you really hear it,” Benjamin said.

Murphy said the city may need to consider other contractors if Transdev’s services don’t improve.

Boston 25 News reached out to Transdev Tuesday for comment and additional information and is awaiting a response.

BOSTON — Firefighters across Massachusetts continue mourning the loss of Boston firefighter Robert “Bobby” Kilduff Jr., who was killed while responding to a third-alarm fire in Dorchester on Saturday night.

Kilduff, 53, a 24-year veteran of the Boston Fire Department, died after falling from the third floor of a home on Treadway Road while battling the blaze.

Boston Firefighters Union President Sam Dillon spoke with Boston 25 News about Kilduff’s legacy and the impact he had on the firefighting community.

Dillon described Kilduff as many others also have, “heart of the firehouse,” saying he represented everything people expect from a Boston firefighter.

“He was dedicated to serving the community. He was passionate about saving lives and not just citizens of Boston, but protecting and standing up for his fellow firefighters,” Dillon said.

According to Dillon, Kilduff had responded to a technical rescue earlier in the day before responding to the Dorchester fire.

Dillon also reflected on Kilduff’s service as a proud Marine Corps veteran and the sacrifices firefighters make every day.

“When you look at what just happened in Boston, and you see someone like Bobby Kilduff, you see all the men and women of Local 718 — there are men and women who are out there who on a daily basis proudly pay the debt of living in a city where you are protected from tragedy,” Dillon said.

“Bobby Kilduff epitomized the type of person who not only shouldered that burden, but wore it with so much pride,” Dillon said. “When it came to being a firefighter, Bobby Kilduff wore his heart on his sleeve.”

“Without hesitation, members of Rescue 2 ran to the piece and went out the front door less than a day after what happened to Bobby,” Dillon said. “That just speaks to the men and women who wear that badge. They will never hesitate to put their lives on the line.”

Dillon said Kilduff will receive the highest honors that can be bestowed upon a public servant in the city of Boston.

Kilduff is survived by his adult son and daughter. He was also a member of Boston Firefighters Local 718, the International Association of Firefighters, and the Professional Firefighters of Massachusetts.

BROCKTON, Mass. — As Massachusetts students head back to school, more of them are going to have the option to become bilingual.

More districts are adding dual immersion programs, which are structured so that all students are taught in two languages.

The sign outside the George Global Studies school in Brockton welcomes students in three languages.

Principal Natalie Pohl said, “Our students are learning half their day in English, and then the other half of the day in Spanish, Portuguese, or French.

The George School houses the city’s dual immersion program.

“We live in a global society, and the skills of multilingualism and understanding people of different backgrounds, cultures, and languages are assets for college, career, and on,” said Kellie Jones, Director of Bilingual Education for the Brockton Public Schools.

She said students from all backgrounds benefit from learning in another language.

“The Manthala George Jr. Global Studies School is the highest performing elementary school in Brockton Public Schools.”

That has made the school very popular. A lottery is held for seats at the school, and there’s a long waiting list.

Dwayne Hines is one of the lucky parents.

He recently stopped by the school to pick up a school uniform for his daughter.

“I just want her to learn different languages. You never know what door it’s going to open for you. I never had a second language, so I do feel it’s going to help her out.”

Nationally, it’s estimated there are more than 3,600 dual language immersion programs.

The most popular are Spanish, followed by Chinese and French.

The Boston Public Schools already have several programs and plan to add one in Cape Verdean Kriolu at the Lila Frederick Elementary School in Dorchester this year.

The Salem Public Schools will start phasing in a Spanish dual immersion curriculum at the Collins Middle School.

“Generally dual language programs are known to be extremely effective, both in terms of proficiency in both languages, but also academic learning,” explained Yasko Kanno, Ph.D., a professor of language education at Boston University Wheelock College of Education and Human Development.

“In other words, kids can learn two languages at no detriment to academic learning.”

Kanno added, “There’s often the assumption that bilingual education really is for kids who are bright or talented in learning languages. Bilingual education really benefits anybody.”

Students can benefit from the way learning a language works the brain.

“What is called bilingual advantage, that bilingualism is good for you. Bilingualism advances cognition and executive function.”

At the George School, Bilingual Coordinator Gloria Cho sees other advantages to these programs, ones that stretch beyond learning another language.

“Those are the ability to recognize the difference and seeing the world differently, ability to collaborate with others who speak different languages and who come from different cultural norms, ability to problem solve and adapt quickly.”

According to the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, about 30 communities across the state now have dual immersion language programs.

The offerings are as diverse at Mandarin and Vietnamese.

Three days before Carney Hospital and Nashoba Valley Medical Center are set to shut their doors, a loud and angry contingent of caregivers and community residents rallied on the State House steps Wednesday calling for action by Governor Maura Healey to keep the hospitals open.

The rally drew more than 80 protesters, many from Carney’s neighborhood in Dorchester and the north central Massachusetts towns served by the Nashoba hospital. They demanded that the governor seize the property housing the two Steward Health Care hospitals by eminent domain as she’s doing at St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center.

“We’re still trying to get her [Healey’s] attention,” said Ayer Selectwoman Jannice Livingston, waving a red-and-white sign reading “No Hospitals No Healey” under the scorching sun. “She can’t just shrug her shoulders and say it’s Steward’s fault. We know that, we’re not stupid. She needs to take this seriously and show that she’s fighting for us.”

Steward put 31 hospitals up for sale nationally this year, including eight in Massachusetts, to pay off creditors. The company filed for bankruptcy May 6 after running up financial losses and falling into debt.

But even as Healey announced on Aug. 16 that bidders had reached preliminary agreements to acquire six of the hospitals, including St. Elizabeth’s, she said Steward hadn’t found qualified bidders for Carney or Nashoba. Both hospitals are slated to close on Saturday.

The closings were approved on July 31 by US Bankruptcy Court Judge Christopher Lopez, who is presiding over the Steward bankruptcy, overriding a state law requiring that hospitals give 120 days’ notice before closures. But speakers at the rally asked why state officials didn’t try to enforce the law, giving the hospitals more time to find buyers.

“They took extraordinary action at St. Elizabeth’s, which I applaud,” said state Senator Nick Collins, whose district includes Carney. “Why can’t they do that for Carney Hospital and for Nashoba Valley?”

Between impassioned speeches beneath the State House dome, rallygoers changed, “Maura Healey, where are you?”

An administration spokesperson released a statement noting that Steward was closing the hospitals while the state has teams on the ground helping their workers find employment elsewhere. The statement didn’t address the question of whether the state could have taken the Carney and Nashoba hospitals’ land by eminent domain.

The administration “shares the frustration of communities and staff regarding Steward’s planned closures of Carney and Nashoba Valley Hospitals,” the statement said. “Unfortunately, these hospitals did not receive qualified bids to continue operating. We have been working with other hospitals and health centers in these regions to preserve access to essential medical services and help patients transition their care.”

While speakers at the rally pressed for an eleventh-hour rescue, many acknowledged privately that it was unlikely. But they insisted that state officials could still act, even after the hospitals close, to find new operators and reopen them for emergency or psychiatric care.

“Whatever happens this weekend, we still think there’s an opportunity for these hospitals to receive bids from new operators,” said state Senator Jamie Eldridge, whose district includes the Nashoba hospital.

Elaine Graves, a nurse at Carney for the past 48 years, came to the rally after cleaning out her locker at the Dorchester hospital Wednesday morning. Like more than 750 of her colleagues, Graves is being laid off this weekend. She said she would have worked longer if Carney remained open but decided to retire to spend time with her new granddaughter.

“I would have stayed,” Graves said. “I love my job. This is going to be a big change for me. My husband says I ought to water the flowers.”

The short notice left Lee little time and few options for relocating and continuing to serve her patients, let alone recouping financial losses. She’s worried about what will happen not just for her family’s sake, but for her patients’, many of whom are elderly, non-English speakers, and otherwise vulnerable.

“They trust us, they always tell us, ‘I will follow you wherever you go,’ so we’re very thankful about that, but we don’t know where to go,” Lee said last week, as the days until closure ticked by. ”There’s not enough time.”

Lee purchased Community Care Pharmacy shortly before Steward’s troubles came to light, and had a lease with the hospital through April 2025. But shortly after the closures were announced at the end of July, Lee in August received an early termination letter from Steward, ending her lease at the end of the month. She was told to be out by Aug. 30, with no offer of compensation nor funds to move.

And she had nowhere to go.

Lee, her husband, and their 22-year-old daughter Taeyeon Kim spent hours daily reaching out to nearby hospitals and commercial landlords, trying to find somewhere they could move the pharmacy on short notice. Initially, Steward suggested the Seton Medical Building next door to Carney Hospital, but the firm that manages that building told Lee — in an email reviewed by the Globe — that she couldn’t move in until Steward’s bankruptcy proceedings in Houston are finalized.

Steward and Carney Hospital declined to comment.

Other places rejected Lee outright or asked for rents she couldn’t afford, if they returned phone calls at all. Then there were matters of timing.

To relocate, pharmacies must submit operational, security, and medication storage plans to the state Board of Registration in Pharmacy. Approval can take two or three months, said Todd Brown, executive director of the Massachusetts Independent Pharmacists Association — time Lee didn’t have. If Carney closed and Lee had nowhere to go, she worried her medications and patient records would be locked in the hospital indefinitely.

She turned to state officials for support, too. Her daughter Taeyeon testified at the Department of Public Health hearing on the Carney closure earlier this month and left more than 20 messages with the department and the governor’s office, she said. Even on the rare occasion when they got a reply, it didn’t come with meaningful help.

Finally, this week, came progress. The family located a spot on Bowdoin Street in Dorchester — more than 2 miles north of Carney — the storefront of the shuttered Hamilton Pharmacy. A lease is not yet finalized, but Taeyeon Kim said a state inspector told her family the space is acceptable, and Lee is now cautiously optimistic they will be able to move and continue serving their patients.

In a statement to the Globe, the Department of Public Health said it is “deeply committed to supporting the Community Care Pharmacy” and helping Lee navigate the transition, including safely storing prescription drugs if needed.

“Our Pharmacy Board staff have been involved in ongoing communication, including conducting on-site visits to assist with the regulatory requirements and logistical challenges involved in relocating the pharmacy,” said Robbie Goldstein, commissioner of the department, in the statement. “We are dedicated to doing everything possible to support the community and work toward continuity of care for those who have counted on the Community Care Pharmacy.”

Lee hopes the move to Bowdoin Street is just temporary and still aims to find a more permanent location in a hospital or other health care facility that will both have enough foot traffic for her business to survive and be close enough to transit that current patients can reach her. Many independent pharmacies operate on thin margins — Lee herself has not drawn a salary since taking over this year — but they provide an essential service to many vulnerable patients, said Dr. Guy Fish, chief executive of Codman Square Health Center in Dorchester.

The Steward crisis, and threat to Lee’s business, also comes amid a wider rash of pharmacy closures, especially in predominately Black and Latino neighborhoods where national chains have pulled back.

“What you lose when pharmacies close, whether they are family-owned or big chain, is the ability to actually go the last mile,” Fish said. That “includes the hand-holding, the education, the advice, the coaching that pharmacists give, particularly family pharmacies, who are staffed by people who are in the profession because of a love of their patients.”

And their patients are whom Lee and her family are most worried about.

After nearly 10 years of working in the Carney Hospital lobby, Lee and her Vietnamese-speaking pharmacy technician, Hung Tran, know their patients personally. They take a lot of pride in the language services that help make their patients, many of whom don’t speak English, feel more comfortable. They know how much it means that they offer home delivery and help patients sync up various medications.

The impending closure of Carney Hospital has been rocky at best, and when even a business-owning pharmacist feels “completely abandoned,” she worries about people with less wherewithal to navigate the system.

“We reached out for help everywhere we thought we could maybe get help, and the state keeps saying that ‘this is going to be a really safe transition, and we’re making sure there’s alternate avenues for everyone impacted,’” Taeyeon Kim, Lee’s daughter, said. “That’s not what’s actually happening.”

For Lyle and several other regular Carney patients interviewed by the Globe, the news that Steward Health Care, embroiled in bankruptcy turmoil, would be closing Carney on Saturday came as a devastating shock. The announcement, made in late July, gave patients, employees, and advocates barely a month’s notice to prepare, fight the decision, or find new work or primary care doctors.

The closing has caused an uproar among hospital staff and political leaders, who say the hospital is a critical fixture of the community and an essential resource for a diverse and historically underserved patient population. Despite calls for the state to intervene and keep Carney open as it plans to do with six other Steward hospitals — including by using eminent domain to take over St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center — Carney Hospital is still set to shut its doors.

“I don’t know what I’m going to do. . . . I have nowhere else to go,” said Lyle. “This is the only community hospital around here. The ambulance takes you here if you get sick. And people like me, older people like me, what am I, what they’re going to do?”

Carney Hospital, founded in 1863, sees around 2,600 emergency department visits every month, according to a state dashboard.

Stephen Wood, an acute care nurse practitioner in the emergency medicine department, said a significant portion of those patients have high needs, and many struggle with homelessness, substance abuse, or psychiatric issues.

He’s worked at Carney for nearly 10 years because, he said, he’s passionate about serving the people who need help the most. His colleagues feel likewise, he said.

“There’s a deep commitment to serving that patient population, and a lot of them are literally my neighbors,” said Wood, who lives in Dorchester. “We are such a tight-knit group that care for each other . . . that I’ve never experienced anywhere I’ve worked previously.”

He said Carney staff go “above and beyond” to also tackle social justice and health equity issues, in addition to providing emergency medical care. That often included helping patients enroll in Medicaid, get access to substance abuse treatment programs, or ensure their children were up to date on vaccinations. They also have diverse staff and robust language support services to ensure the hospital’s many Haitian, Vietnamese, and other immigrant patients don’t have to worry about a language barrier, he said.

Wood said many of his colleagues “immediately broke down” when they learned the hospital would be closing. In the weeks since, many have loudly advocated for the state to keep the hospital open, to no avail.

“They’re not investing in these low-income communities, and that’s a huge problem in this state, is that we haven’t invested our health care dollars equitably,” said Wood. “You’re now leaving an absolute health care desert in Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan, with no thought to what’s going to happen to those communities when this hospital goes away.”

A representative for Steward and Carney Hospital declined to comment. Governor Maura Healey has said Steward determined the hospital did not have a “qualified bid” from an operator interested in taking over the hospital.

To Wood, that sounds like an excuse. “This is an absolute atrocity that she would let this kind of thing happen to this community,” he said.

For Mary Ann Rockett, 62, an emergency room nurse at Carney, the closure “feels like deja vu.”

Rockett had previously worked at the Quincy Medical Center beginning in 2008, until Steward Health Care shut the hospital down in 2020. Quincy was also a very community-oriented hospital, she said.

“It was one of the saddest things that I’ve lived through,” Rockett said. “We know these people so well, we know their limited access to primary care, and we know that we’re the fill-in a lot of times for their access to primary care. . . . When they come through that door, we already know their allergies, their meds, their diagnoses half the time, we know what they’re coming in to complain about before it’s written down.”

When Quincy closed, she said, she remembers hearing about some of her patients passing. Others went to Carney.

“Carney services a true need. . . . What is going to happen to these people when we close?” said Rockett.

Other health centers in the area are also bracing for the hospital’s closing, anticipating they may have to absorb patients.

Michelle Nadow, chief executive of DotHouse Health, a federally qualified health center in Dorchester about 2 miles from Carney, said her organization already sees about 22,000 patients a year, reflecting similar demographics to Carney’s patient population. About 60 percent are on public health insurance, 50 percent prefer to speak a language other than English, and around 85 percent are at or below the poverty line.

Many of their patients prefer to go to Carney for specialty or emergency care, in part because of proximity, as well as language services, Nadow said. And with the health care system in Massachusetts already as fragile as it is, Carney’s closure “most certainly will impact health outcomes and health equity.”

“Places like DotHouse were formed because there wasn’t good access to care for underserved populations, and so these health centers and hospitals were firmly anchored in communities to address those challenges,” Nadow said. “When a piece gets pulled away, it’s like if you shortened a leg of a stool. . . . And then how do you balance that out?”

DotHouse Health’s walk-in urgent care has already seen thousands more patients so far this year than expected, Nadow said. When the wait time exceeds two hours, the urgent care has to pause taking in new patients, which has already happened several times in August. With resources spread so thin, and Carney’s closure just days away, she’s worried that’s only going to continue.

“It’s hard for us to think how we can fill some of those gaps, because we’re a health center, we’re not a hospital,” she said.

Dr. Guy Fish, chief executive of Codman Square Health Center in Dorchester, said his organization is in a similar position. He particularly worries about the loss of Carney’s inpatient psychiatric beds.

“Those patients are not going to go away,” Fish said. “Losing the psychiatric services in a community that has a long history with trauma, a long history with being underserved in and stressed, is going to be devastating.”

Last week, Lyle made the trip to Carney — when she’s feeling well enough she can walk there from her house — to say goodbye to her favorite nurse, who works in the hospital’s community clinic. On the way in the door, she ran into a phlebotomist she knows and stopped to chat.

These days, she said, she cries whenever she’s on the bus and passes Carney.

“Carney is supposed to be a fixture in this community. . . . They saved St. Elizabeth’s, and they saved the other hospitals, why can’t they save this one?” said Lyle, who added she’s still hoping for a miracle. “It breaks my heart to know that Carney is closing.”

The deals mean that two-thirds of the six hospitals Governor Maura Healey sought to wrest from the for-profit Steward may soon be in the hands of new nonprofit owners that will keep them open.

Steward said Thursday that it’s still working to finalize agreements to sell St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton and Good Samaritan Medical Center in Brockton to Boston Medical Center. Steward’s two other Massachusetts hospitals — Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center — are set to close this weekend.

In a statement Thursday, the governor said her administration will work as quickly as possible to complete agreements for BMC to take over operations at Good Samaritan and St. Elizabeth’s, which the state has promised to seize by eminent domain from Apollo Global Management, the investment firm that controls the property of all of Steward’s hospitals in the state.

“This agreement accomplishes our goal of maintaining and protecting access to care and jobs in Southeastern Massachusetts and the Merrimack Valley, while removing Steward Health Care from Massachusetts once and for all,” Healey said in her statement.

By including both the hospitals and their property, the sales deals with Lawrence General and Lifespan remove the millstone of lease payments to outside landowners — a longtime sticking point in the protracted sale talks and a burden at the core of the hospitals’ financial collapse.

But not without cost. The court filings Thursday disclosed the Healey administration has agreed to pay $42 million to Steward to support the hospitals’ operations through the end of September. That sum includes money to cover their payroll obligations. It will come in addition to $30 million in bridge funding the state has already provided.

In all, state officials expect the acquisitions, repairs, and operating support to cost the state, the federal government, and other Massachusetts hospitals as much as $700 million by 2027.

The filing said either Steward or the hospital buyers could terminate the sale deals if they aren’t closed by Sept. 30.

Haverhill Mayor Melinda Barrett, who fought a threat to close Holy Family Hospital in her city earlier this summer, said she received a call from Healey Thursday assuring her it will remain open.

“It’s a happy day,” Barrett said. “Haverhill residents will have a place for care so they don’t have to travel 20 minutes or more to another hospital.”

While the agreements signal that Steward and its creditors are on board with the sales, they still must be approved by Judge Christoper Lopez in US Bankruptcy Court in Houston, where Steward filed for bankruptcy on May 6 after running up debts and financial losses and failing to pay scores of creditors.

Lopez, who has repeatedly urged the parties to come to terms on the hospital sales, has scheduled a hearing for Wednesday. The deals are also subject to state and federal regulatory approvals, clouding the outlook for the hospitals to change hands at the end of next month.

The leaders of Lifespan and Lawrence General, in separate interviews, declined to say how much financial assistance the state has agreed to provide them. Those packages were negotiated separately and weren’t included in the Steward bankruptcy filings.

“We’re going to have to make capital investments for the next several years,” said Lifespan chief executive John Fernandez. “We know what we’ve seen, we know what we’ve done due diligence on. But [when] we get into those hospitals, meet with the leaders, and get a little deeper, then we’ll know more.”

“The state is investing in these hospitals because they found there was underinvestment in them for many years,” said Abha Agrawal, the Lawrence chief executive.

Both hospital chiefs promised to move swiftly to integrate care at their acquired hospital and move forward with repairs and upgrades.

“This is an extraordinary and historic opportunity for us to create a regional safety-net health care system that provides high-quality and, very importantly, local and community access to care,” Agrawal said.

“We think we can add these hospitals to care for patients and make them a sort of thriving nonprofit in our health system by taking advantage of our scale,” said Fernandez.

Unions representing Steward hospital workers applauded Thursday’s news, while calling on Steward and its investors to make good on severance and accumulated vacation pay for employees losing their jobs at the Carney and Nashoba hospitals.

“We are delighted,” David Schildmeier, spokesperson for the Massachusetts Nurses Association, said of the Lifespan and Lawrence General deals. “These hospitals are vitally important for those communities to access health care.”

Negotiations for the six hospitals being sold have been held up for weeks by jockeying among the bidders, Steward, its creditors, Apollo, and other landowners over how to allocate the proceeds of the acquisitions between Steward, which holds the operating licenses for the hospitals, and the investment firms that own their real estate.

While the deals could close in a little over a month, Peter Markell, Lifespan’s chief financial officer, said the transition could take “a year to a year and a half to get all the systems in place and replace the infrastructure [Steward] was providing.”

Lifespan, which operates five hospitals in Rhode Island and already has 30,000 patients in Southeastern Massachusetts, will be rebranded as Brown University Health starting in mid-October. Marcia Neiberg, who is currently Lifespan’s chief strategy officer, will serve as president of the system’s Massachusetts operations for the time being. There is no change planned for the presidency of either hospital, according to Lifespan spokeswoman Jane Bruno.

The sales were welcomed in the communities the hospitals serve.

State Senator Barry Finegold, whose constituents include patients at both Holy Family hospitals, praised Lawrence General’s new leader for bringing the Steward hospitals into the fold. He said it will be important for Lawrence General to make maximum use of all three campuses.

“This will create one top-flight regional health care provider for the Merrimack Valley,” said Finegold. “They could have stayed on the sidelines and let these [Holy Family] hospitals fail. But I applaud Dr. Agrawal for stepping up.”

Leann Chaussee, the owner of Touch of Class, a nonemergency transportation and private car service in North Attleboro, said she had gone months without being paid by Morton Hospital for her services.

“Financially I’m still trying to dig out of the mess this put me in,” Chaussee said. ”As far as Lifespan taking over. . . I think it’s a great idea.”

A long-struggling Boston charter school, the Helen Y. Davis Leadership Academy, won’t reopen this fall after failing to enroll enough students to remain financially viable.

The Board of Trustees quietly voted July 17 to shut its doors permanently, surrender its state operating license, and cancel the upcoming school year. Although the Dorchester middle school notified families this summer about the decision, it made no public announcement about it. The move left families scrambling to find new schools for their children with only weeks before the new year was supposed to begin.

Enrollment in Grades 6-8 had fallen to 56 students in July, well below the 216 students the charter is supposed to serve under its operating license with the state Department of Elementary and Secondary Education.

“This was a difficult decision, but one necessitated by the school’s financial condition due to low enrollment, which was no longer sufficient to support the school’s mission and vision,” Sophia Stephney, the school’s executive director, said in a statement. “The staff and leadership team at Helen Y. Davis Leadership Academy has facilitated the transfer of our students to local schools to help ease the stress with the school closing.”

The independent charter school, which is not affiliated with Boston Public Schools, had been struggling with low enrollment for the last few years, fueled by a variety of factors, including a shrinking school-aged population in Boston.

Another independent charter school, City on a Hill in Roxbury, is preparing to close next June.

The declining enrollment at Davis was increasingly creating financial problems for the school, which operates mostly on per-student state aid.

According to a financial audit previously obtained by the Globe, the school racked up nearly $1 million in operating losses during the 2022-23 school year, representing more than 20 percent of its $4.4 million in annual spending.

Davis failed to rein in spending to compensate for a massive cut in per-student state aid — caused by fewer students enrolling than anticipated — and then it overspent its budget by $260,000, including by hiring more staff.

The state Board of Elementary and Secondary Education placed the school on probation in May due to its enrollment and financial problems, and state education officials warned that the school might have to close in the coming months if it failed to enroll enough students. It was the second time since 2018 that the board placed Davis on probation due to financial problems.

The board will need to vote on whether to accept Davis’s decision to surrender its operating license. The board’s next meeting is Sept. 24.

The Food Project is trying to remedy this issue by providing food to needy families and educating teenagers from the Boston area and Eastern Massachusetts about agriculture and nutrition. It grows around 200,000 pounds of food each year that it sells at affordable prices at project-run farmers markets in Boston’s Dudley neighborhood and in the city of Lynn, the first farmers markets in the state to accept electronic SNAP benefits and pilot a Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program-matching program that’s now used across Massachusetts, according to The Food Project’s website.

It also installs 100 raised-bed gardens each year for local households and organizations as part of the nonprofit’s firm belief in people’s right to grow their own fresh food.

In an attempt to bring more awareness to the problem of food insecurity, Governor Maura Healey’s administration held the state’s first annual Urban Agricultural Week in August showcasing eight local farms, including The Food Project. The Massachusetts Department of Agriculture sponsored tours of the farms, providing transportation between them. People could see how the farms tackled food insecurity and learn about their different programs and initiatives.

John Wang, The Food Project’s co-director of strategy and organization support, said since the project was founded in 1991, one of its goals has been finding which communities are facing food insecurities and why.

“Whether it’s intentional or unintentional, there is a system that doesn’t grant access for local fresh, healthy foods for certain folks,” he said.

A study from The Greater Boston Food Bank showed people reporting the most food insecurity were largely from historically marginalized communities or struggled economically. The study, which surveyed over 3,000 Massachusetts adults from November 2023 to March 2024, found those who reported that they lacked basic access to safe and nutritious food were mostly people from Black, Hispanic, and Alaska Native communities; college students; and LGBTQ+ people.

Danielle Andrews, Boston farms and greenhouse manager at the project, said the organization prioritizes and works with families they can directly impact and educate on how to get fresh foods. She wants The Food Project to address what she said is a misconception that families don’t want fresh fruits and vegetables.

“My experience is that everybody actually really does want them and they can’t afford them, so figuring that out is really just better for all of us and leads to a healthier society,” she said.

During the Aug. 12 tour, people saw that over 20 youth workers were spread out from the project’s garden to the greenhouse in their green Food Project shirts. Some held baskets of harvested crops, and others worked on the grounds, planting.

The Greater Boston Seed Crew is an agricultural youth development program that hires teenagers ranging from ages 14 to 18. The project pays them $15 an hour and teaches them basic agriculture and farming. Students can work in the summer or during the school year.

They learn harvesting, weeding, preparing beds for planting, transporting crops, and managing farming equipment and facilities.

Nox Southard, 17, said more youths should get involved with agriculture. Southard, a peer leader for the crew who was working his third summer with the program, said most people his age don’t participate in agriculture because they have not been exposed to why it’s important and what kind of work is available for them.

“You don’t ever think, ‘I can do this,’ until you get in a real-life space of moving things around, seeing people you’re helping, handing things to people, and even kind of suffering in the heat some days,” he said.

Before joining The Food Project, Southard thought jobs meant having a strict supervisor who dictated tasks to their employees. But he found his supervisors at the project flexible and understanding.

Since the Seed Crew focuses on motivating students to work in or learn more about agriculture, crew members are encouraged to communicate with their supervisors. Everyone working at The Food Project believes in the mission, so those in the crew are receptive to feedback about how they can improve their work on the farm.

Southard said joining the project brought him out of his comfort zone and gave him a new perspective on how youth can influence what food families have access to. He wants to encourage more middle school and high school students to get involved in agriculture and advocate for farmers to open up more space for youth in the profession.

Under the hot sun, Southard loaded newly harvested tomatoes in a truck. He was glad The Food Project gave him a direct connection to farming and agriculture and taught him about food insecurity in the state. He looks to share this hope for change.

In the spirit of conservative individualism, he believes that top-down governmental fixes to address inequality can only go so far. He thinks Black communities’ challenges can be solved not with sweeping institutional redistributions like reparations but with internal cultural change and government policies that would promote economic uplift regardless of race. And while Loury has been a critic of mass incarceration, he rebukes progressive narratives about systemic racism that imply American society is purposely keeping Black people in the Jim Crow era. He writes that he believes there needs to be more focus on issues like “the state of the black family, the black victims of violent crime, and the necessity of building social capital within black communities.”

Loury recounts his political evolution in his tell-all memoir, “Late Admissions,” where he also details falling prey to — and overcoming — many of the vices he cites as plaguing Black communities. Loury has mended his relationship with the son he abandoned to a single mother, he’s beaten his addiction to cocaine, and he has gone from being a self-proclaimed “player” and philanderer to a pensive grandfather living in a sleepy part of Providence. The individualism that makes him critical of dynamics he sees in Black communities also makes him hopeful. “I was raised by some of the most industrious people I had ever met,” he writes. “If I believed that black people were lazy or incompetent, it would have made no sense for me to expend so much energy championing the development of their skills and abilities.”

Sitting in his home this summer, Loury and I discussed the apparent contradictions in his life. Some of the quotes that follow have been condensed.

Glenn Loury makes it sound like being a Black conservative is the most natural thing in the world — though not the easiest.

“I talk a little bit about this in the book — about disappointing family members because of my politics and feeling torn between wanting to be an independent thinker and go where my mind leads me on the one hand and feeling that I am in one way or another perhaps being used by people on the right because I’m a rare representative as an African American conservative of a certain type. Or that I’m betraying in some way or another my people and then I’m losing authenticity as a member of the community by sticking [with] a position that so many in the community reject.

“I’m a neoliberal economist and somewhat conservative culturally. I was a born-again Christian at a point in my life. I am no longer a practicing religious follower, but I have great respect for those traditions and for some of the cultural conservatism that comes out of that. But mainly, I think ‘Black conservative’ is a label that sticks to me because I’m a person who believes in personal autonomy and responsibility, and I think African Americans need — we do collectively as a group — to take control of our lives and to not be dependent upon the benefits and transfers and whatnot that come from people who are trying to make up for the past. And I think the imperative in front of African Americans today is an imperative of development, of realizing the potential that has been created by the success of the civil rights movement and the opening up of American society. And that makes me conservative in the sense of the Booker T. Washington side of the Washington-DuBois debate about the future of Black Americans from 125 years ago. I’m on the Booker T. Washington side. In the contemporary times, that’s a relatively conservative position. The way I’ve put it on occasion is to ‘seize the reins.’ The ball is in our court. The train is leaving the station, America is a great open society.

“I think as I get older, it becomes less of a problem to be a Black conservative. Is it lonely sometimes? Yeah. Is it liberating? Sometimes, yeah. So it’s a mixed bag.”

In the aftermath of George Floyd’s death, how did he feelabout the ensuing protests and the Defund the Police movement?

“The radicals had control of the agenda. I think there was a kind of moral panic, in which everybody felt that they needed to demonstrate their solidarity with a moral position, which is anti-racism, and took the relatively few incidents of police mistreatment, which were egregious, like the George Floyd incident, and [built them] into a general case against the necessity of policing broadly.

“So you end up with this slogan, and that’s all it is, a slogan about defunding the police. It’s not a coherent vision of how you’re going to secure public safety for people who live in dangerous circumstances. So I thought the rhetoric was not well matched to the reality, and I think the history since 2020 of the Defund the Police movement shows that a) the police haven’t been defunded in many places, although the police have been hampered. But b) the politics of Defund the Police has backfired on the progressives and now Democrats are running away from it. ‘We never said that. That’s not what we meant.’ As well as the fact that the crime issue is going to be not helpful to the progressive candidates politically. I think it’s one of the reasons why Trump is doing as well as he is doing. And I think that some of the problems in major cities across the country, in Los Angeles and in Chicago and New York, in Philadelphia and Washington, D.C., and Atlanta and other places where at the local level they’re seeing spikes in violent crime and property crime, people who have to live with that are expressing their disquiet.” [Editor’s note: Loury is right that violent crime was higher nationwide in 2023 than in 2019, but not all property-related crimes have increased.]

“I think it is in keeping with the commonsense observation that if you attack police officers, you can expect to get less out of the police officers, and the community actually depends upon the police for security and safety. I find it interesting that if I were to be talking about another set of public employees — teachers — and I were to say the conditions under which they work and the extent to which they get affirmed by the society affects their ability to perform their jobs, most people would have no problem with me saying that. And I think something like that is also true about policing.”

In Loury’s memoir, he describes an early 1980s House Judiciary Committee hearing held by John Conyers Jr., a Black Democratic representative from Detroit, about police brutality. Having grown up in Chicago, Loury understood how threatening crime can be for residents of Black neighborhoods and felt that Conyers’s focus on policing was missing the main problem.

“The brutality issues of policing in Detroit were minor compared to the criminal victimization issues that his constituents had to confront. There was an outbreak of rapes of teenage girls trying to get to school in the early morning hours. I use that as an anecdote in the book, to say what was spurring me to question the party line about race and inequality, which Representative Conyers was an exponent of — police brutality, systemic racism. And I was saying, ‘Yeah, but what about criminal behavior? And don’t we owe something to the people who have to deal with the consequences of it?’”

Why did he tell Coretta Scott King that the civil rights movement was over during a meeting with Black leaders in 1984? Does he still believe that?

“The civil rights movement of the 1950s and ’60s and ’70s, if you like, was successful. It was successful at getting the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act and the Fair Housing Act and so on. It was successful in promoting an ethos that was very different and much more sympathetic to the aspirations of African Americans than was the case in decades earlier. I think the civil rights movement won.

“But let’s say I take the overrepresentation of Blacks amongst criminal defendants — is that a civil rights problem? I don’t think so. I don’t think that’s a civil rights problem that can be remedied by protest demonstrations or the identification of ‘racist’ laws and then getting them off the books.

“Unfortunately, I think it’s a much tougher problem. This is Glenn Loury here, not everybody’s going to sign on to this: that the root of that problem is the behavior of the people who are being brought under the sway of the law enforcement. And that has to do with a lot of things. It has to do with culture and with their family backgrounds and what kind of values are instilled. I’d accept that it also has to do with economic opportunity and what’s going on in the schools and so on. But I don’t think those, either, are largely civil rights issues — that is, issues turning on African Americans being deprived of the full benefits of citizenship.”

While equality under the law may have been achieved, Black communities still face major challenges. Does he see any place for protest? Yes, he tells me — but when the goals are narrow and targeted.

“I don’t mean to pretend that there aren’t some questions about the way in which certain police departments carry on their duties, that there aren’t certain elements within policing that are racist and so on. And you can talk about what kind of accountability and responsibility police officers who abuse their authority or misuse the awesome powers of their office should be confronted with. Citizens review panels about what happens with policing in a particular place — I’m not necessarily opposed to any of that. But I don’t see a major role for protests unless it’s aimed at ‘OK, the schools in the city aren’t working, we want reform. We have an idea about what that reform should be.’ Let’s say it’s a charter school movement or people who want to try to help parents have more voice in what’s going on in the classroom. ‘We are organizing ourselves in order to make our position known and to make the people who are in positions of responsibility accountable.’

“To say there was no role for protests would be partly like saying that the First Amendment isn’t doing us any good. It can be a vehicle for people to express themselves to the institutions of power. I think that the populist upsurge that we see in the Donald Trump phenomenon is a kind of protest. It’s a kind of way that people without voices are trying to get their voices heard, and I wouldn’t be against that categorically.”

One of Loury’s most controversial views is his opposition to affirmative action. Though he has been the beneficiary of affirmative action programs and believes they have been useful tools in the past, he believes that these programs make the recipients doubt their own worth.

“In the fall of 1970, I was enrolled as an undergraduate with a full scholarship at Northwestern and, of course, that was affirmative action. I probably could have been admitted to MIT [for a PhD] even without a special program because my record was just that stellar. I was taking PhD-level courses as a senior at Northwestern in mathematics and in economics, and I was doing very well in those classes. I was an outstanding prospect regardless of my race, but there’s no way that I can ever know whether or not my admission to Northwestern would have happened even if I hadn’t been Black. Just like there’s no way for me to deny that my appointment as a tenured professor of economics at Harvard in 1982 — just 10 years after I graduated from Northwestern, and only six years after I completed my PhD — full professor, the first Black to have that position in economics at Harvard.

“Well, OK, they brought me in as a joint appointment in economics and Afro-American studies. They wanted to beef up their Black Studies Group. If I weren’t an African American working to some degree on those issues, I’m quite sure that I would not have been offered that position. I had difficulty dealing with the pressures of that position in part because I wasn’t sure that I was ‘good enough’ to pull it off. I was afraid that I was going to fail, and that paralyzed me and I ended up changing the direction of my career in part because of that.

“I think as a historical matter, there was a necessity for something like affirmative action coming out of the period of the Second Reconstruction, out of the post-1960s civil rights environment. But that was 60 years ago. It’s not something that we want to be doing in the second third of the 21st century.”

If systemic approaches like reparations and affirmative action aren’t the right way to go, what is?

“The messages that I would put out within the community’s larger cultural matrix — church basements, popular culture, and things like that — I would want to see be more a message of responsibility and development. Biden goes to Morehouse College and gives a commencement address, and he reminds the students there that this is still America where racism can rear its ugly head at any moment. And he basically says, ‘Support me and I’ll protect you from the racists,’ when what might have been said is ‘You stand on the threshold of greatness. This is an open society. Anything is possible here, hit the ground running, go forth, there are Black billionaires, start a business, etc.’ Affirmative to the possibilities of what can be done in this country and accepting our responsibility to seize the reins of opportunity and to make something of our lives.

“Another thing that I would want to see is transracial politics. I don’t like the reparations stuff. I don’t want to parse the country up into racial enclaves and then get into a quid pro quo negotiation of who’s going to do what for whom. I’d much rather see a transracial, or, if you like, class-based [approach]. So if I take the schools [that] are not working: That’s a problem for everybody. It’s not just a problem for Blacks. If I think that the police are disrespectful, that’s a problem for everybody. It’s not just a problem for Blacks. What about inflation? What about taxes being too high? What about what are we going to do about the climate? These are not racial issues.

“A transracial politics for the larger public space, and an empowerment and seizing opportunity and accepting personal responsibility for the more communal space, is the way I think about it.”

As for Nashoba Valley, the area has suffered from chronic underinvestment in both health care services and basic infrastructure such as transportation, which is an important social determinant of health. The community is already bracing for dire impacts on health, public safety, and municipal finances in a rural region that is stretched thin, with few options for a largely working-class and aging population.

Once the Ayer hospital closes, it will be difficult to reopen it or to repurpose the building for other types of health care uses as the physical plant further deteriorates and workers leave the region for jobs elsewhere.

The time is now for the state to engage the Nashoba Valley community in exploring options and identifying funding to protect health in the region. Investments in primary care and in nonmedical factors that influence health are likely to have the greatest return on investment.

All communities are worthy of the state’s attention and investments to survive, rebound, and thrive after the crisis brought on by Steward Health Care’s collapse.

Amie Shei

President and CEO

The Health Foundation of Central Massachusetts

Worcester

I enjoyed reading Jon Chesto’s commentary looking back at the Market Basket battle of 2014 (“10 years later, Market Basket’s feel-good story,” Page A1, Aug. 28). Arthur T. Backpacks alone would likely run her $200, she said, since they had increased from $25 each a few years ago to $40 to $60 now. She had to temporarily leave her job as a ramp agent at Logan International Airport over the summer, as she lacked child care. So back-to-school shopping will make a sizable dent in her savings, she said.

“It will set me way behind on other things,” she said.

That’s a common situation for many families in the Boston area, said Marguerite Dowd, senior director of operations at Cradles to Crayons, a Newton-based charity that provides children’s essentials for low-income families. The nonprofit will provide 75,000 backpacks and more than 1 million school supplies to Massachusetts students this year.

“With the effects of inflation and increased cost of living, so many families are asking themselves how they’re going to afford any of these basic needs for school,” Dowd said.

At $39 billion nationwide, projected back-to-school spending for all K-12 families is down from last year’s $41 billion, according to the National Retail Federation, which surveyed 7,533 consumers in July.

College students, meanwhile, are expected to spend a total of $84 billion this year, down from $94 billion in 2023. Back-to-college spending is projected to be $1,365 per household, only $2 less than last year, according to the retail federation.

This year’s projections, lower than last year but still high, reflect that consumer spending overall is starting to moderate, though consumers still prioritize what’s important to them, said Katherine Cullen, vice president for industry and consumer insights at the National Retail Federation.

“For families with kids in K through 12 or folks heading off to college, there’s nothing more important or more essential than being ready for that first day of class,” Cullen said.

In Massachusetts, higher inflation and costs compared to the rest of the country could hurt profitability for both small and large businesses and raise costs for consumers, compared to the nationwide projections, said Jon Hurst, president of the Retailers Association of Massachusetts. The goal for businesses is to beat the prior year’s sales at least by the rate of inflation, so the recent plateaus and projected drops in spending are concerning for stores, Hurst said.

“That’s showing a bit of exhaustion from the consumers,” he said. “That’s a direct response to price increases through inflation.”

To be able to purchase the necessary back-to-school items, 47 percent of low-income families will have to cut back on other expenses, Dowd said.

Mangie Beverly, a hospital industry customer service employee from Roxbury, said she saves money on school supplies for her daughters Shayla, 12, and Mikaili, 8, by looking for last-minute sales. But shopping just before school starts means some of the supplies her daughters need are gone, she said.

Since clothes and school supplies are necessary expenses, she said, she generally tries not to think about the price increases.

“I just spring for it, because I have to,” she said.

Consumers who took the National Retail Federation’s survey reported being budget-conscious while shopping for school essentials, Cullen said.

A loyal Target Circle rewards member, sale-savvy Natalia Menard ordered notebooks online because her job in the career center at Tufts University earned her a discount. She seeks out sales and turns to reliable staples, gesturing one recent evening inside Target to a pile of colorful, folded T-shirts with sequins and designs that she’s been buying her daughter, Aili, for years for $6 to $8. This year, though, they’re $12.

“That’s intense,” she said. “How do they justify that?”

With her son, Zeke, starting preschool and Aili entering first grade, Menard said, the back-to-school shopping list is much longer than last year’s and includes some expensive items like headphones. She recalled how her own back-to-school shopping strained her family’s budget when she was growing up.

“It was a really rough time,” she said.

A patient access coordinator, Amado scheduled appointments, sorted insurance claims, and made the diverse and historically underserved patients of the area feel at home. He knew regulars by name and saw some just this week, as they came to say goodbye.

Now, the 26-year-old Amado will go on to find new job, and Carney, which employs 900 people and has served this community since the Civil War, will sit empty.

“The closure was a total surprise,” he said. “They painted this picture that we would be able to make it work, but here we are.”

Both Carney and Nashoba Valley Medical Center, 40 miles away in rural Ayer, will shut their doors at 7 a.m. Saturday. It’s the clearest, keenest loss yet in the financial collapse of Steward Health Care — which is selling its six other Massachusetts hospitals amid bankruptcy proceedings but said it received no qualified bids to buy these two.

Despite weeks of protests and rallies to change the company’s mind or sway the state to step in, that didn’t change.

And so on Friday morning, as ambulances began diverting patients to other hospitals, whole sections of both facilities felt as quiet and somber as a funeral home.

In the emergency room at Nashoba, nurses in scrubs huddled at their station, reminiscing about their years together treating patients rushed in after heart attacks, falls, and drug overdoses. They waited for the final walk-ins on the last full day of operations.

“It’s double hit for us,” said ER nurse Audra Sprague, a 17-year veteran of the hospital, which employs 490 people. “We’re losing our jobs and the place where we get care. And we’ll have to get jobs at hospitals that are already overcrowded and will feel the effects of our closure.”

As the place readied to close, emergency medical technicians making their last visits to the emergency room brought pizza and baked goods for nurses who were busy planning to transfer patients to hospitals in Worcester County or as far away as Boston, Hartford, or Manchester, N.H.

ER nurse Dotty Teehan joked that the closure was just her latest “Steward debacle.” She worked at Steward-owned Norwood Hospital for 20 years until it was closed due to flooding in 2020. Then she briefly worked at the standalone emergency room left over in Quincy after Steward closed Quincy Medical Center in 2014. When Steward shuttered that facility at the end of 2020, Teehan came to Nashoba.

“I think I’m bad luck,” she told her colleagues at the nurses station.

Steward, which filed for bankruptcy May 6, put 31 hospitals in eight states up for sale earlier this year to pay off its creditors. As it closes Carney and Nashoba Valley, the company late Friday reached a deal to transfer operations of St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton and Good Samaritan Medical Center in Brockton to Boston Medical Center.

On Thursday, Steward reached final agreements to sell Holy Family Hospital in Methuen and Haverhill to Lawrence General Hospital, and St. Anne’s Hospital in Fall River and Morton Hospital in Taunton to Lifespan Health System of Providence. The buyouts will come before a Texas bankruptcy judge for approval next week.

But the survival of some Steward hospitals was little comfort to the communities that rely on Carney and Nashoba. Protests have raged for weeks calling on Governor Maura Healey to find a way to keep the two hospitals open, including a rally on the State House steps Wednesday.

Some lawmakers insist that, even as their hospital licenses expire this weekend, Carney and Nashoba could reopen as emergency or behavioral health facilities. On Friday, the Healey administration said it was in talks with UMass Memorial Health in Worcester about the possibility of converting the Nashoba ER into an urgent care center.

But at the hospitals themselves Friday, a stream of longtime patients meandered in to retrieve their medical records — with mixed success.

Jennifer Stewart drove to Carney from Quincy to take her childhood records home. But an employee at the hospital told her that documents before 2008 were not available, locked in a faraway warehouse, and sent her home with a thin white file.

”It’s great that this community had a hospital, somewhere to go to,” said Stewart, who grew up in Dorchester. “But it’s kind of scary that they lost my records. What if there was a medical issue when I was younger and nobody told me? I’d never know.”

Groton resident Sandra LaValley, who grew up in nearby Pepperell, was a lifetime patient at Nashoba. She arrived on Friday to pick up her records and take them to Southern New Hampshire Medical Center in Nashua, N.H., her new hospital more than 20 miles north of Ayer.

“I think it’s terrible,” LaValley said of the Nashoba shutdown. “A lot of people are going to suffer. Not to mention the good people who worked here for so long. If I didn’t come today, I might not get these records.”

Lancaster resident Joseph Brathwaite, a retired engineer, knows people who have been coming to the Nashoba hospital for 60 years. It serves 16 mostly rural communities with more than 160,000 residents.

“I’m 76, and I can get around,” he said. “But what about the older people? They can’t get around. It’s hard for older people to drive to Worcester.”

Outside, housekeeper Kevin Gaguen of Fitchburg parked his white pickup truck — with his green kayak on the roof rack — on the front lawn of the hospital, across the road from an old red barn. Almost every inch of the truck was covered with messages, scrawled with red and blue markers, calling for keeping the Nashoba hospital open.

“Nurses, patients, EMTs all signed it,” Gaguen said proudly. “We even had a doctor sign it. I drove around to different fire departments, and they all signed it.”

In Dorchester, Cassandre Raymond-Millien, a respiratory therapist from Brockton, had already made peace with the fact that something was ending. She’ll be among the last crop of medical staff in the Carney, caring for patients with breathing issues before they are transferred elsewhere.

”We hoped this wouldn’t happen. We thought somebody would do something,” Raymond-Millien said. “Nobody’s coming to save Carney.”

Everywhere, at both hospitals, nurses and other workers could be seen whispering goodbyes and hugging colleagues, teary-eyed.

Michelle Searles, a nurse in the Nashoba hospital lab, said she and her colleagues were at work Friday and had no plans to slow down.

“We’re all pretty sad,” Searles said, “but we’re still working all day at our jobs, supporting patients. Right till the end.”

Steward Health Care has reached agreements to transfer operations of the last two of its hospitals in Massachusetts that were up for sale, St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton and Good Samaritan Medical Center in Brockton, to Boston Medical Center, the company and Governor Maura Healey’s office confirmed late Friday.

The agreement includes an outright purchase of Good Samaritan by BMC. For St. Elizabeth’s, BMC will take over the operations, although for now, the underlying hospital property appears to remain under the control of the mortgage holder, New York investment firm Apollo Asset Management.

While the finalizing of those last two deals augurs the end of for-profit Steward’s time in Massachusetts, the battle over its hospitals is not over. Healey has proposed taking the St. Elizabeth’s property from Apollo by eminent domain, and in its statement Friday the state said it is proceeding on that course.

Apollo has already rejected the state’s offer of $4.5 million for the large campus and promised to “vigorously challenge” the proposed sale price.

A document in Steward’s federal bankruptcy case in Houston Friday did not make clear the ultimate purchase price of the hospitals, because of various contingencies. In its statement, the Healey administration did not disclose terms or how much the state would offer in financial aid to facilitate the transfer, as it has in the sale of four other Steward hospitals.

A Steward representative declined to share details of the deals.

These latest agreements come one day after Steward announced Thursday that it had reached final deals to sell four other hospitals to nonprofit systems: Lifespan Health System, based in Providence, will pay $175 million for St. Anne’s Hospital in Fall River and Morton Hospital in Taunton, while Lawrence General Hospital will pay $28 million for the Holy Family Hospitals in Methuen and Haverhill.

“We’ve said from the start that our focus was on protecting access to care, jobs and the stability of our health care system — and getting Steward out of Massachusetts,” Healey said in the statement. “With this third agreement signed, we are delivering on those promises. We’ll continue to press ahead with our plans to take St. Elizabeth’s by eminent domain to keep that hospital open.”

BMC chief executive Alastair Bell added in the statement that the agreements will allow his institution to continue to provide “vital health services for these communities,” and said next steps include “finalizing the transaction, integration planning and efforts to support the workforce and community.”

The latest agreements were announced just as Steward’s two other Massachusetts hospitals, Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer, were winding down operations in preparation for closing permanently on Saturday. Steward said it was forced to close the two because neither received qualified bids during the bankruptcy process.

Two weeks ago, Healey announced preliminary deals for all six hospitals, but BMC’s purchase of St. Elizabeth’s, in particular, appeared to be complicated by the plan to seize the hospital’s real estate by eminent domain for a price far lower than its assessed value.

Earlier Friday in US Bankruptcy Court in Houston, Ray Schrock, a Steward attorney from the New York law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges, seemed to indicate the operations of the hospitals, at least, will soon all be in new hands.

“I’m pleased to report that we did sign asset purchase agreements for the six Massachusetts hospitals. Those are scheduled to go forward,” he said. “It’s been a tremendous amount of work.”

The deals are subject to approval by federal bankruptcy Judge Christopher Lopez at a hearing in Houston next Wednesday.

Uncertainty over the fate of St. Elizabeth’s, the flagship Steward hospital in Massachusetts, had created anxiety and led to departures at the Brighton medical center. Department chiefs were told on Tuesday that the hospital had signed an asset purchase agreement with BMC, according to employee emails shared with the Globe.

But on Thursday, Steward said it was still working to finalize agreements with BMC to acquire St. Elizabeth’s and Good Samaritan.

In a city where socializing and pet care often vie for attention, Park-9 offers a solution. The company opened a venue in Everett last year that combines a dog park and a bar so people can have fun with their friends without having to worry about leaving their pet at home. Park-9 recently launched the Fenway pop-up which will be open through the end of October. The group plans to have the pop-up again next spring.

Park-9′s Everett location has both outdoor and indoor dog parks, a bar that offers beer, wine, cocktails, and a doggie day care. The Fenway venue is outdoors. Both spaces employ park rangers who separate dogs if they get too frisky.

Dog bars have been popping up all over the country from Missouri, Oklahoma, Maryland, Nebraska, Washington, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, Colorado, and Florida. Each location has a dog park, a bar, and sometimes even a full-service restaurant.

Park-9 was founded by Emily Gusse, a Harvard College alum, her wife Tess Kohanski, who received a master’s degree from Boston University, and her brother Chris Kohanski.

The company got its start because the three wanted to bring the dog park bar idea to New England for their dog, Nora.

Nora is a golden retriever who loves spending time outdoors but overheats easily, which causes her to seize. She doesn’t handle running around most dog parks well because of their hot pavement.

On a road trip to Minnesota with Nora, Gusse and Kohanski wanted to stop somewhere the dog could cool off. They spotted a dog park that seemed different then most.

It was a dog park bar that had dogs running around without a leash while owners were relaxing and socializing over a drink.

Gusse wondered why a similar dog park bar didn’t exist in New England. The idea to create Park-9 was born.

The Park-9 chain of dog bars is different from “dog-friendly” bars since pups are allowed to run about without a leash. Most bars and dog parks in Massachusetts require a dog to be on a leash, mainly for safety reasons. The park rules and regulations say leashes are allowed up to a length of 8 feet, permitting dogs to run while the owner retains control over their pet.

“There’s nowhere you can legally have a dog out without a leash on between the Commons and here,” said Alex Rossetti, 27, who works at Boston IT Services.

In Fenway, Rossetti said he gets ticketed if he lets his dog run around. Once, he got one for $125.

The exceptions for leashes are in the designated dog recreation spaces, such as Downer Avenue Playground, Garvey Playground, and Ronan Park in Dorchester; Peters Park in the South End; and DeFilippo Playground in the North End. Downtown, there’s the Friends of the Public Garden, which has a subgroup called Common Canine. The Common Canine, located at the Boston Commons, is an off-leash space, and it rotates to different sections of the park.

While the list of places to let your dog freely move without restriction is expanding, Park-9 is the only in the area to incorporate a treat for the humans as well as the pups.

“It’s really interesting and fun to grab a beer and watch a dog,” said McNulty.

It is also one of the only places that have resources to prevent dogs from overheating during extreme temperatures such as having a swimming pool, sun coverings, and air conditioning in the Everett location.

On that Friday evening, Jessica Amanambu’s dog, Roman, wagged his tail and ran across the park to play with the other dogs. Amanambu, 24, said she drives 20 minutes from Dorchester to bring her dog to Park-9 because she likes the bar’s environment.

Amanambu, a project manager and scientist at Vertex Pharmaceuticals, said her miniature dachshund, Roman, can jump around with the other dogs and play more freely because the park is fenced in.

“There’s no dog park like Park-9,” said Amanambu. “It’s not a real dog park because it’s closed off, staff helps, and there’s drinks to relax.”

Mat Giladi, 25, an incoming student at Stanford University’s business school, said Park-9′s rangers make the park safe so he doesn’t have to constantly be monitoring his dog. Giladi, who currently lives in the South End, said he can work on his laptop while his girlfriend talks to her mom on the phone.

He brings Basel, their 8-month--old Bernese mountain dog, to Park-9 because it’s a perfect place where dog owners get the responsibility of walking their dog out of the way while also making time to hang with friends.

“I don’t need to sacrifice one for the other,” said Giladi.

As the day fades and the owners begin to tire, the dogs are still buzzing with energy, sprinting from one end of Park-9 to the other.

Every day, police officers respond to reports of all sorts of events and nonevents, most of which never make the news. Here is a sampling of lesser-known — but no less noteworthy — incidents from police log books (a.k.a. blotters) in our communities.

On Aug. 16, a prowler was found lounging in the rafters of a bar at the Sunset Tiki Bar and Grill in Westford. This was not a two-legged prowler, but a four-legged, furry one. It was a Friday afternoon, and Animal Control Officer Kirsten Hirschler and Officer James Antonelli responded to the call reporting that an “angry raccoon” was refusing to leave the bar. The manager reported that a few employees had tried to scare the creature out and “this had caused the animal to become agitated,” Hirschler said. “At the time of the call, there were approximately 150 people at the establishment so the manager was rightfully a little nervous about the whole situation.” When Hirschler and Antonelli arrived, they were told that keg taps were open and beer had spilled everywhere. Several bottles were moved out of the way and Hirschler was able to climb up, secure the raccoon, and place him safely into a crate. “He definitely wasn’t happy about being moved from his little nook and was soaked in beer,” Hirschler said. “The raccoon was then released beyond a fence on the property where he quickly shot out of the crate into the woods. I think he learned his lesson and won’t be looking to tap the keg anytime soon.”

At 10:02 a.m. Aug. 12, Wakefield police checked out some suspicious activity on Audubon Road, where a woman with blonde hair was reportedly seen walking around with a pair of scissors and a samurai sword. Police discovered that the situation wasn’t as bizarre as it appeared, since the item the woman was carrying was just a “wooden walking stick that looked like a sword.”

At 4:50 p.m. Aug. 24, police were called to Burger King on Route 1 in Norwood after employees reported that an 18-wheeler truck went through the drive-through the wrong way. “After being confronted by employees, the operator became agitated,” the log entry stated. Police reported that the truck was sent on its way, and there was no damage caused to the restaurant.

At 11:50 a.m. Aug. 23, Duxbury police were notified of a missing child in the town forest off Mayflower Street. A command post was established and four officers began searching on foot, along with an officer riding an ATV. The Duxbury Fire Department was requested to come to the scene to help, and Kingston police notified dispatch that it also was available to assist. Soon after the search started, Officer Michelle McDonnell located the child a half mile into the woods. The child was then reunited with its family. “Great job by all Officers and assisting departments involved,” police wrote on Facebook.

A lot of anger has been directed at MBTA buses lately. One recent example occurred around 6 p.m. July 22, when an MBTA bus had to be taken off its route in the area of Washington Street and Forest Hills in Boston after a man kicked and broke one of the door windows. According to Transit Police, he was angry because the bus driver would not pick him up at a non-designated stop and decided to express his frustration by kicking the window, causing a spiderweb crack to form. There were slight delays as the bus was removed from service, police said, and the man fled the scene.

At 11:45 p.m. July 27, someone outside Nubian Station in Roxbury threw a metal object at an MBTA bus that shattered the back window. Service was delayed as the bus was taken out of service for repairs, police said, but no injuries were reported.

At around 10 p.m. Aug. 24, a similar scenario unfolded in Chelsea, when a juvenile male on Cabot Street punched a door window of a bus, causing it to break. Once again, service was delayed. Transit Police said they would be conducting a follow-up investigation.
