A former author of children’s books and teacher at schools in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, Mr. Feinstein, beginning in the 1970s, amassed millions through his subscription newsletters, including “Alan Shawn Feinstein’s International Insider’s Report.”

Mr. Feinstein’s wealth was also collected through sales of direct-mail collectibles featured in his publications – such as presidential autographs, coins, and stamps – with a money-back guarantee, as reported in a 2004 profile in The Providence Journal.

After he was made aware of food scarcity in Providence in the early 1980s, Mr. Feinstein began donating money to food pantries and other public service programs, and by 1986, his $1 million gift launched the World Hunger Program at Brown University to help combat the issue on a global scale, backed by a matching $1.5 million from the Ivy League institution.

“So many people go to bed hungry in this country, about 10 percent if not more, and that’s a disgrace for the richest country in the world,” Mr. Feinstein told the Globe in March 1998. “There is no shame in hunger; there is shame in knowing about hunger and doing nothing about it.”

The Feinstein Foundation launched in 1991, working under the mission to inspire children to “do good deeds and be kind whenever possible.”

More than 600,000 kids have since participated in the Feinstein Leadership school program, earning the title of “Feinstein Jr. Scholars” – a designation that gives them complimentary access to attractions throughout southern New England – as they pledge to “do good deeds to make our world a better place,” the foundation’s website states.

Tax filings for 2023 valued the foundation at just shy of $30 million and indicated the organization served 265 schools that year.

In her statement, Leila Feinstein recalled how important the Jr. Scholars were to her father.

“Knowing that Feinstein Jr. Scholars were doing good deeds every day brought my dad tremendous joy and comfort,” she said. “It gave him peace in his final moments knowing our work will continue even though he is no longer with us.”

Born in Dorchester, Mass. on June 25, 1931, Mr. Feinstein was a graduate of Boston University and Boston Teachers’ College, and once taught at schools in Mansfield and Newton, Mass. as well as in Bristol, R.I., according to his death notice. He was married to Dr. Pratarnporn “Pat” (Chiemwichit) Feinstein for 61 years. The couple had three children and five grandchildren.

A funeral service for friends and family will be held on Sept. 21 in Providence and also streamed online, followed by a private burial, the obituary said.

In a post on X, formerly known as Twitter, Governor Dan McKee described Mr. Feinstein as not only a philanthropist, but as“a change agent who invested in the lives and futures of Rhode Island’s children.”

“We will always remember him, not just for his impact on education but for his kind and full heart,” McKee said.

US Senator Jack Reed said Mr. Feinstein’s “memory will live on through the countless lives he touched and improved,” pointing to not only the foundation’s work but also his efforts “to feed millions around the world through initiatives with leading universities across our region.”

“Above all, Alan urged us all to be kind and compassionate toward one another,” the senator said in a statement. “He knew that good deeds reverberate throughout our neighborhoods and that every one of us can make a difference.”

Speaking to the Globe in 1992, a year after his foundation launched, Mr. Feinstein reflected on the difference he himself hoped to make someday.

“Hopefully when I go,” he said, “there will be a few less hungry people in the world and a few more compassionate ones.”

Now a criminologist, Joyce has produced a groundbreaking study of Boston’s street gangs and gang culture, “It Started With the Hats: The Life Experiences of Boston’s Founding Street Gang Members,” the heart of which are his in-depth interviews with 30 original gangbangers: one-on-one.

“The book’s credibility is that it’s based on their words, the men who lived it,” Joyce says of the “OGs” who participated — some of whom he arrested decades ago. They came from a cross section of gangs that mostly take the name of their street or housing project, like Castlegate, the Corbet Crew, the Humboldt Boys, or the Franklin Hill Crew.

The interviews confirmed a suspicion Joyce had way back at the start of his policing career: that outrunning and arresting gang members wasn’t enough to combat gang violence. “Even when the violence was out of control, we’d talk in the unit about how these kids, many were talented. Real smart. Or athletic. And we’d wonder about their potential if different pathways were offered. The pull of the street was just so strong.”

His book, which will appeal to policy makers, youth workers, and public safety officials confronting gun violence, also offers the first deeply reported origin story of the Boston street gangs that terrorized neighborhoods and killed at a record-setting pace. The broad outlines of that history are known — how crack cocaine first arrived in the mid-1980s via gangs encroaching from Detroit and New York City, setting the stage for homegrown armed gangs to pursue for themselves the profits from trafficking in cocaine. The Corbet Crew, the city’s first and most powerful gang, was dominant until its charismatic kingpin, Tony Johnson, a star athlete who’d gone to college, was gunned down in June 1988 next to his Dorchester home. Mayhem followed as street gangs scrambled to solidify and prevail.

“By the fall of 1989, Boston was in the midst of its most violent time,” Joyce writes. “Gang violence was a driving force behind over 100 people being shot or killed in a forty-day period” in an area covering only about 1.7 square miles. The next year Boston experienced a record number of homicides — 152.

Joyce expands on this history with both new information and the personal and at times heart-wrenching perspectives of former gang members who were at war. “Nobody seen that coming,” an ex-Corbet Crew member told Joyce about the killing of Tony Johnson, the gang leader who’d seemed invincible. “Then things turned up heavy,” he said. “People wanted revenge.” Said another Corbet Crew member about Johnson’s death: “Turned the city upside down. He kept the peace in a lot of neighborhoods. Once he passed away, all bets were off.” Joyce writes that the impact of Johnson’s death “cannot be overstated.”

Joyce, who joined the police force in 1983 and retired in 2014 as a superintendent, was part of Boston’s first tactical response to the emerging gang crisis, the Citywide Anti-Crime Unit, formed in 1988. He then played a key role implementing Operation Ceasefire, the innovative and nationally acclaimed partnership of Boston police, religious and community leaders, and Harvard criminologists that achieved a dramatic drop in homicides in the 1990s. Not your typical cop, Joyce has moved from the street to the classroom, earning first a master’s degree at Boston University and then, in 2017, a PhD in criminology and justice policy at Northeastern University. He now chairs the criminal justice and criminology department at Salve Regina University.

In his studies, Joyce knew he wanted to dig deeper into gang culture. He found plenty of research on the front end — when teens joined a gang. But he saw little that had been done examining a gang member’s later life, whether he “desisted” or “persisted.” “The final phase of gang membership — the long-term changes that occur over time when gang membership comes to an end — has been understudied,” he writes. To help recruit participants for his interviews, he reached out to two former youth workers and a Boston police detective who knew many ex-gangbangers. He nicknamed them his Boston Street Gang Advisory Group, and together they enlisted 30 Black and Latino men between the ages of 35 and 54. Joyce spent three years conducting interviews, one-on-one, at locations of their choosing — their workplace, a community center in Roxbury, an office at Northeastern, or a restaurant. He promised to use pseudonyms to protect their privacy and, possibly, to prevent retaliation.

He knew they’d be doing something that went against their street code — talking to cops about the gang. “Getting the subjects to open up and share with me their life experiences was difficult due to my past profession as a police officer,” he writes. But in time he won their trust; some he interviewed helped him recruit new subjects. Joyce compiled more than 1,300 pages of transcripts.

Joyce painstakingly asked his subjects to recall the emergence of street gang culture in Boston and the role they played. Their responses are raw, blunt, and often emotional. “They did not hold back,” Joyce says.

There’s Reggie, who joined a Jamaica Plain street gang at age 14 and told Joyce about the impact of crack. “It made everybody instantly rich,” he said. His family was broke, and suddenly he had $465 after selling “a package.” “It was like so much money.” He could now buy pizza, or whatever. “Like for us, that was a big thing, eating. It was like we’re able to eat.”

Reggie became an enforcer, and guns were easy to obtain. “I came across MAC-10s, TEC-9s, shotguns, .38 revolvers, all different kinds of guns.”

Then there’s Edward, an enforcer for a gang in Dorchester, who “changed best friends three times because they kept getting killed.” He told Joyce about an emotional deadness that set in from killing and seeing others killed. “I’m numb to murder,” he said. “When people used to get murdered, I’d be like, ‘Damn, that’s [expletive] up,’” then switch topics in an instant: “‘Who do you think the Celtics are going to draft this year?’”

From those who have “desisted,” Joyce learned that willpower alone, while essential, was not enough. The gang was family, the camaraderie and friendships deeply embedded. Leaving that life, he found, required “human agency” in combination with some other turning point, something that helped them resist the pull to return to the gang and the quick money from selling drugs. For one ex-gangbanger, that meant leaving Boston for a stretch. For others, it was parenthood, education, religion, a mentor, or work.

Tony, who bore scars from being shot and stabbed 17 times in 12 years, told Joyce: “Being in the gang, selling drugs, doing shootings, getting shot. Other kids went to school, graduated from college; I went to jail. I had choices, and I made the bad choice.” After prison, Tony was determined to move on. For him the key was steady work, despite “temptations all the time to get back in the streets.” He learned to cook. “I’m a chef,” he told Joyce. “I love to cook, and I like working with people.” It’s not been easy, though. Tony ran afoul of the law several times, but he had been crime-free for six years when Joyce interviewed him.

Joyce hopes the “set of rich and thick narratives” will prove useful to officials here and elsewhere in devising comprehensive approaches to teen and gun violence, a responsibility he says must involve “multiagency partnerships and a balance of public safety and public health services.” In Boston, he noted, Police Commissioner Michael Cox, whom he’s known for years, was a young cop during the city’s worst years of gang violence. Cox, he says, “gets it; he knows it.”

For the book’s jacket, Joyce turned to a Boston graffiti artist, or “tagger,“ named Alvin “Acoma” Colon, who was barely a teenager in the early 1990s when he “was tagging everything but a canvas.” Colon and his tagger friends, guided by a teacher at the Martin Luther King Middle School, were eventually steered to practice their art on approved walls; they became known as the “Young Graffiti Masters.” Colon, now an airbrush artist and sculptor, told me he worked out the cover design on a blank wall in Norwood, using the tone and spray-paint style of ’80s graffiti to portray Boston’s street gang lifestyle. His colorful mural depicts a housing project, a cemetery, bejeweled gangbangers, and the fists of one gangbanger breaking free of the bonds of handcuffs.

To help Colon get a feel for the book, Joyce gave the artist the manuscript. “Oh, man,” Colon said, exhaling deeply, recalling his reaction to reading oral histories about a violent time when he was just a Roxbury kid trying to survive. “Tears came down my eyes.”

Why? Because Boston’s school desegregation and busing crisis was the single most important event in Boston in the past 75 years. Aspects of the desegregation orders of Judge W. Arthur Garrity Jr. from the 1970s are still present and the legacy of desegregation and busing is still with us as our schools face today’s challenges.

This includes the student assignment plans where parents apply for three choices out of 10 to 12 schools for their child, who isn’t likely to attend their nearest neighborhood school. And the goal of hiring 25 percent Black and 10 percent Latino and Asian teachers and administrators has still not been met.

As a community organizer back then in Dorchester, Boston’s largest neighborhood, I got to see the racial tensions up close. For a year or more after busing began, the only place in all of Dorchester that both our white and Black students felt safe going to a meeting at night was at the then-Grover Cleveland School in Fields Corner. Buses carrying Black schoolchildren were frequently showered with rocks. Racial epithets were yelled by adults and teens. Fights were started again and again at certain high schools.

A Haitian man was attacked by a mob in South Boston and saved by an off-duty police officer who fired his gun into the air. A white truck driver was pulled out of his truck in the South End and beaten and died days later. Black community leader Ted Landsmark was attacked by protesters who were outside City Hall demonstrating against busing. One wielded an American flag on a flagstaff at him like it was a spear.

Listening to white community members of Dorchester back then, I heard their anger over their court-ordered inability to send their kids to their neighborhood schools. Attending neighborhood schools existed in most school districts everywhere. I later learned that the Boston School Committee had a great deal to do with creating the need for desegregation by intentionally drawing the districts, especially for middle and high schools, to make them racially segregated.

The Black community had been advocating for decades for better schools, asking for improving the schools in their neighborhoods or transporting students to better-resourced white schools. But the all-white Boston School Committee rejected all their proposals. So in 1972 the Boston NAACP filed a case in federal court and won a desegregation order in the decision by Garrity in Tallulah Morgan vs. James W. Hennigan on June 21, 1974. And the Latino and Asian communities also organized to get their educational issues considered with some success.

It was true and should be acknowledged that most schools remained opened and stayed peaceful once desegregation with busing began. Garrity did not just order busing but made education reforms in ordering hiring of more Black teachers and principals, setting up integrated parent councils in every school, and beginning bilingual and special education programs.

We learned some lessons. In 1977, anti-busing politicians Louise Day Hicks, John Kerrigan, and Pixie Palladino were defeated. John O’Bryant was elected that same year as the first Black member of the School Committee. And the 1983 mayoral race between Mel King and Ray Flynn was another turning point toward starting to heal the racial divisions in our city.

Both King and Flynn campaigned on the need to heal racial divisions. When Flynn became mayor he carried this out by creating a special police unit on racial attacks, desegregating Boston’s public housing developments, strengthening the resident jobs policy on hiring people of color on construction jobs, and creating laws for equity in renting. In 1987, public housing developments were integrated so that people of color started to move to South Boston, Charlestown, East Boston, Roslindale, and Hyde Park.

Living and working in Dorchester in the 1970s, I learned a great deal about how racism limited opportunities for people of color, the many ways in which Black people experienced disrespect and even hatred in their daily lives, and how class limited opportunities for both white people and people of color. They sometimes even blamed themselves for their troubles rather than an unfair system.

Fifty years on, what do we want for Boston Public Schools? It’s complicated. There is declining enrollment as high housing costs push people out of the city and parents choose charter, parochial, private schools, and METCO because they don’t have confidence in BPS. There are thousands of kids coming to school who are homeless and a large percentage of students are immigrants and/or have learning disabilities.

We can’t stay with the status quo. The state almost put Boston schools into receivership in 2022 and BPS has not completed the long list of turnaround goals.

Superintendent Mary Skipper, Mayor Michelle Wu, and the School Committee need to work with parents, students, and their organizations in reforming the school system, including doubling down on the hiring of more teachers and administrators of color, finalizing a facilities plan that is implemented with a racial equity tool, and building more student-focused, long-term partnerships with Boston’s many businesses and health care, higher education, and cultural institutions.

With US civil rights history as part of the curriculum, schools should make sure Boston’s own history is included and cover the actions of community leaders like Ruth Batson and Ellen Jackson and student activism like the Freedom School Stay Outs, as well as the more widely known violent responses in some communities. To benefit students with special needs and English Language Learners, BPS needs to increase inclusion of special education students into regular education classes and must protect and maintain specialized classes for English Language Learners.

On this momentous anniversary, we can reflect on the hard-won lessons learned from integrating Boston schools and make our schools ones that educate and launch our students to have successful careers and be good citizens. It’s up to all of us to step up.

When contacted, the realtor said she had changed the wording.

While the description was ultimately edited, its presence signified a particular lack of candor or misinformation that can rear its ugly head in real estate listings. Occasionally, this can land agents in court. In the 2006 lawsuit Seit-Olsen v. Reliance Appraisals, LLC, a Michigan buyer sued a realtor over the square footage represented in the listing, among other complaints. The plaintiff argued that the home was 938 square feet because the basement couldn’t be counted. The realtor ultimately prevailed, but Reddit is rife with complaints about alleged inaccuracies in listing descriptions.

In the Massachusetts case Schoembs v. Schena, Robert and Kimberly Schoembs sued sellers Robert and Christine Schena, the real estate brokers, and the home inspector in July 2007, alleging that the house they bought in Medford had “significant structural issues” and was smaller than the square footage the listing cited, according to research by attorney Mark S. Einhorn of Marcus Errico Emmer & Brooks. The court sided with the defendants, ruling that the statute of limitations period had lapsed, and noted that the appraisal had the correct square footage, that the buyers should have noticed the square footage discrepancy during the walk-through, and that they purchased the property “as is.”

But for prospective buyers attempting to navigate a chaotic market amid a housing shortage, surfing through online listings can mean inaccuracies ranging from doctored photographs to address fibs.

Many realtors say inaccuracies in listing descriptions can simply be the results of typos, auto-population, or lack of experience. Other times, listings include subtle acronyms to take the responsibility off the seller’s agent like “BATVAI,” which stands for “buyer’s agents to verify all information.”

In the Boston area, Jason Niles, a realtor with Coldwell Banker Realty-Cambridge, notices a lot of inaccuracies regarding a property’s ZIP code or neighborhood.

“Sometimes people will have a place in Roxbury, and they want to make it be Jamaica Plain,” Niles said. “You’ll have Jamaica Plain 02131. No, that’s Roslindale.”

Kate Ziegler, a realtor with Arborview Realty in Boston, said many of the inconsistencies she sees in listing descriptions are associated with a home’s systems. She once took clients on a showing to a property listed as having a new heating system. But upon examination, Ziegler realized that while the water heater was new, the boiler was “fully depreciated.” Her clients’ interest in the property soon disappeared.

Listing photographs often can be the source of inaccuracies. While virtual staging can transform a space, agents are supposed to disclose that they used the technique, whether it appears in the text in the listing or on the photo itself. Sometimes agents will follow the staged photo with a picture that shows the space empty. And while drones provide great photography, the click of a button to zoom out can make a property appear much closer to the ocean than it is.

“In real estate, that’s called puffing,” said Ryan DeLisle, a realtor with Coldwell Banker Realty in Marblehead.

Some realtors argue that saying that a home is within “walking distance” to an attraction violates US Department of Housing and Urban Development fair housing laws. Einhorn said the wording does not break the law, but advises realtors to use more mindful language, such as “convenient access to,” “less than 100 yards from,” and “two blocks away.” “This approach ensures that the language is inclusive and considerate of all potential buyers and tenants,” he told the Globe.

Michael McDonagh, general counsel for the realty firm Lamacchia Cos., said agents should also avoid saying whether an area is “safe.” McDonagh said the word is subjective and “even the safest neighborhoods have crime.” He also advises Lamacchia Realty agents to avoid mentioning the quality of the schools, because it may imply that the seller is looking for a particular type of buyer: a family.

Back in June, Laura Alix went to visit a two-bed, 1.5-bath condo in Somerville listed for nearly $600,000. While she thought the space looked a bit dirty in the listing photos, she realized the level of filth only when she arrived in person. Plus, the description didn’t mention the stench (“it just smelled so basement-y,” said Alix, a business writer) and the “ominous” stains.

At a time when prospective buyers feel burned out by their home search, discovering that a description is misleading can be particularly disheartening.

“There’s not a lot on the market anyway, and usually you’re trying to compete with people. It’s a whole other job to go look at places and try to put in an offer. It’s an emotional suck,” said Sarah Rodewald, broker and owner of SR Realty in Boston, who noted that it’s important to remain ethical while still serving her client. “It just doesn’t feel good.”

According to a representative for the Better Business Bureau of Eastern Massachusetts, Maine, Rhode Island, and Vermont, no listing inconsistency trends have been reported to the New England bureau’s ScamTracker. The bureau encourages people to research their agent and use realtors who are BBB accredited.

To combat misleading listings, Ziegler tells her buyer clients early on to send her every listing they look at, even if they’re not serious about it yet. While prospective buyers may be bright-eyed and excited at the start of a home-buying journey, repeatedly showing up to properties that look great online and terrible in person can lead to significant frustration.

“Thirty years ago, you wouldn’t have seen a space online before deciding to go see it,” Ziegler said. “I can take a look and tell you what I see because I notice things that you don’t.”

Steph Lewis got the kind of call that few tenants want to get, two days before Christmas: The landlord was putting the home of the nonprofit that Lewis leads, The BASE, up for sale, almost immediately.

Rather than looking for a new place, Lewis and his team decided they would figure out a way to buy their existing home. The BASE uses sports — baseball, softball, and basketball — to help build kids’ teamwork skills and self-esteem, and couples athletics with mentorship and preparation for college and careers. The location at 150 Shirley St. in the Newmarket Square area is ideal for The BASE because it’s next to the ballfields and basketball court at Clifford Park, and it’s in Roxbury, where many of the kids live.

Lewis wasn’t about to let that slip away. And with some aggressive fundraising that brought in $2.5 million, including $1.5 million from the Yawkey Foundation, The BASE was able to complete the deal in August.

The nonprofit bought its 9,600-square-foot industrial building and a small lot next door, for $3.5 million from Kensington Investment Co. As a result of the Yawkey grant, the BASE facility will be renamed the Yawkey Urban Sports Complex: Home of The Base. Many individuals donated, too, along with The Boston Foundation and Eastern Bank, and Eastern helped with a loan.

“We had a will to make sure this thing happened, and it did,” Lewis said.

The BASE and its 23 full- and part-time staffers serve more than 800 Boston children and teens every year, at no charge to them. Lewis said owning the building will not only stabilize the nonprofit’s future, it will also position the BASE for future expansion. Lewis’s father — Robert Lewis Jr., now the CEO of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Boston — started the nonprofit in 2013 in Egleston Square and relocated to Newmarket Square in 2019.

Now, Lewis hopes to take the money that the BASE used to spend on rent, and spend it on programs instead.

“There aren’t many Black- and brown-run nonprofits that own property [in Boston],” Lewis said. “We could be one of the few in this city. This is a big statement of our commitment to our young folks and to this community. ... We are truly saying to the Roxbury community that we are here to stay.”

“Ricky needs new glasses. . . . He can’t touch the ball!”

“Yeah . . . well . . . you going to need glasses when I slam the ball and hit your big head, Tony!”

“You crazy . . . thinking you can hit like Fred Lynn!”

We’d banter and play until we stopped the game to organize our coins for Popsicles and sodas and honey buns. Sitting together on park benches, we’d review the day’s games. In baseball, kids like me from Villa Victoria, the mixed-income housing development in the South End, shined like the stars of the ‘75 Sox.

Those of us who met for these daily pick-up games didn’t share family history, racial identity, or faraway motherlands. Our bond was the experience of coping with changes in our public schools in 1970s Boston, each of us absorbing the heat that simmered in the city.

Growing up, you knew to walk the streets with a conscious acceptance of your inherited place in the city. Proud Southie Irish. Black child from the ‘Bury. Eastie strong. Townie to the end. Puerto Rican kid con fuerza in the Villa.

We found common ground in the city playgrounds and ballparks where we banded together for games of baseball, or basketball, or tag football. The environment we created was wholly different from what played out in the halls of government.

We were a collective of around-the-way kids playing in the shadows of the downtown buildings, blocks away from City Hall and the State House. There, local politicians were wrangling over the 1974 federally-mandated school desegregation court order. Meanwhile, city kids like us were traveling the public school bus circuit.

My family had left New York City in 1973 for Boston, a city long set in its tribal parochialism. We moved into student housing at Boston University, where my father was completing his doctorate, and my mom was preparing for her career as a Boston public elementary school teacher. In 1976, we moved into the recently-developed Villa Victoria.

My childhood identity as a Puerto Rican kid in Boston was shaped in the public schools, but even more so on those neighborhood playgrounds where everyone knew my name. Most weekend mornings, the Villa would come alive early with an army of us on our stoops calling out for whoever would become our squad of the day.

“Hey, Eldin, we playing football at Peters Park with the kids from Cathedral, and los blancos from Eastie!”

We all looked the same once we hit the field, both sides draped in Patriots jerseys. We didn’t play one neighborhood against the other. Most days we mixed it up, maybe three Puerto Rican and two Black kids, with one Italian, on a team.

“That kid, Stevie, sucks at throwing, like Jimmy Plunkett!”

“Just throw it, man! Jamal will catch it!”

The playground was the equalizer.

Hungry mid-game, we’d break and together make a run to the nearby bodega that sold lunch specials of pollo with arroz con gandules (pigeon peas). And we’d stain our faces with cherry-flavored Limber icees.

We had no phones to stare at, much less to receive calls from home, so day games suddenly turned to night games. And as soon as our stomachs began to growl, we’d bike back to our families before supper was gone. Sometimes a teammate would follow me home to sample a plate of Mama’s Spanish food. Mama would often ask herself — aloud — “¡¿Y quién es este niño?!” And who is this boy?

“He’s from Eastie, Mom. Can he eat with us?” I’d ask.

“OK, he’s here, he must be hungry.”

A meal at a friend’s house was just as foreign to me, a window into a world of new foods, home decor, and aromas. At a buddy’s home in Charlestown I tasted cabbage for the first time and learned not every family keeps Salsa Picante hot sauce on hand.

Supper at a friend’s became the simplest space for sanctuary. Because any differences between the adults — school choices or busing routes or, in any real way, racial or ethnic — were outweighed by what we kids shared.

Eldin Lynn Villafañe is a writer and communications strategist in Boston. Send comments to magazine@globe.com.

Below is a collection of responses we received:

“I started high school in 1974. My parents got caught up in the scare tactics used by Louise Day Hicks and the others. My father was a Boston police officer. All city employees were told they would be fired if they moved out of the city. My parents moved us to parochial school in 1972 because they knew it would be crazy trying to get in if busing was forced on the city. We had six kids. Catholic school nearly bankrupted my parents.” -Robert Darling, Plymouth, Mass.

“I went to the elementary school in Charlestown...not as a student but as one of the five Black teachers sent there to desegregate the staff. I was the only Black teacher in a school of all White teachers who refused to speak to me all year. On the way to school I was harassed and called names. That was 1974, before Black students were bused to Charlestown. The second year when busing did start, I experienced rocks and snowballs thrown at my car every day upon leaving. It was a tense, unsafe, unfriendly atmosphere with little support for Black staff. Fortunately this was the beginning of my teaching career so I ignored the outside and totally focused on my students that I felt were all wonderful even if one of their siblings was the one throwing the rocks each day! Hindsight is 20/20. Sitting in an integrated setting did not further the education of Black students. We neglected to see that the White students weren’t being educated either...” -Patricia Kelly, Boston, Mass.

“I was a senior at South Boston High School that year. So many terrible memories. I don’t think people realized how dangerous and unsafe it was for all students. I look back and realize my class were the lucky ones. We only had to live this nightmare for one year and we graduated.” -Nancy Costigliola, South Boston, Mass.

“I was a Boston Latin student in the mid 70s and there were several student walkouts leading up to the start of busing where the predominantly Black students of Boston English would come to BLS and demand we join them to protest racist School Committee policies. That radicalized me to be anthracite before the racist riots started and I remained a lifetime activist ever since.” -Greg Perkins, Long Beach, Calif.

“I was bused in 1974 for first grade from Jamaica Plain to the William Monroe Trotter in Roxbury. I had a great experience at the Trotter for five years and made many Black friends that I would’ve never been friends with due to segregation. I credit this experience and my progressive parents as the reasons I’ve been a public defender in Boston and Brockton for the past 25 years!” -James Greenberg, Jamaica Plain, Mass.

“I was a White second-grader living in Dorchester when busing started. I got bused to the Dennis C. Haley School in Roslindale. I loved it. Ms. Krumpleman and Ms. Wise were the best grade school teachers I ever had, and the school was innovative and clean. Brother Blue came to tell us stories, and a Japanese dance troupe entranced us with a folk story about a fisherman who rescued a turtle. We went to the Children’s Museum and the Science Museum. My best friend, Sarah Baston, was mixed race, smart, and very funny. I remember people throwing rocks at the bus, which seemed weird, but most of the things adults did seemed weird. My mom, who had just had a baby with her second husband, told me that we were going to leave because ‘Boston was no place to raise a child.’ I didn’t understand that, because I was already being raised in Boston, and it was fantastic. We moved to Maine as part of White Flight. Ironically, many of the kids I knew in Maine died tragic deaths — Tim fell out of a pickup truck, Jamie was washed off a breakwater, Fred died diving into a quarry. My Maine school taught at a level about two years behind what I was used to in Boston, leaving me bored and not sure how to fit in. I never got used to Maine, and I moved back to greater Boston as soon as I could. If the decision had been up to me — which it surely wasn’t — we never would have left.” -Amanda Mathiesen, Arlington, Mass.

“It’s how I ended up in Catholic school. Public school was uphill one way, Catholic school was uphill the other. When the school up one hill was no longer a guaranteed assignment, I went up the other hill. I was only 7. I have older friends who dropped out of school or were terrified of school.” -Marla Smith, Boston, Mass.

“I didn’t experience the chaos of the 1974 busing decision. My parents did. My dad lived in Roxbury and was assigned to South Boston High School. I can remember him recounting stories of having to fight White kids inside Southie High. For years later, my father refused to step foot in South Boston. I was told repeatedly as a teenager to never enter to that neighborhood because the Irish were violent. Andrew Square was the only place in South Boston I ever entered. I’m 40 and I can clearly remember my grandmother telling me that as a teenager. My mother was an immigrant from Trinidad and Tobago. She grew up with British colonialism. Trinidad and Tobago is majority African and Indian. Whites in Trinidad and Tobago were few. Coming to America was a shock as a 13-year-old teenager. And then to be placed on a bus and sent to Brighton High with other West Indian teenagers and to be pelted with rocks by local Whites was traumatic for her and my aunt.

My parents never really forgot their experiences. My father eventually transferred to Madison Park. My mother transferred to Boston English and graduated from there. Their stories of battling the Irish and Italians for a semi-decent education stuck with them. They passed those traumatic stories down to me and have probably affected me slightly in how apprehensive I act when dealing with White folks in Massachusetts. Why? I can’t be certain. My parents are in their 60s now and have mellowed out tremendously since 1974. Honestly, I don’t think they ever fully forgave the Irish and Italians for their treatment as teenagers during the busing crisis of the 70s. I am glad that trauma didn’t get passed on to my kids the same way it was passed on to me in the 80s and 90s.” -Eric Depradine, Norwich, Conn.

“Busing was the worst experience any middle and high school child could experience. Because I was Black but lived in an all-White area of Boston, I wasn’t bused. The result was I was hated all day at school and found no respite at home in my neighborhood because I was treated as the problem. My experience was that of complete, total, psychological, emotional, physical rejection and isolation. There are still the reverberations of this experience with me today.” -Janine McLaren, Boston, Mass.

“I did classroom observation in Brighton High School in the late 1990s while working on my M.Ed. (I completed my degree, taught high school briefly, then ended up on the faculty at Berklee College of Music.) I also did classroom observation at Boston Latin, and my student teaching at Brookline High School. My experience at Brighton High School was really sad.

Every class there were multiple students asleep. How could I blame them? They had to get up at 5:00 am to make the bus, and there’s no way these teenagers were asleep at 9:00 pm! Many times I would encounter students who were really struggling with math. I’d suggest they take advantage of the free tutoring offered after school, and nearly every time the reply was ‘If I do that then I’ll miss the bus, and if I miss the bus it’ll take me two hours to get home on public transportation.’ So not only were students not getting the help they needed, but organized after school activities in general were a pale shadow of what I saw at other schools.

Before observing in a school, I assumed that busing was a wildly expensive way to achieve integration, but otherwise fairly benign. It was only being there that I saw its real destructiveness. Whatever noble goals there might have been, I was watching children’s education being shortchanged by the system.” -Kevin Block-Schwenk, Brighton, Mass.

“I entered my senior year at Hyde Park High School in the fall of 1974. The first year of forced busing in the city of Boston. I remember how fearful my friends and I were that summer wondering if we would be bused somewhere else in the city. Most of us were not but Black students from other parts of the city were bused to Hyde Park. There was violence and riots daily. More police presence than I’d ever seen in and outside of the school. I was one of the few females that continued to show up daily. Most were too fearful but I was quiet and minded my business and was never bothered by anyone, White or Black. I often sat in classrooms that were mostly empty that year which was my final year. I witnessed a White teacher being chased in the hallway by a group of Black students. I witnessed White parents yelling racial slurs at the busing coming and going. A lot of rock throwing from both sides. A stabbing. Entered the school through metal detectors. I was 17 in 1974. Now I’m 67 years old and the memory of it all is still distressing. It was an experiment gone wrong at our expense. It changed the city neighborhoods forever and not in the best ways.” -Lorraine Quinn, Walpole, Mass.

“I was a student in the fifth grade at Elihu Greenwood School, attending since kindergarten. They had a gifted student program that I tested into, which was for the fifth and sixth grade. After receiving notice that summer, I boarded a bus in the fall to the Frank V. Thompson Middle School in Dorchester. Our bus was routinely hit with rocks as we rode along Blue Hill Avenue. There was virtually no learning happening that first year of busing. The principal told us students who were bused in to lock ourselves in a classroom in the event of violence. I was scared, lost my sense of community, and to this day cannot understand how putting children on buses away from their communities and friends would improve schools. My new school didn’t get the resources it needed to improve educational outcomes. Getting home safely each day was the priority for all involved. The money spent on that failed integration experiment would be better spent improving all schools, so that students in every area of the city could have quality schools in their neighborhood. Judge Garrity failed the children of Boston.” -Joyce Fagerberg, Plymouth, Mass.

On the 50th anniversary of the federal court decision to integrate Boston schools, a group of 20 people stood on the red brick walkway in front of the Massachusetts State House at one of the first stops of a walking tour of key events in the city’s history of desegregation and busing.

The group of people, some in suits and some in jeans, stood under the beating morning sun, intently listening to advocates give personal testimonies of the brutalities they witnessed and their fight to defend students’ right to equality.

The tour was organized by the Boston Desegregation and Busing Initiative, a committee seeking to teach the public and students about the history of desegregation in Boston through forums, exhibits, partnerships, research, and interviews. Thursday’s event was a preview for community leaders and the media of a public tour the committee is hosting on Sept. 14.

In addition to visiting meaningful historical landmarks, the tour incorporates important voices and photos from the movement.

Lyda Peters, a longtime desegregation and education equity advocate, encouraged her audience to “take on the mantle” of fighting towards equality and justice.

“Move forward and learn from what we did,” Peters said.

The first day of busing in Boston was on Sept. 12, 1974, after a federal judge ordered Boston to integrate its public school system. Black families hoped the decision would lead to better educational opportunities and fairer outcomes for their children, but it sparked outrage. Protestors launched rocks at a bus carrying Black students to South Boston High School and spewed slurs at them.

The first leg of the tour ended at the courthouse where Judge Arthur Garrity ruled in 1974 that Boston’s schools were segregated by the Boston School Committee. Busing would begin that September.

A yellow school bus rolled up to the courthouse to take the tour group to South Boston High School. Tour organizers handed each person a golf ball once they were seated on the bus to symbolize the violence targeted at innocent kids.

The tour group was led to the school’s auditorium to listen to community leaders talk about their advocacy efforts. The speakers’ voices echoed and bounced off the walls.

During busing, Ira Jackson, chief of staff to former mayor Kevin White, said the school resembled a prison.

He said police officers and state troopers were stationed inside the corridors of the school after the first day of busing to ensure Black kids were safe.

Jackson described horrific events he witnessed during the period, such as mothers throwing bananas at Black children and yelling slurs. Someone from an angry mob spat on a Black patrol officer’s shield, a friend of his.

The Sept. 14 tour will also cover events like Freedom Stay Out Day in 1963. Gloria Bourne Lee, one of the tour’s speakers, participated in the event as a young teen. A youth leader at a Cambridge church she belonged to said people would be going to support Boston students.

She doesn’t remember much of the actual event, but what sticks with her are the emotions that rushed through her that day.

“I remember feeling, ‘Oh, I’m doing a good thing. We’re doing a good thing,” Bourne Lee said in a phone interview. “We’re making progress. We’re going to help these students.”

Bourne Lee went on to become a teacher, and her first job was at the New School for Children in Roxbury, one of the alternative schools opened for Black students failed by BPS.

“I’m happy and proud that I was part of all that,” Bourne Lee said.

Fifty years ago, busing changed my life. I was raised in East Boston, and mine was the first Black family to move into the Maverick Projects. I was an athlete, a good student, and had a close-knit group of Black and white friends. East Boston was my home. I bled blue and gold, East Boston High School colors. Eastie forever.

Then, at 16, one of my friends firebombed my family’s home. We were forced to move out of the neighborhood I loved. The busing and desegregation era had unleashed a wave of racism in Boston that I had never experienced. Overnight, our city became a symbol of division, and the stain of that reputation continues to haunt us.

The day our house was firebombed, I made a decision that shaped the rest of my life: I would dedicate myself to bringing people together. That traumatic moment ignited a passion for issues of race, class, and equity. It set me on a path of activism and youth development, which has been the cornerstone of my life and career, now working closely with nearly 40,000 youth and their families each year at the Boys & Girls Club of Boston.

If it wasn’t for that experience, I would not be who I am today. But my focus has always been on the future — on what society at large can build together, rather than the divisions of the past.

Today, the city of Boston spends close to $160 million on transportation for students and is one of the most diverse school districts in the United States. And while some progress has been made, Boston youth are still facing a number of challenges.

Approximately, less than 20 percent of third-grade Black and Latino students in Boston are performing at grade level in English or math. Black and Latino boys, in particular, face significant disparities across every social determinant of health. More alarming is the 23-year life expectancy gap between Roxbury and the Back Bay — neighborhoods just 2 miles apart. And the current national teacher and health care provider gap will only put more youth at risk.

How can we call Boston a world-class city, renowned for its higher education, cutting-edge hospitals, and booming innovation economy, yet continue to fail our young people? This is not just a matter of race or class; it’s about moral failure. It’s unacceptable.

The real opportunity before the city is how we can shift our thinking, disrupt entrenched systems, and build a future where we are not repeating the same failures 50 years from now. We must rise to the occasion, ensuring that we do not look back and say we’ve had a century of ineffective systems for our young people, and make Boston the beacon of hope it aspires to be for youth, families, and communities.

To become a city of genuine opportunity, we must address the systemic inequities in education, health care, and economic mobility. This is our moment to launch an action-oriented innovative agenda — one that moves beyond rhetoric and centers on accountability and measurable outcomes.

First, we need to return to a time when neighborhoods were a source of community pride and strength. That begins with rebuilding neighborhood schools. When I was young, there was nothing better than competing in sports against teams from Charlestown, Southie, Jamaica Plain, and Roxbury (Madison Park). Those games brought parents and neighbors together as spectators. Sports have always been a powerful unifier, capable of breaking down barriers. We must tap into that power to rebuild communities.

Second, collective action is essential. As a city, we must invest in integration, opportunity, and progress.

▪ The business community must invest in the city’s talent, ensuring that young people are equipped with the skills and education needed to thrive in Boston’s 21st-century innovation economy. They are the solution to the looming labor shortages that many industries will face.

▪ Colleges and universities must play a pivotal role, extending academic support to K-12 students through tutoring, mentorship, and access to their resources. Simultaneously, Boston charter, parochial, and public schools must also collaborate to ensure that all youth are well-equipped with experience, knowledge, and a plan once they graduate from high school.

▪ Philanthropists can help fund the next generation of leaders by investing in programs that create real pathways to success for young people.

Let’s stop underestimating what’s possible for Boston. We have the resources, talented young people, and the opportunity to lead the nation by example. But it requires all of us to come together, to think bigger, and to commit to building a Boston where every child — regardless of race, class, or neighborhood — can thrive.

With this in mind, I encourage the Boston community, business leaders, families, and, most important, our youth, to place a higher expectation on themselves and each other so that together we can reach our highest potential. Let’s strive for greatness.

It’s time to move beyond our painful past and focus on what we can build together in the next 50 years. Boston’s future depends on it.

Robert Lewis Jr. is Nicholas president and CEO of the Boys & Girls Club of Boston.

KAY WALKINGSTICK / HUDSON RIVER SCHOOL Renowned painter Kay WalkingStick, who is Cherokee, has made a lifelong project of landscape painting from an Indigenous perspective. She subverts the romantic gaze of colonial Europeans who regarded North America as an untouched wilderness and supplants it with visions of the so-called New World as a cradle of North American culture and civilization for centuries before them. In this show, her specific target is the Hudson River School, who filtered the terrain of upstate New York through beatific visions of Christian providence; her responses resituate those treacly notions in the true context of an ancient people that were there long before. Through Feb. 2. The Addison Gallery of American Art at Philips Academy, 180 Main St., Andover. 978-749-4000, addison.andover.edu – Murray Whyte

CONJURING THE SPIRIT WORLD: ART, MAGIC, AND MEDIUMS The confluence of art and quasi-mysticism is deep and centuries old — pick an animist faith, and you’ll find no shortage of expressive imagery to accompany it. But the Spiritualist movement of the late 19th and early 20th century in Europe and North America emerged as a unique counterpoint — and in some cases, complement — to the rise of Modernism, with its science-minded empiricism. At their intersection, inevitably, was art, capturing their radically different ways of understanding an increasingly complex world. This show explores that intersection with an array of paintings, posters, photographs, stage apparatuses, costumes, film, and publications. Through Feb. 2. Peabody Essex Museum, 161 Essex St., Salem. 978-745-9500, pem.org – MW

Those memorable words feature in a climactic scene in “Is This America?”, Watkins’s new opera about Hamer’s life and work, which runs Sept. 20 through 22 at the Strand Theatre in Dorchester in its world premiere stage production by Boston-based opera company White Snake Projects.American mezzo-soprano Deborah Nansteel portrays Hamer at the head of an ensemble cast, which also features Puerto Rican bass-baritone Eliam Ramos Fuentes

Watkins, who was in her mid-20s during the peak of the civil rights movement, followed the news but was “never involved in the marches or the sit-ins,” she said during a rehearsal for “Is This America?” at the Brookline home of co-librettist and White Snake impresario Cerise Lim Jacobs.

However, as the composer — now based in Oakland, Calif. — was casting about for a civil rights-related operatic subject several years ago, a few friends suggested Hamer. It wasn’t long before the composer realized she’d unknowingly seen Hamer’s speech all those years ago.

Through her research, Watkins learned that on the way home from a 1963 Southern Christian Leadership Conference training, Hamer and a handful of other Black activists were arrested in Winona, Miss., jailed, and brutally beaten; the ordeal left Hamer with permanent damage to her kidneys. “And this was all about voting,” Watkins said.

The fact that Hamer was a singer herself only inspired Watkins further. “Music was what saved” the activists in dangerous situations, Watkins said. “They were frightened, and so they would sing their way through these episodes.” Since the civil rights movement was partially rooted in the Black church, the musical traditions of the church transferred, too, Watkins explained. “So I tried to bring to life that spirituality in the music that drove them.”

“Is This America?” evolved out of an earlier incarnation, called “Dark River: The Fannie Lou Hamer Story,” which premiered at Oakland Opera Theater in 2009 before being performed in workshop and concert a few times. Conductor Tianhui Ng, now music director of White Snake, led performances of “Dark River” at Mount Holyoke College and in Washington, D.C., in 2014 and 2015, and some of the music is the same. However, Watkins has made significant alterations to the piece, and “Is This America?” is shorter, she said.

“There were things that could be cut because it really wasn’t necessary to Fannie Lou Hamer,” Watkins said. Nearby, Ng and a rehearsal pianist — a last-minute replacement for White Snake’s usual, who had come down with COVID-19 — went over some last-minute revisions to the score.

When writing “Dark River,” Watkins had initially looked for a Black librettist who “understood experientially the problems that were in the South,” but didn’t find the right fit. In the meantime, during her research, she had a “habit of writing down stuff,” she said. That led to her imagining conversations between the characters, and she ended up writing the libretto on her own.

Jacobs, who founded White Snake Projects in the mid-2010s, worked with Watkins to revise that original libretto after Ng suggested it as a project for the company.

“My mission was to make this piece performable not just for White Snake but for other opera companies, and on the other hand respecting all the research that Mary put into the original,” she said. “We also added new scenes as a result of Mary’s desire to focus more on who this woman was.”

In one of these new scenes, Hamer reacts to learning that she’d unknowingly undergone a full hysterectomy while under anesthesia for removal of a uterine fibroid. This forced sterilization was so commonly performed on poor Black women in the region that Hamer popularized the term “Mississippi appendectomy” to refer to it.

“She spent so long trying to have children,” Jacobs said. “It’s an incredibly timely conversation for now, when we’re focusing on reproductive freedom, reproductive rights.”

The timing of the “Is This America?” premiere deliberately lines up with the final approach to the 2024 presidential election, said Jacobs. “We all knew that 2024 was going to be a doozy,” she said. “And because of our mission, we could not come into an election year and not be right in there.”

Because White Snake is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, it can’t participate in too much political lobbying, but it can do “engagement, education, encouragement, everything that an arts organization should be doing,” Jacobs said. In conjunction with “Is This America?,” White Snake planned several community events at two Boston Public Library branches, the Museum of African American History on Beacon Hill, and Milton Community Church. The “Sing Out Strong” community series solicited lyrics from nonprofessional writers on the theme of voting as freedom. Four of the writers selected are students at Boston International Newcomers Academy, a Boston public high school oriented toward immigrant English learners.

Asked what message she hoped audiences would take home with them from the opera: “Vote,” Watkins said simply. “We don’t like the way things are, so let’s make sure we vote.”

IS THIS AMERICA?

Sept. 20-22. Strand Theatre, Dorchester. Presented by White Snake Projects. www.whitesnakeprojects.org

Since then, tens of thousands of patients have been scrambling for alternative emergency care options while the emergency responders on the front lines find themselves stretched increasingly thin.

“Pretty much every hospital is overwhelmed and overloaded right now,” said Kevin Rosado, director of operations and communications at Beauport Ambulance Service, a private medical transportation provider. “So, kind of as a rule right now, we expect to have an extended delay.”

Gloucester-based Beauport, under an agreement with state officials, is currently stationing an ambulance at Carney on a temporary basis in case patients unaware of the hospital’s closure arrive seeking emergency care.

That precaution was not part of the initial closure plan that Steward presented to the state. Instead, it was recommended by a bankruptcy court-appointed ombudsman after a report that a patient with a gunshot wound walked into Carney’s ER the weekend before its closure, according to a court filing, and secured by the state.

Since Carney closed, Rosado said Beauport has transported around 30 patients from the Dorchester hospital to nearby emergency rooms. Dozens more have approached Beauport responders on-site, apparently unaware that their hospital was closed.

Most of the medical emergencies have been minor, he said. But the volume at Carney was high enough that the state recently extended the contract for another week, until Sep. 13.

“Everyone’s kind of feeling the pinch,” Rosado said. “Longer wait times mean less ambulances in service. Obviously, if we’re detailing a truck there to the Carney, that takes away from our other customers. But it also takes away from our resources to help provide backup services to the city of Boston.”

Boston Emergency Medical Services also continues to operate a paramedic ambulance out of a garage at Carney for nearby calls — though its future at the site is unclear. The agency has also stepped up recruiting in order to staff additional front-line ambulances, including one covering Dorchester on a 24-7 basis. During peak operating hours, it staffs five paramedic ambulances for high-priority emergencies, along with 21 EMT ambulances that provide more basic care, according to Nicholas Mutter, a spokesperson for the city’s EMS union.

Boston EMS transported over 6,000 patients to Carney in 2023, according to an agency spokesperson, or approximately 17 people per day. Most of those calls originated in Dorchester or nearby Mattapan, though the hospital also saw patients from Milton and Quincy — areas that were already reckoning with limited care, particularly after Steward closed Quincy Medical Center’s emergency room in 2020.

Carney’s patients, many of them from low-income and marginalized communities, will now need to seek treatment elsewhere, with the nearest ER being about a 15-minute drive away at Beth Israel Deaconess Hospital-Milton. Both Brigham & Women’s Faulkner and Boston Medical Center are roughly 20 minutes away — though that’s without traffic on the Southeast Expressway.

“Now we’re going to see Quincy ambulances at Boston Medical Center, so that’s going to be more patients there,” said Matt Anderson, a paramedic and president of Boston’s EMS union. “Same thing at Milton Hospital — if we have multiple crews in Milton, they’re going to be backed up a lot more. And we already know that Milton is small. They don’t have the capabilities for a large patient population.”

Patients in rural Ayer, meanwhile, face a roughly half-hour drive to either UMass Memorial HealthAlliance-Clinton Hospital in Leominster or Emerson Hospital in Concord — a journey that many point out could be a matter of life-and-death.

The increased transport times have “certainly been challenging” over the last two weeks, according to Ayer Fire Chief Timothy Johnston. The small fire department, which staffs two ambulances with four paramedics, used to send nearly all of its calls to Nashoba Valley. Now, it has to stray far outside of its response area for every emergency medical call, and that means, less often, there’s an ambulance close to home.

“I can tell you that, the last couple weeks, the station has been empty more than it ever has,” Johnston said.

With its two ambulances almost always on the road, Ayer has had to rely on nearby mutual aid departments “anytime there’s a third call,” Johnston said. In the surrounding Nashoba Valley community, fire chiefs say that the extent of the problem remains to be seen.

The rural Nashoba Valley region is home to a large population of low-income senior citizens and veterans, many of whom can’t drive themselves and rely on quick response times, according to Steve Adams, president of the Community Foundation of North Central Massachusetts.

“We seem to be putting the most burden on the people least equipped to deal with it,” he said.

But it’s not just transport times that are longer. With ambulance traffic for the closed hospitals diverted elsewhere, the burden will be shifted to other nearby ERs — many of which are already swelled, understaffed, and overcapacity.

That means that triage times may also balloon. Ideally, first responders are able to transfer their patients to hospital staff within 20 minutes of arriving, Mutter said. But now, crews are often calling in “L-20s” — meaning that they anticipate being at the hospital for longer than 20 minutes — frustrating dispatchers and patients alike.

“If you’re just sitting there with the patient on your stretcher waiting to be triaged, you’re out of service that whole time,” said Stephen Wood, a former paramedic and nurse practitioner at Carney who now works at St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton, and who conducts EMS training for the Quincy Fire Department. “Then when you get triaged, you go back and get them settled, which takes another 20 to 30 minutes. And then to get the ambulance back in service, clean it up, get ready for the next call, that’s another 20 minutes. So for each call, the turnaround time from drop-off to being back in service can be two to three hours.”

That’s a sharp contrast from Carney, which was considered to have relatively short turnaround times. Ambulances would normally turn around “pretty quickly” in Dorchester, according to Anderson, the paramedic — in large part because Dorchester is the “busiest area” for EMS crews.

But now Carney is gone, and other emergency rooms will have to take up the slack.

“They’re limited by staffing, and how many vehicles they can staff on a given day,” Wood said. “So they’re moving some chess pieces around. You’re stealing from Peter to pay Paul.”

The transportation problems in BPS have persisted for more than a decade, even after the state began intervening. It’s not due to a lack of money: BPS expects to spend $172 million this year on transportation. As part of a wide-ranging improvement plan struck with the state two years ago, BPS is supposed to get 95 percent or more of its buses to arrive punctually each month. But it has repeatedly fallen short: The highest monthly average BPS achieved during the last school year was 90 percent in March.

BPS entered the state improvement plan to avoid a state takeover. But the agreement, which also encompasses special education, facilities, and other problematic areas, does not have a mechanism to force BPS to follow through.

At a City Council meeting Wednesday, several city councilors demanded BPS fix the bus problems immediately, and the council subsequently passed a motion to hold a hearing in the future. Councilor Julia Mejia said the council needs to stop giving BPS a free pass, noting she and others supported BPS in its fight against state receivership.

“We cannot continue to let our families down,” she said. “Every year, we face similar problems, and it’s time that we get this right.”

A day later, City Councilors Edward Flynn and Erin Murphy sent a letter to the state Board of Elementary and Secondary Education, requesting an investigation into the late buses and a detailed action plan to resolve the problems.

Wu and Skipper insist they remain committed to getting the buses to run punctually but need more time, pointing to other unexpected issues. For instance, late school registrations and sign-ups for transportation caused a surge in last-minute adjustments to bus routes, resulting in route changes for about two-thirds of drivers.

The new Zūm app, they say, also holds promise in improving efficiencies by enabling drivers to follow routes on tablets affixed to their dashboards and keep track of which students have boarded and which ones haven’t. The latter could result in canceling stops where students never board.

“We’re rolling out a new technology ... that we think is going to be a real game changer and really revolutionize transportation for us,” Skipper said in an interview, but she added the new technology comes with a learning curve.

Instead of drivers simply greeting students as they get on, they now need to mark on their tablets which students boarded, which entails getting to know each student by name and getting comfortable with the technology. Those adjustments, Skipper said, likely contributed to the increase in tardy buses.

The new initiatives build upon past efforts to improve bus punctuality, which has included consolidating routes and stepping up driver recruitment and training amid a national shortage. The Wu administration also secured changes two years ago in the bus driver union contract, which included cracking down on driver absenteeism.

Wu declined an interview request, but she addressed the busing problems during an appearance on GBH News’s “Boston Public Radio” Tuesday, chalking up the late arrivals to the new app and the surge in last-minute registration of students.

“We are going to keep pushing,” she said, noting she wants all buses to arrive on time. “Major challenges are being addressed day by day, year after year.”

Wu has said addressing late buses is a top issue. She experienced the problems firsthand roughly a decade ago while raising her sister in the city and her bus was constantly late.

Russell Johnston, acting commissioner of elementary and secondary education for the state, said in a statement his agency continues to monitor transportation efforts, but noted that, despite missing benchmarks, BPS’s overall rates have improved over the last two years.

Figuring out how to deploy buses is a massive undertaking. The district dispatches over 600 buses and private vans to transport approximately 22,000 students to more than 200 public, charter, and private schools.

Under the district’s school assignment system, families can choose to apply to any school within a one-mile radius of their home and also others further away if there is a shortage of seats or not enough quality schools near their homes. The broad selection means buses are often transporting kids over several miles in a city with among the worst traffic congestion in the nation.

Late school buses hit a crisis level in 2010 when BPS attempted to modernize its operations by replacing hand-drawn bus routes with ones generated by software, which enabled the district to consolidate routes.

Drivers criticized the routes for being too jam-packed and poorly timed out, while scores of students waited a half hour or longer for buses. Then-mayor Thomas M. Menino, irate over the fiasco, repeatedly demanded improvements. More buses got to school on time but often not enough of them and the problems persisted for years.

In a bold move to snuff out late buses in 2017, BPS teamed up with MIT researchers to optimize efficiencies, but on the first day of school even more buses arrived late than the previous year and high tardiness persisted well into the fall. BPS had cut dozens of bus routes, saving $5 million.

Other districts nationwide, such as New Orleans, Milwaukee, and Washington, D.C., have grappled with late buses in recent years. But those challenges have provided little comfort to Boston families who are desperate for BPS to resolve the chronically late buses.

“It’s the worst it’s ever been,” said Kyle Sinclair, a West Roxbury father, whose daughter’s afternoon bus has been running severely late since school started. He drove to the Ohrenberger School after dismissal on the first day to pick up his daughter because the bus hadn’t arrived at the school yet. Inside the cafeteria, he said, dozens of students were waiting for bus rides. “It’s a disaster.”

Today we’re looking at the Great American Beer Hall, the passing of a beloved tarantula, and Rhode Island cheap eats. But first, I’m handing over Today’s Starting Point to my newsletter partner, Jazmin Aguilera.She hosted and produced a special podcast about Boston’s traumatic busing effort to desegregate schools 50 years ago that features a conversation with one of the Black parents who sued the School Committee for equal treatment.

Fifty years ago yesterday, yellow school buses rumbled across the city of Boston, for the first time carrying Black students to mostly white public schools and white students to schools that had a majority of Black students. In response to a lawsuit by Black parents and the NAACP, federal Judge Arthur Garrity had ruled that the city of Boston was deliberately ignoring state racial segregation laws, and the School Committee was discriminating against majority Black schools by withholding funding for supplies, letting school buildings deteriorate, and preventing Black students from attending better-funded white-majority schools.

His remedy was to force desegregation via cross-neighborhood busing.

On that first day of classes, most students stayed home. But when buses carrying Black students arrived in the predominantly white neighborhood of South Boston, angry white protesters crowded around the buses, hurling rocks, bottles, and eggs and yelling racial slurs. It was the start of what came to be known as Boston’s busing crisis, a period marked by violence and racial tension.

Fifty years later, Boston Globe reporters, editors, audio producers, videographers, and photographers, as well as an independent team of graphic novel illustrators, joined forces and reached out to the community to tell the stories of the original plaintiffs of that remarkable court case.”

While a lot of the stories in this project are looking at the state of [our schools] at present and where we have to go from here, we did want one historical story, looking back at the original ‘Freedom Fighters,’ so to speak,” reporter Ivy Scott told me. “And what motivated them to do something this bold.”

One of the elements of the comprehensive reporting package is our new occasional podcast series that will feature premium audio journalism from the Globe. In this episode, we hear Earline Pruitt, who lived in Dorchester, describe her decision to sue the School Committee, and the toll that decision took on her daughter, Denise Garrow-Pruitt, then a 14-year-old high school freshman who was bused through an angry mob of protesters on her way to Hyde Park High. Reporter Ivy Scott interviewed the women; I hosted and produced the episode, which you can hear here.

”We didn’t really, you know, think about the danger or the trauma it will cause us,” Denise said. She remembers feeling a responsibility to see it through, even though in the back of her mind she thought about what she had seen happen at civil rights marches just a few years before. “I was hoping nobody was going to hose me down.”

”The fight was there,” her mother Earline remembered. She was torn between the drive to improve Boston schools and the maternal instinct to protect her children. They all sat down as a family before agreeing to take part in the busing order. But seeing the reality of the crisis plagued Earline.

”It was doing a job on me psychologically,” she remembered. “I wanted to hurt somebody the way, you know, they were hurting my children.”

– Jazmin Aguilera

The bus shuttles are free to riders. But they’re a costly, albeit unavoidable, expense for the MBTA.

Since the agency began working to eliminate slow zones systemwide last year, alternative bus service has been a main way for riders to get around. Commuters often bemoan the delays and typically slower travel times. Meanwhile, the bus vendors are making plenty of money as the T replaces degraded rails and ties, a symptom of years of inadequate investment.

How much money could the T be on the hook for with all those shuttle bus companies? The total value of all contracts could reach $193.5 million, if it utilizes all possible buses, according to the T. So far, the T has paid out more than $50 million with more bills coming.

September will be costly. With the weeks-long shutdown of the Red Line’s Braintree branch, commuters have been lining up and packing into yellow shuttle buses operated by A Yankee Line Inc. The Boston-based company is one of several vendors that the T has contracted with to provide shuttle service through the duration of its track improvement program.

“I don’t want to pay an expensive Uber to TD Garden, but I can’t rely on these buses,” 20-year-old Madison Leuchte said recently at Quincy Center station, adding that there were not enough shuttles for all the commuters. “There needs to be more than one or two buses for everyone here.”

A Yankee Line is being paid $6.45 million during the 24-day closure between JFK/Umass and Braintree stations, the biggest diversion so far, according to the agency. The T turns to Yankee Line the most during its scheduled shutdowns, and the overall contract is valued at $159 million — a substantial increase from initial estimates of $30 million in 2021.

At the T’s board of directors meeting in June, Yankee Line was singled out for being “uniquely successful” in meeting the T’s requirements. As a result, the company has been awarded more than 90 percent of the T’s business, increasing the cost of the contract.

Aside from Yankee Line, which has been paid or invoiced approximately $51.2 million for track improvement weekday diversions, the T has used Academy Bus and Paul Revere Transportation, along with A&A Metro for accessible van service.

Not including diversions that occurred solely on the weekend, there have been 12 shutdowns since October, when the Ashmont branch and Mattapan lines were closed for track work, according to the T. The cost of shuttle service for the first 11: $53.67 million (the agency has not received invoices for the latest).

The most expensive closure, by far, occurred when the Red Line was closed in July. Shuttle bus service cost the T nearly $14 million.

More diversions are planned through December, meaning: more shuttle bus service.

T general manager Phillip Eng said in an interview there’s no way around it: “Giving the riders alternative travel is essential.”

Although critics might bristle at the high price being paid for shuttle service given the T’s funding crisis, Brian Kane, executive director of the MBTA Advisory Board, called it “a necessary cost.”

“We can’t leave people stranded,” said Kane, a member of Governor Maura Healey’s transportation financing task force. The agency itself is not equipped to operate their own buses during all of the diversions, he added, so employing the services of the private sector helps to avoid issues such as staff driver burnout.

Eng said the agency is on pace to have all speed restrictions cleared by the end of the year.

But unexpected future shutdowns are inevitable with any large transit service, and moving forward, Eng said, the T aims to be able to manage diversions differently. The agency is continuing to hire bus operators and “we hope to have a lot more of the shuttle buses being done in-house,” he added.

“There’s always going to be need for third-party support, but really the goal is to be able to have the ability to manage even alternative service from within as we grow our workforce,” Eng said. “If we need to provide alternative service, that is our intention: to make sure the public can always rely on public mass transportation.”
