Re “Housing but hardly habitable” (Page A1, Sept. 1): Danny McDonald’s portrayal of the conditions at the Franklin Field public housing project in Dorchester represents just one example of the widespread intolerable condition of much public housing across the Commonwealth. As Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority, noted, these dreadful conditions are primarily a result of the lack of annual operating and capital improvement funds.

There is reason for hope for tenants of Massachusetts’ public housing in the past legislative session as lawmakers, following Governor Maura Healey’s lead, authorized a major increase in bond authority to address the capital needs. Yet these funds will flow only if the governor seeks them through bonds in her annual capital improvement plans. Meanwhile, the level of operating funds for state-owned public housing ($218 per unit per month, by our estimate) remains less than half of the still-inadequate amount we estimate the federal government pays for the upkeep of its public housing units ($562 per unit per month).

Just as a budgetary matter, it doesn’t make sense to maintain so many unused seats. But the core problem posed by under-enrolled schools isn’t financial. Students’ educations are harmed when schools have so many empty seats that it’s not viable to offer sports teams, clubs, and a wide variety of classes.

“When some of the schools are larger, but then some are very small, at that tiny scale, it’s very, very difficult to sustain the range of academic offerings” and extracurriculars that students, “especially high schoolers,” need, the mayor said last year.

The Globe profiled one of the high schools bearing the brunt of enrollment declines last year. The Jeremiah E. Burke High School in Roxbury, where enrollment is half what it was two decades ago, lacks extracurriculars like a school newspaper and the range of academic offerings that other high school kids take for granted.

Districtwide, 32 of the 119 school buildings have “utilization rates” below 84 percent over the past five years — which the district considers “not ideal.” And several enroll less than half their capacity. The five-year utilization rate at the Burke (which was recently renamed Albert D. Holland High School of Technology) is 58 percent, according to the district.

A long-range facilities plan released by the district in January suggested that as many as half of the district’s buildings could close in the most extreme realignment scenario, though Skipper said the district wasn’t contemplating closing that many.

There are many reasons for the enrollment decline, including the inescapable demographic reality that families are having fewer children. BPS also faces competition from private, parochial, and charter schools, as well as from the Metco program, which buses some Boston kids to suburban public schools.

The problem has been known, and largely ignored, for years. In 2013, this editorial board wrote that “[d]emographic shifts point to sparsely attended high schools for many years to come.” Two years later, an audit commissioned by former mayor Martin Walsh said the district could save millions by closing undersubscribed schools. At the time, BPS served about 57,000 students; the figure was just under 48,000 last year.

From a political standpoint, mayors know they’ll take plenty of heat from teachers and parents for school closures — but likely won’t get credit for any of the long-term improvements that might result from an efficiently run district that spends more of its money in the classroom and less on heating, maintenance, and duplicative staff. When spring 2024 came and went without any major closures or consolidations, some education advocates feared the Wu administration was joining its predecessors in kicking the can down the road.

Still, Skipper said in an interview with the Globe editorial board last week that addressing the district’s facilities was a high priority. “We see this as urgent work,” she said.

If Wu and Skipper are serious about finally right-sizing the district, they deserve the public’s support through what is bound to be a contentious process. But the public deserves something too: a specific and detailed vision from the city, with measurable goals, for how the district will reinvest money freed up by consolidation.

The downsides and dangers of school closures are abundantly clear. They’re disruptive for parents, staff, and students, and can harm neighborhoods that lose local institutions. Children from closed schools can feel stigmatized, especially at the high school level. In cities that did not handle closures well, such as Chicago, they have dealt academic setbacks to some affected students.

But those are reasons to approach closures carefully, not reasons to avoid them. The cost of not closing and consolidating schools is high, too, even if it’s harder to see. A conservative estimate is that the district would realize about $40 million in annual savings if it had no under-enrolled schools; that’s what the district pays in “soft landing” funds to schools whose enrollment goes down (the district’s overall budget is about $1.5 billion).

Over the next few weeks, the Globe will outline some ideas for better ways the district could use that money — adding more high-dosage tutoring, for instance, or offering more bilingual education. It’s not meant to be an exhaustive list. But those are the kinds of ambitious investments that the district should be promising to students and families as schools are closed, merged, and reconfigured. The goal should not just be fewer schools, but fewer schools that are consistently better.

In an interview with the editorial board, Wu said that school reconfigurations would be “a multiyear process to manage transitions thoughtfully and individually” and that her promise to families was a “guarantee that every person who is disrupted by this, it’s because there’s benefit that they experience from it.” The district has developed a rubric to evaluate schools that focuses on three main criteria: the utilization rate and two measures related to the building’s physical characteristics.

Wu and Skipper didn’t offer a specific timetable but said some changes could be voted on by the School Committee in spring 2025. Wu said the process would leave “enough planning time for families to adjust and and plan their lives around it.”

Let’s hope they stick with it and succeed. Education is vital to maintaining Boston’s viability as a top-tier city. More than ever, the city needs to prepare students for careers in a changing economy and hold onto middle-class families. To accomplish those things, quality schools for all students are essential. As painful as it will be, the process that the city is contemplating is essential to meeting those goals, both by getting kids out of under-enrolled schools and investing the savings back into education.

Opposition — and there’s almost certain to be opposition — will focus on the hardships of closing schools, which are real. But Wu, Skipper, and the city’s political and business leadership can’t cede the conversation to skeptics who dwell only on those downsides. At every opportunity, officials ought to be offering a positive vision for how reconfiguring the district is a chance to give more students in Boston what every one of them deserves: a quality education.

Say, for instance (like me), you missed out on eating at The Tasty Sandwich Shop in Harvard Square before it closed and a CVS took its place. To see it depicted in that indelible “Good Will Hunting” scene, then, is to more fully grasp the romantic, bohemian vibe that is still suffused through the neighborhood. Meanwhile, more contemporary entries into the Boston canon — like Elif Batuman’s 2017 novel “The Idiot” or the 2023 film “American Fiction” — help illuminate the diversity of Boston experiences for even the most seasoned townie.

“This is a way of just complicating your vision of a place and giving it those layers of history,” said Lee Stabert, host of the podcast “Explain Boston to Me” and a Philadelphia native. Particularly for a transplant like her, Boston-focused pop culture, she said, is a way to make her adopted city feel more like a hometown.

“The idea that you walk down the street and you know what business was there 10 years ago, you know what was there 20 years ago,” she said. “I don’t have that here, but I can give my world more texture by digesting this pop culture.”

With all that in mind, we put together a guide of Boston-focused pop culture artifacts to read, listen to, and watch as a sort of tour through the city’s zeitgeist, past and present. Some of the entries we chose because of their portrayal of Boston itself; others, because of what they say about the kind of city that would produce them.

We tried to stay away from the ol’ reliables you’ve surely encountered — nothing else from the Damon–Affleck cinematic universe, “Cheers” and its spinoffs, etc. — opting instead for a more under-the-radar selection, compiled from suggestions from Stabert, Globe colleagues, and dogged Googling. If we missed one of your favorites, be sure to let us know in the comments.

“Funny Ha Ha”: Though it was made more than two decades ago, this progenitor of the “mumblecore” genre still captures that offbeat flair that defines Allston. Watch as our hapless heroine weaves through a postgrad haze of late nights in friends’ apartments, awkward romances, and temp work.

“Fever Pitch”: In this 2005 flick, Jimmy Fallon plays a Boston Red Sox fanatic who has to balance his love of the team with his budding romance with a Sox-agnostic woman (played by Drew Barrymore). It’s over-the-top, to be sure, but it might help you brace for Boston sports fandom culture — and the sort of bedlam you’re sure to witness outside Fenway Park on game day.

“American Fiction”: The Oscar-winning film follows a Black author, played by Jeffrey Wright, who achieves career success only when he pens a novel laden with racial stereotypes. It’s a laugh-out-loud movie that explores the region — from West Roxbury to the South Shore — and also digs into the quintessentially New England intersection of race and literary prestige.

“Stronger”: Whereas the movie “Patriots Day” took a birds-eye view of the Boston Marathon bombings, “Stronger” zooms in on one victim: Jeff Bauman, who lost his legs in the blast. The 2017 film, which stars Jake Gyllenhaal as Bauman, gives an intimate look into the spirit of “Boston Strong” that followed the tragedy at the finish line.

“Spenser: For Hire”: One of the few Boston-set television shows that was actually filmed on location, this ABC drama (based on Robert B. Parker’s series of novels) followed the hardscrabble life of the title character, who works as a private eye. It’s a tour through the Boston of the ‘80s — snowy winters and all.

Dunkin’ SNL skit: It might be a mere 108 seconds long, but the faux Dunks commercial from “Saturday Night Live” starring Casey Affleck conveys just about everything you need to know about Bostonians’ favorite coffee brand — and the sort of people who might be ahead of you in line ordering a coffee regulah. (Be forewarned, the clip is not exactly safe for work.)

“The Friends of Eddie Coyle”: This novel by George V. Higgins (the basis for the 1973 feature film) is an unvarnished account of crime and the people caught up in it — the titular character is an arms trafficker trying to avoid hard time. It’s a classic primer into the sort of underworld narratives Boston produces time and time again (see: “The Departed”).

“Interpreter of Maladies”: This collection of stories by Jhumpa Lahiri won the Pulitzer Prize for its depictions of characters bridging Indian and American culture, particularly in the Boston area. Just consider the setting of the story “Sexy”: the Mapparium, a place where, Lahiri writes, “all the countries had seemed close enough to touch.”

“The Idiot”: Elif Batuman’s debut novel follows a Turkish American student making her way through freshman year at Harvard University. A Globe review called it “a cutting satire of academia,” which is a five-word summary of Boston if there ever were one.

“Common Ground: A Turbulent Decade in the Lives of Three American Families”: This nonfiction book by J. Anthony Lukas, another Pulitzer winner, is often considered the defining account of the city’s busing crisis. The story of the saga is told through people caught up in the racial dynamics that fueled it —dynamics that remain divisive even a half-century later.

“Explain Boston to Me”: Stabert’s weekly podcast cuts out the middleman altogether, inviting guests to explain the stories behind Boston’s cultural guideposts. Episode topics range from the city’s dive bar scene to the region’s housing crisis to the phenomenon that is Allston Christmas.

“The Big Dig”: Debuted last year, this nine-part podcast series, produced by GBH News, provides a comprehensive history of the mega-project that rewired the city’s streetscapes. The next time you take the Ted Williams Tunnel to the airport or stroll through the Rose Kennedy Greenway on a lunch break, you’ll have some context for your commute.

“Hemenway” by Tiny Habits: To understand the sort of talent the area’s colleges and universities teem with, look no further than this tune by Tiny Habits, a trio with its roots at Berklee College of Music. Named after a street in the Fenway neighborhood, the silky-smooth harmonies artfully convey the pain of a college situationship gone sour.

“M.T.A.”: Ever wonder where the CharlieCard got its name? It’s from this 1959 ditty recorded by The Kingston Trio. The song concerns a commuter who, due to being short a nickel for exit fare, is destined to “ride forever ‘neath the streets of Boston.” (Hey, at least he didn’t have to deal with slow zones.)

“Twilight in Boston” by Jonathan Richman: Performed more like a spoken word poem than a song, “Twilight in Boston” is the Natick native singer-songwriter’s love letter to the city, which he maps from the Public Garden to Fenway to the Jamaicaway with sparse lyrics. (For extra credit, listen to “Roadrunner” or “New England” by The Modern Lovers, for which Richman was the frontman.)

“Sweet Caroline” by Neil Diamond: Love it or hate it, this 1969 hit is woven into Boston’s ba-ba-ba-seball history. Come for the tradition — it’s been crooned by the crowd at Fenway every game during the eighth inning since the early aughts — and stay for the melodic camaraderie: It’s so good, so good, so good.

“I wanted two people on every instrument, so two bass players, two guitarists, two keyboard players, two drummers. The majority of the members also identify as being part of the LGBTQ+ community. In a city where queer spaces— specifically, sapphic spaces — are limited, most of the musicians, including Katsumata-Smith, said the lack of representation extended to their experiences working in the wedding industry.

“For the first time in my life, I was around so many out and proud queer women,” she said.

Meanwhile, for multi-instrumentalist Vee VanRemoortel of Marblehead, the Femmes became an integral support system for her opening up as a trans woman while onstage. “I was out as trans in all of my circles,” she explained, “except for my performing world.”

Being a wedding professional can come with unpredictable encounters — ranging from revelry to rambunctiousness — and then substitute musician VanRemoortel, not knowing if she’d be accepted as her true self on the day, would present as male for performances. Their most requested song of 2024? Pretty much “anything” from Roan.

The married couple still attends every public Femmes performance they can: “We are Femmes groupies for life.”

Despite that, Alaia now primarily speaks English. In fact, while both of her parents mostly speak to Alaia in Spanish — and always have — the 8-year-old has lost her ability to easily understand and speak Spanish. “It is sometimes very hard to speak with her,” González said. “She’d say, in Spanish, ‘mami, no entiendo lo que me dices, ¿cómo se dice en inglés?’ And I repeat it to her in Spanish but she insists that I tell her in English.”

Alaia has struggled to learn because she has never been taught in Spanish — her biggest asset, her primary language — at Orchard Gardens, according to her mom, whose proficiency in English is limited. González and her husband are now in the process of switching Alaia to the Hurley K-8 School, one of BPS’s eight schools that offer bilingual education for English language learners, which the couple said they didn’t know was an option in the district. “It’s very hard for me to help her with homework because I don’t understand,” González said. “I had to put her in an after-school program so they can help her with homework because I can’t.”

Educating students whose first language isn’t English, like Alaia, is one of the most urgent challenges facing the Boston Public Schools.

A third of students in the district — or about 16,800 — are classified as English language learners. At the younger grades, the ELL numbers are even higher:47 percent of kindergartners and 51 percent of pre-kindergarteners are non-native English speakers.

For this group of students, the district has to juggle two tasks: teaching them to speak and write English, as required by federal law, while at the same time teaching them academic subjects like math and science.

It’s a daunting challenge — one the district hasn’t always met.

Consider the district’s latest test scores, which paint an abysmal picture for English language learners. Only 4 percent of ELLs in grades 3-8 and 2 percent of ELLs in grade 10 met or exceeded expectations on the English MCAS test in 2024, while 8 percent of ELLs in grades 3-8 and 6 percent of ELLs in grade 10 did so on the math MCAS test.

Academic research suggests that the best way to serve these students is through bilingual education programs that deliver some instruction in their native language, while also teaching them English — like the one at the Hurley. Decades ago, bilingual education was controversial — Massachusetts even banned it for a time.

Now, though, legal restrictions are gone and the barriers are staff and money. Bilingual education is expensive, qualified bilingual teachers are hard to find, and Boston’s bilingual education offerings are relatively scarce.

There’s no magic formula to solve those problems. But there’s also no question that expanding the district’s bilingual education offerings for families like González’s would be a far better use of money than keeping underutilized school buildings open. Boston needs to consolidate schools so that it can direct as many of its resources as possible into closing gaps that have festered for far too long.

For English language learners, the recent history in Massachusetts has been bleak. A political movement in the late 1990s and early 2000s spearheaded by conservative Silicon Valley millionaire Ron Unz drove voters in Arizona, California, and Massachusetts to pass restrictive language laws — so called English-only laws — which severely limited the use of the native language in the education of English learners. The Commonwealth’s voters approved English-only education in a 2002 referendum.

In Boston, the impact was immediate. A University of Massachusetts Boston study found that, from 2003 to 2006, high school dropout rates for English learners almost doubled and that MCAS test score gains for them were lower than those of other student populations; as a result, achievement gaps between ELL students and other BPS groups widened.

In the next decade, things didn’t improve — despite federal intervention, task forces appointed to address the needs of ELL students, and, in 2017, state legislation that effectively repealed the 2002 law. “The district has not created equitable conditions to ensure that all English learners progress both academically and in English language development,” read a comprehensive audit of BPS by state education authorities released in spring 2020, just as the COVID-19 pandemic began.

In 2018, the four-year graduation rate for English learners was the second-lowest among all student groups at 63 percent. Between 2015 and 2018, the dropout rate for English learners grew by roughly 34 percent and was the highest among all groups.

Recent BPS data show that the graduation rates of multilingual learners in Boston are much lower than the average; their dropout rates are nearly double the average.

At the crux of these poor outcomes is the insufficient amount of bilingual education the district offers.

Research shows that programs that use English learners’ primary language in instruction — like dual-language programs, which form part of what is known as bilingual education — are more likely to close achievement gaps. A large-scale, longitudinal study published in 2017 found “that English-only and transitional bilingual programs of short duration only close about half of the achievement gap between English learners and native English speakers, while high-quality, long-term bilingual programs close all of the gap after 5–6 years of schooling.”

And yet, according to figures provided by the district, only 7 percent of English learners — or about 1,200 students — are currently enrolled in the district’s dual-language programs. The rest, including Alaia, learn under what is dubbed an English immersion approach, where teachers teach academic subjects in English with limited support in students’ native languages. Lessons are typically taught in English, but the teacher can use various tools or techniques — like speaking slowly, using simple words, or offering visual aids like pictures and videos — to help students follow along even if their English proficiency is low.

English learners are often described as the fastest-growing student segment in K-12 education nationwide. About 1 in 10 American K-12 students is an English language learner. In the Bay State, the share of public school students with ELL status more than doubled between 2003 and 2018 — from 6 percent to 14 percent.

Additionally, many English language learners have special needs, which further complicates the challenge of educating them. In Boston, nearly 1 in 4 English learners has a disability.

The majority of English learners in the district are native Spanish speakers. But ELLs who speak Haitian Creole as a first language are an emerging demographic — Boston has the third-largest population of Haitians in the country. Small numbers of native Portuguese, Vietnamese, Chinese, Arabic, and Somali speakers attend BPS, according tolast year’s data from the district.

In an ideal world, all ELLs would be enrolled in bilingual programs — which could also serve as attractive options for English-speaking families who may want their child to learn a second language. But Boston only has eight verbal dual-language programs (it also has an American Sign Language program). Dual-language programs include the Mario Umana Academy K-8 in East Boston (Spanish-English), the Mattahunt Elementary School in Mattapan (Haitian Creole-English), the Rafael Hernández K-8 School in Roxbury (Spanish-English), and the Margarita Muñiz Academy in Jamaica Plain, the district’s first and only dual-language high school (Spanish-English).

Building these bilingual education programs requires money, primarily to hire certified bilingual teachers. But there is fierce competition nationwide to hire qualified teachers since so many districts are also contending with rising numbers of ELL students. In fact, the national shortage of bilingual teachers is the main reason why districts across the country aren’t expanding bilingual and dual-language education, according to a recent paper from The Century Foundation, a public policy research nonprofit.

Many school systems have been offering targeted cash incentives like hiring or retention bonuses for bilingual educators — for example, up to $8,000 in Houston for new hires. In Boston, though, according to a district spokesperson, bilingual teachers’ pay is not differentiated from non-bilingual educators’ pay. The spokesperson said BPS would like to explore bonuses for bilingual educators and had discussed the idea with the teachers union.

Rebuilding all the infrastructure needed for bilingual education in Massachusetts takes time, given that the pipeline of bilingual teachers withered during the time the policy was illegal. More than anything, it will take millions of dollars — for sustained investment in curriculum, training and certification of specialized teachers and staff, professional development, and even emerging AI tools to support bilingual education.

In an interview, a BPS spokesperson said the district submitted to state education authorities nine new program proposals to teach multilingual learners. Of those, two are dual-language programs. “That’s a big first step and we want to continue to grow that,” the spokesperson said. “But we are trying to balance doing this well and doing this quickly.” (In the spring, state officials rejected 17 out of 19 new program proposals for multilingual learners the district wanted to implement this fall because they fell short of state criteria.)

Boston does have a program to train bilingual educators: The Bilingual Educators and Accelerated Community to Teacher Program, launched during the 2023-2024 school year, is a 12-month program that’s free to accepted applicants. The district’s spokesperson said the program had 18 graduates last year and the current cohort has 89 participants. Graduates are not required to teach in BPS, but they are strongly encouraged to. BPS is also offering a new bilingual inclusive education initiative, in which graduates of the accelerated teacher program can apply to be a teacher resident next school year at one of the district’s bilingual schools and earn a discounted master’s degree through a partnership with Stonehill College, the spokesperson said.

The district should launch more grow-your-own programs. These programs could help bilingual paraprofessionals or school staff become licensed teachers and create a career pathway for multilingual high school students to become educators.

To the disappointment of many experts and community leaders in Boston, though, the district doesn’t seem to be going all-in on bilingual education.

Last fall, Boston officials announced a new model to educate multilingual students. The approach involves educating non-native speakers in full-immersion general education classes. The idea is that they will have access to multilingual services but not guaranteed instruction in their native language.

Nine of the 13 members of the task force appointed to advise the Boston School Committee on multilingual education resigned in protest.

“The current plan is incomprehensible in its ignorance of what constitutes optimal educational practice,” Miren Uriarte and Rosann Tung, two of the members who resigned, wrote in a Globe op-ed. Indeed, the district could not point to research or studies that would support the plan.

“This is an English-only dumping operation,” Roger Rice, executive director of Multicultural Education, Training and Advocacy, said of the plan last year.

“We are trying to do something very different than we have in previous years. This is the first year of rolling out inclusion differently,” the district’s spokesperson told the Globe last week. “We are on month two of doing that and we’re doing it at very specific grades. We have to give it some time.”

BPS insists that the plan allows multilingual learners to be taught in the least-restrictive environment. They borrow that terminology from the special education world, where inclusive practices are encouraged, such as teaching students with disabilities in a general education classroom.

Mainstreaming special education students leads to better academic outcomes, social skills development, and many more benefits for students with disabilities. But students with disabilities and English language learners are two different populations, and what works for one isn’t necessarily best for the other. The way a former district official put it, BPS’s definition of inclusion, in the context of English learners, is misguided. The definition of inclusion, the former official said, should be celebrating different cultures and different languages and fully embracing multilingualism.

It remains to be seen how the district’s new approach will fare. But it is clearly not ideal. In the long term, increasing bilingual offerings — by attracting more bilingual teachers and rebuilding the pipeline to train them — is the most promising way to give non-native English speakers the education they need.

Hewitt cracked jokes about the bride’s neat-freak tendencies — “Andria loves a good load of laundry” — but got serious, too. Andria was her “best friend,” her “sister,” Hewitt said, and theirs was “one of the most important and cherished relationships in my life.”

Hewitt described how much Andria’s support meant to her. “She doesn’t judge or make assumptions based on where you come from or mistakes that you’ve made,” she said.

Although Hewitt didn’t get into many details in the toast, Andria knew what her friend had been through. Hewitt struggled after the loss of her mother, and was working hard to overcome eating disorders, anxiety issues, and even a tendency to develop over-the-top attachments to certain people, such as her therapists.

Andria “always offers non-judgmental compassion and empathy,” Hewitt told the guests. “She lets you be exactly who you are, at any given moment.”

Andria didn’t know it yet, but Hewitt’s words would come to haunt her. Because who Shelby Hewitt was, at any given moment, changed in ways Andria never could have imagined.

The next summer, Andria was at home watching TV with her husband when she got a text from a friend. It was a link to a news article: Hewitt, then 32, was being investigated by police after allegedly spending months masquerading as a teen student in three Boston schools.

The story sent Andria reeling. She felt even worse the more she learned in the weeks and months that followed.

On Andria’s wedding weekend, for example, Hewitt mingled with guests as her usual self: highly-educated, charming, a full-time social worker for the Massachusetts Department of Children and Families. She’d recently bought a condo in Worcester for some $377,000, apparently paying cash from a family inheritance she told friends exceeded $1 million.

But in the days just before and long after that weekend, she was living a fabricated secret life, posing as a destitute, sex-trafficked foster child she named Daniella. Living this double life as a traumatized teenager, she’d managed to enroll as a special needs student at Jeremiah E. Burke High School in Dorchester. She joined the basketball team and made friends with real teens, yet also pretended she could barely read and sometimes erupted in dramatic tantrums that brought grown-ups running to help.

As Andria absorbed more details with horror, she recalls, “I felt sick to my stomach.”

Hewitt had also lobbied to move into the Jamaica Plain home of her former therapist at Walden Behavioral Care, an eating-disorder treatment center where the fictitious Daniella first emerged around 2020. Rebecca Bernat, a top-ranking administrator, agreed to this ethically questionable arrangement, which now has her facing disciplinary hearings by the state licensing board.

Hewitt created an entire supporting cast of additional characters to smooth her way through Walden and Boston schools, often drawing on aspects of her real life. She invented DCF social workers, forging documents she’d lifted from her actual job at the agency. And when she was at Walden, she said she was financially supported by a wealthy former prostitute — the name she chose was Andria, spelling it just like her friend did.

Over time, the real Andria came to realize Hewitt had lied to her “for years and years.” Andria had long thought she’d found a soul mate in Boston, someone to share their ups and downs. But she’d actually gotten pulled into the life of one of the most sophisticated con artists Massachusetts has ever seen.

All the affection that Hewitt conveyed in the wedding toast now feels like a violation. “None of this,” Andria says, “was genuine.”

SINCE HEWITT WAS CRIMINALLY CHARGED in July 2023, Andria has found herself part of an unusual group of women who share a rare form of heartbreak. They’ve known Hewitt in her different identities — whether as Shelby or Daniella, or by a nickname like Ella — and found one another on social media and through word-of-mouth. Turning their feelings of betrayal into action, they’ve also mobilized into amateur investigators — a kind of Shelby Hewitt detective squad — pooling the carefully curated bits of information Hewitt shared with each of them to try to paint a fuller picture of the person they thought they knew.

Many reached out to me after I wrote a Globe Magazine story in May about Hewitt’s secret lives. In it, I explored how so many people and institutions — the Boston school system, the state Department of Children and Families, the privately run Walden Behavioral Care — were duped by Hewitt’s elaborate hoaxes. After that article, and a shorter follow-up, I talked with many former clinicians, co-workers, and close friends, Andria among them. They were consumed with answering the most difficult question of all: Why? Why did she do it?

These people all had substantial relationships with Hewitt — she told at least four they were her best friend — though not everyone knew her by her real name originally. (Nearly all did not want to use their last names in this article, lest they get pulled into the criminal prosecution or the state’s ethics probe into Bernat’s actions.)

They’ve spent hours poring through Hewitt’s past communications with them, including text chains, emails, letters, photos, and videos, trying to figure out what it all means.

There are never any simple answers about the motivations of imposters, and Hewitt’s case is especially complex. Most imposters chase prestige and money, creating a glitzier life than they really have. But Hewitt did the opposite: Casting herself in a life filled with pity and misfortune.

And that makes her friends wonder, What could possibly have been in it for her?

Hewitt herself, now 33, declined my interview request through her lawyer. She has said almost nothing publicly, except to utter the words “not guilty” at her arraignment last December. She faces numerous charges, including document forgery and identity fraud. But her lawyer, Timothy Flaherty, plans to argue in Suffolk Superior Court that she deserves leniency because she has a mental health condition.

Instead, Flaherty tells me, Hewitt suffers from dissociative identity disorder, or DID, a serious psychological condition that controls her behavior. (It was once known as “multiple personality disorder.”)

Experts say this disorder usually originates from childhood trauma, and those who suffer from it generally can’t control when their alternate identities emerge, or remember what these other identities did or said.

Flaherty told a judge that a mental health expert has evaluated Hewitt and reached this diagnosis.

“Shelby Hewitt is a young lady who has suffered from DID for years,” Flaherty explains to me in a statement, “and despite receiving significant in-patient care, she continues to live with the pain and suffering caused by the disruption in her consciousness, memory, and identity by this disorder.”

Andria also heard about that psychological diagnosis, from Hewitt herself. After Hewitt’s hoax was uncovered, she realized she needed to better understand what was going on. She left a message for Hewitt at McLean Hospital, one of the places where she has been treated in recent months.

Over three subsequent phone calls, Andria says, Hewitt offered a range of explanations, including that dissociative identity disorder dictated her behavior, and she didn’t know what she was doing. But Hewitt also said she posed as a foster child to get the stable family life she said she’d never had. And, in a third explanation, she said she was advised by a psychic to return to her childhood to heal past traumas.

The psychic? Andria thought. The calls only left her feeling more confused and deceived.

Some of Hewitt’s closest friends have received similar calls, and listened to similar explanations and apologies. Many of these women come from mental health or medical fields, where they learned not to abandon someone in crisis, or have experience in therapy, and know the importance of grace. Still, none of them are taking anything said by Hewitt at face value. Not anymore.

They all think a lot about what motivated their friend, as they reluctantly find themselves inside Hewitt’s troubled circles of make-believe. They can’t help but see her as a master manipulator who could con anybody — and wonder if Hewitt has some kind of psychopathy, where empathy is always faked, not real.

“She is very good at preying on people with very big hearts,” says a former Walden patient who grew close to her. “Shelby’s the smartest person you’ll ever meet, and she’s very calculating.”

Another woman, who thought of Hewitt as her best college friend, sees an emotional genius within her. “She is able to connect with people on a very deep level, very easily. She disarms people,” she says. “You meet hundreds and thousands of people throughout your life, but very rarely do you meet someone like that.”

Even as these women take stock of what Hewitt took from them, they recognize she had the ability to, somehow, first give them something they needed: A show of deep empathy when they were down, or a wise counselor during a dilemma, or just a goofy buddy on Halloween. Like a social chameleon, Hewitt could change to be just what they needed.

They sometimes wonder now about themselves as well. Was there a vulnerability in them that Hewitt spotted and then exploited?

“You can feel infatuated with her personality,” says the former friend from Walden. “Meeting her, it was like I realized I was missing a part of myself that I didn’t even know I was missing. And she completed me.”

THE HEWITT FAMILY’S ranch-style home on Maskwonicut Street in Sharon would blend into any number of well-off suburbs, with its wide lawn shaded by towering pines. But looks can be deceiving. In the 1990s, when Hewitt was growing up, money was often tight.

Her father had been a photographer, but his business fell apart, in part due to his drinking and substance abuse, leaving him to work odd jobs in retail. Her parents filed for bankruptcy protection more than once, and nearly lost their house to foreclosure. Still, her mother worked numerous jobs, including as a fund-raiser for a public radio station, finding money to buy her only child North Face jackets and Uggs like those her classmates wore.

Friends say Hewitt’s household was among the poorer in the affluent town, a fact that she felt acutely. “It was definitely not as ‘nice’ as my parent’s house, in terms of cleanliness and coziness,” says Katie, who considered Hewitt her best friend growing up. “Shelby preferred to hang out at my parents’ house. And she would mention to my mom how nice and clean our house was.”

The two girls first met at a summer camp. Shelby lived some 20 miles away from Katie, so they spoke for hours on the phone during the week, and often had sleepovers on weekends. They talked about wanting to go to college and their dreams of working in the helping professions, such as social work. “We liked the same things,” Katie says. “We were almost the same person.” They’d giggle while trying on makeup and outfits, sometimes trying to look older than they really were.

Katie remembers Shelby as a self-confident teenager throughout high school who didn’t need any extra support. But the truth was Hewitt was getting lots of it. She was just keeping that side of herself secret from her best friend.

By Hewitt’s junior year at Sharon High, her grades plunged and she was placed in a special program that offered one-on-one academic help. She was also given a pass to leave class anytime to see a particular guidance counselor she’d grown close to. “She had carte blanche to see her,” recalls one school staffer.

Hewitt sometimes spoke about frequent arguments with her mother, but that didn’t strike anyone as unusual for a teenage girl. Once, when she was 16 and home alone, she called 911. When police arrived, she explained her parents would be at work late into the night, and “she had no friends or relatives to call and nowhere to go,” according to a police report.

Officers contacted her parents and concluded it wasn’t an “emergency situation.” But the police said they would notify the state child protection agency to follow up, conceivably to provide extra support beyond what she was getting at school.

Looking back, friends of Hewitt believe high school was when she began to realize, for better or worse, that appearing psychologically troubled brought her extra attention. And the more disruptive her behavior, the more the adults rushed to help.

To the Sharon High staffer, there was something enigmatic about the high schooler, who displayed deep vulnerability, and yet also an ability to exert a measure of control over how she expressed her needs.

“There was always a sense of — you don’t know with this kid,” the staffer recalls. “She appears in distress, but you wonder, How genuine is this?”

HEWITT HAD LONG WANTED to help people, and in college and graduate school she put in the work to do so. At Wheelock College, she studied human development and counseling psychology. Then, while pursuing her master’s in school counseling at the University of Massachusetts Boston, she worked at schools and a psychiatric hospital that gave her real-world experience.

What she saw and heard may have, in the years to come, informed how she portrayed characters in her double life.

While earning her master’s between 2013 and 2016, according to a résumé I obtained, Hewitt worked at three public schools in Somerville and Dorchester, focusing on students with emotional and behavioral challenges. During that same period, she also worked as a residential treatment counselor in Brighton at Franciscan Children’s, an institution for young people with serious medical and mental health needs. There, according to her résumé, she learned to apply “intervention techniques to assist in crisis situations and de-escalation of patients.”

Andria recalls Hewitt describing tense moments at Franciscan, and wonders now if she was filing them away in her memory. She’d see patients soil themselves and let out head-rocking screams, she told Andria. She also spoke of patients who had “dissociative” tendencies, who were undergoing trauma flashbacks so acute they behaved erratically in ways they’d later forget.

But Hewitt also spoke with some cynicism about “tantruming” behaviors she witnessed, Andria recalls. To Hewitt, some patients appeared to be manipulative, modulating their behaviors to get something they wanted. It apparently worked on other people, but she seemed to have the ability to see through it. “She was totally faking it,” Hewitt said after one patient’s outburst.

These powers of observation would prove useful when, less than a decade later, Hewitt returned to that Brighton neighborhood. She wouldn’t, however, be there as a counselor for troubled teens at Franciscan. Instead, she’d be walking into Brighton High School, directly across the street, persuading everyone she was a troubled teen herself.

HEWITT’S FRIENDS SPEAK OF hearing a consistent grievance from her: She didn’t have a good childhood. “She felt cheated,” Andria says. “She said her parents didn’t meet her emotional needs. She felt she was the parent.”

In Hewitt’s late teens and early 20s, friends say, she started showing a desire to form deep ties with strong women in her life. Hewitt’s fascination didn’t seem romantic, though it had some of that intensity. Instead, Hewitt seemed intent on receiving vast amounts of attention, the kind so enveloping it can feel like unconditional love.

“She’s obsessed with conventionally attractive females who have authority roles, like therapists,” is how her friend Katie puts it.

A former Walden patient made a similar point, just more bluntly: Hewitt had “mommy issues.”

At Wheelock, Hewitt became fixated on a campus housing administrator and grew obsessed with attracting her attention. But Hewitt’s neediness eventually got to be too much, and the administrator stopped responding to her messages. “She tried to distance herself because Shelby would just blow up her phone,” says Hewitt’s friend from college.

Hewitt later told at least one friend that she may have fabricated some stories from her childhood — including about a sexual assault — to try to elicit sympathy from this administrator. “I needed her to love me,” Hewitt said.

After college, Hewitt seemed to grow similarly fixated on a therapist helping her work through issues with eating and anxiety. But this woman, too, became uncomfortable and decided to end the therapist-patient relationship. Hewitt told Katie and Andria that her ensuing emotional collapse was so intense she briefly went to an emergency room.

As Hewitt courted the attention of mother figures, her real mother’s health was failing. She had a debilitating stroke, and eventually needed round-the-clock attention in a nursing home. In May 2018, she died at age 65.

Hewitt, 27 at the time, expressed much grief. “You know, her mom loved her very deeply,” says the friend from college. “Her mom would do anything for her.” By the next summer, Hewitt still seemed to be struggling.

Andria understood — she’d lost her own father, and the two had grown even closer talking of their experience. She had the idea to bring Hewitt to a psychic. “I had met with a few different mediums after my father passed away,” Andria says. “I found that it helped with grief, trying to connect with a loved one who passed on, whether it was real or not.”

Andria settled on a psychic named Ruthie Larkin, who is said to have powers to connect with the dead and comfort the suffering. Years earlier, Larkin was named in a book as one of the top 100 psychics and astrologers in America.

When Andria and Hewitt visited, in July 2019, they sat in on each other’s sessions. As Larkin focused on Hewitt, she spoke of sensing something troubling in her past, Andria recalls. It had to do with “witnessing something traumatic as a child.”

That particular insight didn’t seem to affect Hewitt in any serious way at the time, Andria says — the friends went out for pizza afterward. But recently, she’s had to wonder: Did Hewitt take more out of it than she remembered?

After Hewitt’s con was exposed, she told Andria she had earlier gone to see a psychic alone — she didn’t say who she visited — and took a pivotal message away from the encounter: If she wanted to heal her past wounds, she’d have to find some way to return to her childhood.

DANIELLA was screaming again.

The teenager’s wailing was so loud it could be heard through the walls of a consult room at the Walden Behavioral Care center in Dedham. Yet some staffers barely reacted, it seemed, as if they’d gotten used to it — yet another outburst from Daniella, the high-maintenance patient many called Elle.

But for one of the teenage patients, Daniella was impossible to ignore. “There was screaming, bloody murder,” recalls this patient, who considered Daniella her best friend at the time. “I start freaking out. And I’m like, I need to go see what’s going on.”

When she stepped into the consult room, she saw Daniella — she was wild-eyed and had stripped naked. This was how she sometimes acted when she was experiencing flashbacks to being sexually trafficked, this patient knew.

The patient turned to Walden staffers with alarm, saying, “How the [expletive] are you guys leaving me alone in here to deal with this?!”

Hewitt had long created confusion at Walden. The first time she was admitted, in 2019, it was under her real name and birthdate. But not long after, she told staff she was actually a teenager named Daniella Blake Herrera.

But even from the beginning, she was describing her situation to staff in horrifying terms: “a homeless young adult prostitute who had been sexually trafficked from a young age, had no idea exactly how old she was, and was illiterate,” therapist Rebecca Bernat wrote in a filing with state licensing officials as she defended her role and conduct in Hewitt’s case.

Over roughly a half-dozen stays at Walden, between 2019 and 2022, Hewitt would prove to be “an extremely difficult patient,” wrote Bernat, who oversaw Walden’s residential programs. The patient would rock back and forth, hit herself on the head, soil herself, and sometimes end up in what appeared to be a catatonic state, among other worrisome behaviors. In calmer times, however, staff say she tended to speak in a meek, childish voice.

Over time, many from Walden told me they suggested Daniella needed a more intensive psychiatric facility than one focused on eating disorders. But they recall higher-ranking Walden staff — Bernat included — waved off their concerns.

Since the start of Hewitt’s criminal case, Walden executives have remained virtually silent about how the institution missed so many red flags during her stays there. In declining comment, a Walden official cited patient confidentiality and the ongoing criminal case. (The official did acknowledge Walden abruptly ended Bernat’s employment after police exposed Hewitt’s double life.)

But I’ve been able to piece together considerable information by interviewing numerous former Walden staffers and patients, as well as by obtaining the extensive, written statement Bernat submitted to the state licensing board. (Through her lawyer, Bernat declined to be interviewed for this story.)

In her statement, Bernat alleges she was the victim of a multi-year, orchestrated effort by Hewitt to con her and other Walden staff.

Bernat said Hewitt created a number of fake characters who communicated with Walden officials about her care. Among the first she made was Andria, who Hewitt painted as a wealthy former prostitute who was her benefactor. Posing as this older woman online, Hewitt wrote emails and texts to Bernat and other Walden officials, and used a Venmo account to pay for special services.

“Hi Becky,” the fictitious Andria wrote in one message about the logistics of an upcoming appointment for Daniella. “Will work on the following week for the neuropsych, but is there any way I can send her in a cab on monday?”

Andria’s name came up so often related to the patient’s care and expenses that one former Walden staffer recalls hearing a colleague ask, somewhat suspiciously: Has anyone ever actually met Andria?

Nobody had.

Bernat and others also heard from two DCF social workers who were really Hewitt in digital disguise: Michelle Delfi and Michael Kornetsky. Over email, Hewitt used these identities to describe Daniella’s extensive needs, suggested she was abused in foster homes, and implored staff not to abandon her.

Bernat has also insisted she spoke directly to at least one of these purported DCF staffers, raising questions about whether Hewitt had an accomplice, or used a voice-altering app to disguise her voice on the phone. When Hewitt was working as a social worker for DCF, several of her adult friends recall her talking about downloading such apps. She said she needed them for an undercover work assignment at DCF.

Hewitt spun her stories so persuasively that Bernat said there wasn’t much doubt at Walden about what they were hearing. Daniella told staff she’d been using the name Shelby Hewitt — which she said actually belonged to her half-sister — to hide from her sex traffickers.

Daniella also pointed Walden staff to an actual news article about a man with her last name, Herrera, who’d been arrested for running a brothel in Framingham. She implied he was her father.

Bernat said in her statement that Walden officials had a discussion about insurance coverage, because it was initially under Shelby Hewitt’s name. They questioned if Daniella could use her half-sister’s insurance this way, Bernat wrote, but ultimately concluded Daniella “could do so.”

Going forward, Walden staff were instructed to refer to her as Daniella, or by one of her nicknames, such as Elle or Ella.

As Bernat tells it, the biggest concern at Walden was whether Daniella was safe. After hearing that she was a scared, sex-trafficked teenager, Walden staff called in the FBI, only to find that Daniella refused to speak with them when they arrived.

One of the only people Daniella seemed to trust at Walden was Bernat, who often got pulled into helping her. “Becky was always right there with her. She was like the crisis manager for Elle,” recalls Jessica, another former patient. Eventually, Daniella also began seeing Bernat at her private practice for additional individual therapy.

Although Daniella was deeply connected to Bernat, a large portion of her attention was also focused on another therapist, according to former staffers and patients, a woman with a speciality in adolescent treatment. The two grew close and worked together often. At some point, Daniella asked to move into the woman’s home. Those requests soon turned into pleas.

The therapist, however, couldn’t do it for several reasons, including that she was expecting a baby.

Soon after the birth, Hewitt’s attention seemed to focus entirely on Bernat. According to her statement, she began receiving requests from Hewitt’s fabricated DCF social worker to intervene in Daniella’s deepening crisis. By the summer of 2022, the requests were bigger: Bernat was being asked to become Daniella’s co-guardian and take her into her home.

IN MANY WAYS, BERNAT was just the kind of woman Hewitt had obsessed over in the past. She was in her 40s, fashionable, and had a big job — overseeing some 200 staff in the Walden system, as well as running her private practice. She and her partner, John Smith, didn’t have children of their own, but Bernat loved taking her nieces and nephews on adventures.

Former Walden employees say Bernat was not the warm and fuzzy type at work. She could be intimidating, like a no-nonsense school principal who’s seen it all before.

In her statement, Bernat said she wasn’t comfortable with the idea of having Daniella move in — and Smith was initially against it. But Hewitt was known to be persistent. Over months of “significant pressure” from the purported social workers, Bernat said she was led to believe that Daniella needed her — and only her — desperately.

In March 2022, a time she was complaining about her treatment in a foster home, Daniella arrived at an appointment “bruised and soiled,” Bernat said. Worried Daniella was being abused, she says she and another therapist filed reports with DCF. At other times — such as when Bernat was “not available at all hours” — Daniella only got worse. Bernat believed DCF was telling her “that they needed to finally break the cycle of ‘Ella’s’ abuse.”

Bernat finally gave in. But before that, she said in her statement to state licensing officials, she terminated her therapeutic relationship with Daniella in April 2022. She said she knew it was a professional transgression for therapists to let patients move into their homes.

SOMETIME AROUND THE start of the school year in September 2022, Daniella wore a birthday-themed tiara, looked at the cake before her, and smiled.

She told Bernat it was the first birthday celebration she’d ever had.

Hewitt was finally getting the life she wanted — in a family that cared for her in exactly the way she wanted. “Becky made me feel my needs were met,” she told her friend Katie much later.

Daniella had been having occasional sleepovers at the Jamaica Plain home of Bernat and Smith since the summer. But she would begin to stay over with the couple more regularly while attending Burke High.

While posing as Daniella and starting in school, Hewitt was busy in her real life. She had a full-time job for DCF as a social worker, responsible for assessing safety risks for children under state supervision and visiting families at least once a month — a friend recalls Hewitt once temporarily caring for a DCF infant in her apartment. That September, Hewitt also closed on her Worcester condo.

Around the time school started, Hewitt smiled for a photo in front of an ice cream sundae at Cabot’s in Newton. Showing the picture to her friend Andria, she asked, “Don’t I look like a kid?”

In Jamaica Plain, Daniella was eventually given her own bedroom in the couple’s two-bedroom condo. She joined the Burke basketball team, and Smith frequently went to games. When Daniella wasn’t sleeping at their condo, Bernat understood she was staying at a foster home in Worcester. She did not say if she ever made contact with that alleged foster parent to coordinate care.

By the time Christmas rolled around, Daniella was excited. She’d picked out scented soaps to give Bernat, and Bernat would give her a set of AirPods and new clothes. For Christmas Eve, she joined relatives of Bernat and Smith for a fancy dinner around a beautifully decorated table, according to Bernat’s lawyer Paul Cirel.

“I’m finally going to have the Christmas that I deserve,” Hewitt had told a friend.

THAT WINTER AND into the spring, Hewitt’s life grew exceedingly complex. She didn’t tell her adult friends about her double life, but she did say she was moving into an apartment in JP with “Becky and John.” That seemed unusual to friends, since she had her own condo, but they figured it must be some kind of roommate arrangement.

In her statement, Bernat suggested there was no time she had suspicions that Daniella was an imposter. Hewitt was apparently very careful around Bernat, such as making sure to park her car blocks away from the JP condo.

At Walden, not everyone knew that Bernat had taken Daniella into her home, though it apparently wasn’t a secret either. After one person heard about it, she approached Bernat at work. “I congratulated Becky when I heard she was going to be a guardian,” this former employee says.

Bernat helped support Daniella’s education, including by communicating with school staff, sometimes from her Walden work email address.

In the spring of 2023, Daniella transferred to Brighton High, where she sought more intensive special education services. But Hewitt still found time to be with her grown-up friends.

On Memorial Day weekend in 2023, Hewitt joined her childhood best friend Katie, and two other longtime friends, on a holiday getaway.

After Daniella’s school day in Brighton, Hewitt hustled to Logan Airport for their flight to Colorado. They toured Boulder in a Jeep, and rented a mountainside cabin near Garden of the Gods Park, snapping photos of themselves at hiking trails and impressive rock formations.

Friends had been noticing, with some curiosity, that she was trying to look younger. She’d gotten braces on her teeth, and started wearing clothes fashionable among Gen Zers. Some suspected she was getting Botox and lip filler.

The Colorado trip was so much fun, no one but Hewitt wanted to leave. “Shelby was adamant about needing to return for work,” Katie recalls. “I asked if we could shift the trip or stay another day but she said she absolutely couldn’t because of work and she didn’t have any PTO.”

In reality, Hewitt needed to get back to Bernat’s house and to her teenage identity.

Daniella’s behavioral problems in Brighton High were getting worse. By early June, 16-year-old Daniella had disappeared from Brighton High. For reasons that remain mysterious, Hewitt reappeared as a newly enrolled 13-year-old student named Elle Blake at English High.

Even for someone as intelligent as Hewitt, it was getting difficult to keep all the details straight.

An adult friend once spotted her wearing an “Elle” bracelet and asked what it meant. Hewitt brushed the question off, saying it was her nickname at Walden.

Somewhere around this time, she also appeared to slip up with Andria. Hewitt had claimed that she switched jobs and was working as a school counselor at Burke. But then, not long after, referenced working at English High.

“I thought you mentioned Burke?” Andria asked.

Hewitt didn’t miss a beat. “You have such a bad memory,” she snapped.

Looking back, friends realize she often reacted that way when she was challenged.

The student known as Elle wasn’t at English High for a week before she allegedly complained that school bullies were mercilessly mocking her. Some classmates said she looked too old to be 13, more like she was in her 30s.

Looking into the alleged bullying, English’s principal noticed something odd about Elle’s DCF social worker’s email address — the domain name didn’t match what is used for all DCF employees. She contacted police and, within days, years of Hewitt’s intricate stories had come unraveled.

Before long, Hewitt was making something like a confession to Bernat.

“I lied to you about something big,” she said.

The last time Bernat saw her in person, she said, Hewitt was in the back of a police cruiser and the JP condo was being searched. Not long afterward, though, Hewitt began repeatedly contacting Bernat by phone, saying she was in an emergency room. Bernat tried to ignore Hewitt, but finally responded.

Bernat said she had no idea who Hewitt really was, and didn’t want to hear from her again until she “was ready to tell her the truth.”

Hewitt hasn’t contacted her since.

AFTER HEWITT’S HOAX was revealed, she’s been periodically admitted at mental health facilities for treatment, according to her lawyer. But she has also sought out another type of counselor — Ruthie Larkin, the psychic she’d originally seen with Andria in 2019.

Larkin agreed to speak to me about Hewitt’s half-dozen sessions with her, starting in the fall of 2023, several months after her arraignment.

Over one meeting by Zoom and the rest by phone, Hewitt made clear she was in big legal trouble, Larkin says. She also “unloaded” about growing up and the pain of her mother dying. It was clear to the psychic — who sees herself as a “spiritual adviser” helping others — that Hewitt had “major problems and major disturbances over her childhood.”

Larkin acknowledges she once met with Hewitt after her mother’s death, possibly with a friend, but insists she never advised Hewitt to regress back to childhood.

When asked why she led this fabricated life, Larkin says Hewitt didn’t elaborate. But she did say she was “trying to take care of her trauma.”

Although Larkin knew she was hearing from a person who might falsify information, she wasn’t interested in trying to parse truth from fiction. Hewitt was speaking “her truth,” Larkin says.

As Larkin tells it, attending Boston Public Schools wasn’t part of Hewitt’s plan. She just got stuck, feeling like she had to attend school to keep up her image as a needy child in the eyes of Bernat and Smith.

“It wasn’t like an idea,” Larkin recalls Hewitt saying, “it was just something that happened.”

Hewitt also told Larkin how happy — truly happy — she’d been with Bernat and Smith. “She met this couple. They treated her like a child,” Larkin says. “She loved that family. They nurtured her.”

Although Hewitt said she knew she’d eventually be caught, her biggest preoccupation was how she had hurt Bernat and Smith.

“Ruthie, will they ever be friends with me again?” she asked the psychic.

Hewitt’s last session was apparently in January of this year. She was feeling like everything was her fault. Among the advice that Larkin left her with was this: “You have to forgive yourself before you can feel better.”

THOSE WHO KNEW SHELBY or Daniella have gone on with their lives, but can’t help revisiting their relationships with her.

Even now, some of Hewitt’s friends can feel her draw. “Sometimes I want my old friend back,” says her best friend from Walden. “But then the reality kind of sinks back in, and I don’t think I can get over the damage that’s been done to my mental health.”

That former Walden patient has cut a lot of friends out of her life, but not because any of them did anything wrong. “It’s just because I can’t get over my trust issues,” she says. “I have lost a lot because of her.”

So has Hannah, another former patient at Walden. She and the person she knew as Elle participated in trauma support groups at the center, where patients discuss their most private matters. Hannah now feels horrendously betrayed. “I shared things I’ve never shared with anybody in my life,” Hannah tells me, beginning to cry. “And she’s not a real person.”

For her part, Andria sometimes uses humor to try to get by. She recently edited the contact she used for Shelby’s number in her phone. Now it reads: “Shelby? Elle? Who the [expletive] knows.”

But shock and anger still overtake Andria in waves. Hewitt had the gall to stand by her side at her wedding, and lie to her for years. She took Andria’s own name for a fake prostitute she made up to further her cons. And, Andria later heard, Hewitt told people at Walden she was once raped by that fake Andria’s husband. To back up her story, Hewitt showed a picture she’d lifted from Facebook — it showed the real Andria and her brother.

Andria hasn’t spoken to Hewitt for nearly a year. If Hewitt were to call again, she thinks she would tune out anything she’d say.

“It’s psychobabble. She says nothing. It’s like, ‘let me repeat a bunch of these therapy words,’” Andria says. “She wants to feel like the smartest person in the world. She wants me to believe her, so she can feel powerful. Maybe superior.”

In one of her phone conversations with Hewitt, Andria confronted her about the bizarre story she’d heard from former Walden patients.

Did you really use the name “Andria” — my name — for the made-up benefactor for Daniella?

Hewitt said she did. She apologized.

But Andria wasn’t done: And did you tell Walden clinicians that this “Andria’s” husband raped you, and as “proof” showed them a picture of me with my real brother?

Hewitt apologized again.

“I haven’t been a good person,” she said, as Andria recalls. “I’m not the person I want to be.”

The secret lives of Shelby Hewitt, 32-year-old high school imposter

What did therapist Rebecca Bernat know about the 32-year-old who impersonated a teen student in Boston schools?

After years of underinvestment, the neighborhood is showing new life. Apartment buildings have sprung up, especially near stops on the Commuter Rail’s Fairmount Line. New bus lanes are coming too, to be installed in the center of Blue Hill Ave. A long-discussed neighborhood plan is now official, with zoning that aims to spur along new multistory, mixed-use buildings and support smaller, locally owned businesses. And there’s hope that a tranche of new liquor licenses designated for Mattapan will bring more restaurants and places to linger.

That sounds a bit like the Mattapan Square Ali-Salaam grew up in. Back then there were two movie theaters, bakeries, and a Brigham’s ice cream shop.

“There were places that, if you were a young teen, you could walk down to the square and sit down and have an ice cream sundae,” she said. “Now it’s not that type of atmosphere.”

There’s a lot at play, but one shared goal of the various plans is for business and development to radiate up Blue Hill Ave., creating opportunities for residents and entrepreneurs alike. Today, the road can feel like a mini-highway, with 40,000 cars a day, many of which are simply cutting through Mattapan on their way somewhere else. Those who do often double park in front of businesses and takeout joints, only clogging traffic further.

The zoning changes aim to encourage more housing and even office space. Taller buildings, yes, but also a more pedestrian-friendly sidewalk with room for street-level businesses. A few have already arrived.

Just this month, Marcia Satchell opened a new location of her Blue Mountain Jamaican Restaurant in The Wellington, a new 39-unit apartment building on Blue Hill Avenue in the Wellington Hills section of Mattapan. She’s already welcoming regulars, and she’s excited to contribute to a vibrancy she feels is long overdue here.

“Some of what’s happening throughout other parts of Boston are now happening in Mattapan,” Satchell said. “I think the continuation of development and building is going to be key, and ensuring that Mattapan gets equal opportunity for business growth as other communities.”

New housing is a key ingredient to all that, said Dariela Villon-Maga. The developer and Mattapan native is working on three projects along Blue Hill Avenue, has a bid in for a city-owned parcel on Cummins Highway parcel, and is proposing a mixed-use building near Mattapan Square that would also house an arts complex.

In each project, Villon-Maga says she’s hoping to prioritize the neighborhood’s values. That means emphasizing affordable homeownership over rental units — so that residents will know they can stay. She’s also created a community board to vet occupants of ground-floor space, which those businesses, too, would ultimately own, not rent. All of it, again, aims to enliven Blue Hill Ave.

“The community has really been vocal about their want for more activation along Blue Hill Avenue: More destinations, more places for them to go, whether it’s cafes, restaurants, or art galleries,” Villon-Maga said. “It’s the ability to kind of walk to a destination versus having to go downtown or having to go kind of outside of their neighborhood.”

That’s part of what the city aims to do as well. Five years in the making, Plan:Mattapan aims to enable more buildings that can both bring more residents and a wider variety of commercial spaces to Blue Hill Ave.

Some, yes, would likely be taller than what’s there now. But the idea isn’t to remake the corridor entirely, said Aimee Chambers, who leads planning and zoning at the Boston Planning Department. It’s to make the most of what’s already there.

“We want to make sure that we’re not encouraging demolition of buildings or anything like that,” Chambers said. “Rather, we want to create circumstances where we can work with existing building owners to think about ways to be more creative.”

Still, even among supporters of that vision, there are concerns about growing pains from all this change. Villon-Maga hears a lot of worry about traffic and the new bus lane project that’s now under public review. The $44 million plan would create three miles of designated center bus lanes, 2.25 miles of protected bike lanes, between nine and 11 new pairs of raised bus stops, and more than 14 new crosswalks.

All of the potential construction is on the minds of local entrepreneurs who have invested in the neighborhood, too.

“I’m concerned about the thriving businesses around here,” said Denise O’Marde, the owner of Cafe Juice Up, a juice bar that sits across the street from the Blue Mountain restaurant.

O’Marde sees herself as part of the change: She opened her business in 2018 to bring a healthy food option to a section of Mattapan where convenience stores reigned supreme. The business survived the pandemic, but she’s now worried construction on Blue Hill Ave. could result in more traffic and congestion — and less foot traffic into her shop. “While I support a change for the future — and I understand that it’s so our children will have a nice Blue Hill Ave. for the next 50 years — I’m scared,” she said. “I have anxiety when I think about that.”

Then there’s that perennial concern that comes with new development in working-class neighborhoods: displacement.

Rising rents and home prices have already pushed many Black families out of this part of Boston, something the Rev. Willie Bodrick sees every Sunday when he looks out at his congregation at 12th Baptist Church in Roxbury.

“There are families who come from Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan,” he said. “Now they’re living in Canton, Randolph, Brockton.”

Along with being a pastor, Bodrick’s also a housing developer, work he sees as deeply intertwined with his goal of building community. He and his brother Winston cofounded Ambry Development and are launching three residential buildings, including one on a parcel they acquired from the city, off Blue Hill Avenue near Harambee Park. It’ll be 18 units, all set at affordable prices for lower- and middle-income buyers. And it will be all for sale, not rentals, so that not just current residents but also their children and grandchildren can have a place to call home.

“We know there’s a lot of movement in this neighborhood. And we know we’re in the midst of a housing crisis,” Willie Bodrick said. “We want people to be able to stay in this neighborhood.”

Staying and being part of the evolution of Mattapan is important to small business owners like Derick Foster-Toney, whose family has owned the Chez-Vous roller rink for four decades. The rink, which sits on the border of Mattapan and Dorchester and has been in business since 1933, is one of the few entertainment venues in the area, and has long served a rare role in the neighborhood: a community gathering place. “The fabric of what Boston truly is,” he said, “is defined by places like Chez-Vous.”

Foster-Toney said he’s been buoyed to see new development crop up along the Blue Hill Ave. corridor, and he’s hopeful to be part of it, saying he hopes to obtain one of the new liquor licenses that will be distributed to the neighborhood.

“This area that was forgotten and overlooked because of stigmas,” he said. “It wasn’t the fault of the people,” he noted, but rather a lack of city support. “We have the greatest opportunity to change that narrative and restore a sense of pride.”
