“HUD relies on public housing agencies to ensure that public housing units funded by HUD are decent, safe, and sanitary,” HUD Acting Inspector General Stephen M. Begg said in a statement.

The results of the audit come amid a housing crisis that continues to plague the region. BHA oversees about 10,000 public housing rental units in the city. Established in 1935 to provide stable affordable housing for low- and moderate-income residents, the authority is run by Administrator Kenzie Bok, a former Boston city councilor appointed to the post in August 2023 by Boston Mayor Michelle Wu.

In a statement responding to the audit, the authority said the quality and safety of its housing is “extremely important” to both Bok and the mayor, and the agency has already implemented reforms that will help fix the issues identified in the federal review.

Bok, according to the statement, “completely overhauled” the agency’s maintenance system since taking the reins of the organization, reducing the total number of work orders agency-wide in BHA units from more than 17,000 in March 2023 to 3,100 as of the end of February.

“BHA changed its processes so that every BHA unit is now inspected by an expert licensed staff inspector every year,” the statement said.

Last year, the authority digitized its entire work order system “to ensure that every emergency issue is tracked and rapidly addressed in real time,” according to the authority’s statement.

The audit found that not only did the authority fail to comply with federal requirements, but it also failed to meet its own policies requiring maintenance superintendents to inspect the authority’s buildings and grounds quarterly.

According to the audit, the authority provided the last quarterly inspection report for only seven of 24 buildings that were identified as having deficiencies. It could not locate the last quarterly report for the remaining 17 buildings.

In addition, the audit reviewed the inspection history of 55 units, finding that the authority failed to perform 37 of the 103 required inspections during the agency’s 2022 and 2023 fiscal years.

Problems also riddled building exteriors and common areas in the vast majority of buildings the audit examined, with officials faulting heating and cooling equipment on the sites, fire exits, and fire control panels, plumbing, and infrastructure such as stairs and railings.

For instance, at the Franklin Field development in Dorchester, toilet leaks and rodent infestation were observed in a teen center community bathroom. Residents told officials that such conditions were a recurring issue. Next to the center, water leaks and standing water was spotted near electrical equipment. Elsewhere in that development, a hallway light was improperly wired.

In recent months, Franklin Field tenants have complained about shoddy maintenance and poor living conditions. Last year, allegations of disgraceful living conditions at Franklin Field drew the attention of the state’s attorney general, who sued the authority over its handling of a tenant’s complaints about a unit infested with mice and mold.

Last year, Bok, the authority’s administrator, said the many complaints at Franklin Field, a sprawling complex off Blue Hill Avenue, reflect not a failure to care but a shortage of resources.

“People get tired of hearing how underresourced public housing is, but it really is,” she said at the time.

The vast majority of Franklin Field’s 1,000-plus residents are people of color, and the units are intended to house the working class and the poor. There are three separate housing programs that make up Franklin Field. For all three, the average household income is below $30,000 a year. For one of the three, it is below $14,000.

The audit also found problems at other locations, including some instances of the authority failing to identify glaring problems in its own inspections.

For instance, mold and mildew were observed in a unit at the Alice H. Taylor Apartments near the Roxbury-Mission Hill line. The authority failed to identify that issue in a March 2023 inspection, according to the audit.

Similarly, at the Roslyn Apartments in Roslindale, the authority failed to identify a rodent infestation in a March 2023 inspection.

“The Authority lacked staffing resources to inspect all units, create work orders, correct the deficiencies identified in the Authority’s properties during its own inspections,” read a portion of the audit’s conclusions.

The audit was triggered at least in part by media attention and public concern about the condition of subsidized housing properties, according to inspector general’s office.

In the units that had deficiencies, problems with windows were most common. Such issues were present in more than 40 percent of the problem housing units. The review also found issues with bathroom appliances such as tubs, sinks, and toilets, ventilation, electrical hazards, kitchen appliances, pest infestations, and air quality.

In chaotic political times, when our health and spirits feel low, a long walk may be just the restorative medicine we need.

On Dec. 6, 1854, Thoreau visited Providence to deliver a lecture on reform at Union Station’s Railroad Hall. He arrived early in the day and another transcendentalist writer, Charles King Newcomb, served as his host and guide during his two-day stay. The two men explored Providence, from Olneyville to Narragansett Bay. Thanks to their journals, letters, and some suggestions from local historians, we can recreate their saunter through the city, learn more about Rhode Island’s history, and see why Thoreau felt that “an early morning walk is a blessing for the whole day.”

Start the walk near the Wall of Hope behind the modern-day Union Station, which is about 100 yards northwest of the original depot where Thoreau gave his talk.

He would have seen a row of commercial buildings and unpaved roads filled with horse-drawn carriages. In his journal, he wrote that he was struck by the train depot’s twin spires and lengths of red brick. It was the largest railroad complex in America at the time. That station burned down in 1896, and the station that stands today is its replacement.

Today, walking through the tunnel to the front of the depot, and past the clock tower, you will see the city skyline, Waterplace Park, the Providence Place Mall, and the Rhode Island State House, which occupy the land in and around what was once the Great Salt Cove, a mile-wide salt marsh that once existed between Smith Hill and downtown Providence.

Thoreau and Newcomb probably walked along Steeple Street to get to Newcomb’s home, which, according to former Providence Journal editor and columnist John Kostrzewa, may have been on Benefit Street. Steeple Street becomes Thomas Street, and at the intersection of Thomas and North Main streets stands the First Baptist Church in America, which was built in 1775.

The church was founded in 1638 by Roger Williams, the Puritan minister who founded the settlement of Providence, which went on to become Rhode Island. Thoreau, who had an interest in Williams, likely would have been interested in seeing the church. Tours of the building are offered after the Sunday worship services, and on Tuesdays and Thursdays at noon, 12:30 p.m., 1 p.m., and 1:30 p.m. More information is available on the church’s website.

The Benefit Street area is home to some of the most historic buildings in the city, including the Providence Athenaeum (251 Benefit St.), a stunning circulating library that opened in 1838. It was known to be frequented by gothic fiction writer Edgar Allen Poe, and Thoreau stopped by during his visit.

Go inside the library and take a self-guided tour. (Admission is pay-what-you-can, but a $5 donation is suggested.) The library has an original copy of Thoreau’s “Walden,” purchased in 1854, in its private collection, but in the main reading room, there are other copies of Thoreau’s books, including “Walden.”

After the library, stop by other historical spots on Benefit Street and the side streets off of it: The Providence Marine Corps of Artillery building at 176 Benefit St., was built in 1839; the Old State House at 150 Benefit St. was built between 1760 and 1762; Sullivan Dorr House at 109 Benefit St. was built in 1809; and the Sarah Helen Whitman House at 88 Benefit St., was where the poet and transcendentalist writer lived from 1783 to 1794.

There’s also the Stephen Hopkins House, a classic picket-fenced red colonial home at 15 Hopkins St. where a signer of the Declaration of Independence lived. The First Unitarian Church, which was raised in 1816, is at the corner of Benevolent and Benefit streets. The massive John Brown House — the first mansion built in Providence — is on the corner of Benefit and Power Street. Brown was a statesman, merchant, slave trader, and benefactor of the university. His home is now a museum.

There are two beautiful parks in the vicinity, both of which are connected to Roger Williams: The Roger Williams National Memorial, at 282 N. Main St., where Williams’s followers allegedly settled near a spring, and Prospect Terrace, at 60 Congdon St., where a 14-foot-tall statue of Williams was erected in 1939 to honor the 300th anniversary of the founding of Providence.

From Newcomb’s neighborhood, Thoreau likely walked south on Benefit Street to Power Street, and then turned left to Gano Park, which is across the street from Slate Rock. The pair could also have walked by Brown University – Newcomb’s alma mater – by following Waterman Street to Gano Park.

The Rhode Island Historical Society calls Slate Rock Providence’s “most historically significant” landmark. The boulder was the site of Williams’s arrival in Rhode Island, but it was accidentally blown up with dynamite while workers were building the Roger Williams Landing Monument. Pieces of the boulder can be found around Providence, according to the New England Historical Society: Remnants are in the floor of the Central Baptist Church on Wayland Avenue, in Brown University’s Waterman Avenue gates, and in the pedestal of the university’s Brown Bear statue.

At Gano Park, you will find an informational sign on the bike path along the Seekonk River that talks about Williams’s 1636 arrival in Rhode Island. When Thoreau took his walk, the spot where this marker is now was part of the river.

Thoreau also crossed the Seekonk River to visit Fort Hill. It can be reached from Gano Park by taking the East Bay Bike Path across the Washington Bridge and following it to the hill near Veterans Memorial Parkway and Mercer Street.

After the walking tour of Providence, Thoreau and Newcomb returned to Railroad Hall, where Thoreau delivered an original speech, “Life Without Principle,” about righteous living.

He wrote in his journal that the talk failed to connect with his audience’s interest.

“I fail to get even the attention of the mass. I should suit them better if I suited myself less. I feel that the public demand an average man, — average thoughts and manners, — not originality, nor even absolute excellence,” he wrote. “You cannot interest them except as you are like them and sympathize with them.”

A good, long walk, it seems, can only go so far to soothe the troubled soul.

The surprise plea averted a jury trial in a crime that shocked Highland Park, Ill., a lakefront suburb of Chicago. Eric Rinehart, the Lake County state’s attorney, said Monday that he had been prepared to go to trial and present overwhelming evidence that would prove Crimo’s guilt.

In 2023, the elder Crimo pleaded guilty to seven misdemeanor counts of reckless conduct for his role in helping his son own firearms. He sponsored the application for his son’s gun permit, despite indications that his son was capable of violence.

“Not even water?” is such a common question Muslims get during Ramadan — the Islamic month of fasting — that it’s become an inside joke. Malak Ahmed, the social justice chair at the Islamic Society of Northeastern University, even has a hoodie displaying the question.

The answer is: not even water. Fasting means nothing is supposed to intentionally pass your lips — food or beverage — from sunrise to sundown.

“You feel hungry, you feel thirsty, but it allows you to recognize that on a daily basis you have access to food, access to water, you have access to all sorts of comfort,” Ahmed, a sophomore, told me. “Fasting at its most basic level, at its core, it really just brings you down to earth.”

The holy month, which began Saturday, is a special time of reflection and spirituality for the Muslim community — one whose visibility has grown in Boston, as today’s newsletter explains.

Community highlights

Greater Boston has dozens of mosques, and many of them offer special Ramadan prayers, meals, and programming.

The Islamic Society of Boston runs two mosques: One in Roxbury that is the largest in New England, and another in Cambridge, the city’s original mosque. They provide a no-cost iftar — the evening meal to break the fast — every day of Ramadan, and serve around 5,000 meals during the month, according to a mosque official.

The Islamic Center of Boston, Wayland also serves community-sponsored iftars every Saturday of Ramadan and on select Sundays. My colleague Camilo Fonseca visited the center after the first day of fasting and highlighted the strong community there amid a time of heightened anti-immigrant rhetoric and episodes of Islamophobia, especially since Hamas’s 2023 attack on Israel, and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza. Muslims and others across the country, including in Boston, have rallied to oppose Israel’s treatment of Palestinians there.

Yusuf Mosque in Brighton offers a nightly iftar and Tarawih prayer (the practice of reading the entire Quran during Ramadan).

The Islamic Center of New England has locations in Sharon and Quincy, and hosts special iftars throughout the month. The Quincy location is New England’s oldest mosque, built in 1964.

The City of Boston is hosting its annual Community Iftar on March 14 at the Bruce C. Bolling Building in Roxbury. In past years, the event has been held at City Hall. But Hawa Yusuf, the city’s civic engagement project manager, told me that the Bolling Building was chosen to make it accessible to the community — it’s just blocks from the Islamic Society of Boston.

Tips for working professionals

At least 50,000 adults in Massachusetts are Muslim, as indicated by a check of the voter rolls by the Council on American-Islamic Relations. Many people who celebrate Ramadan build their schedules around prayers and when the fast starts and ends. That can make it a challenge to accommodate sleeping, eating, and working.

Yusuf, the city’s civic engagement project manager, told me that communication with one’s employer is really important. For example, employees could ask to leave work an hour early in exchange for not taking a lunch break. Or they could ask to start their work days earlier, since some are already up for suhoor (the meal before sunrise that precedes the day’s fast).

Although more people throughout Massachusetts now know what Ramadan is, Yusuf also suggested that those who observe it could do a presentation during a weekly team meeting to educate coworkers about the holiday. And to optimize the day, they could ask their bosses to avoid scheduling meetings in the late afternoon out of consideration for those who have been fasting all day.

Tips for students

Many of the Muslims in the Boston area are students, and for some, this Ramadan could be their first away from family — a daunting and isolating experience, given that community is central to the holiday.

“I just remember freshman year, being very scared, like, ‘Oh, I have to break my fast in the dining hall. No one around me is going to be fasting,’” said Reda Samari, a senior at Boston University.

Samari, the vice president of the Islamic Society of Boston University, told me that his fears quickly subsided after getting involved with ISBU. He felt “engulfed within the community” with nightly iftars and prayers with fellow students, and now encourages other students to seek community around them.

Universities in Greater Boston have varying degrees of accommodations for Muslim students during Ramadan, such as suhoor to-go boxes, shuttles to the masjid (another name for mosque) for evening rituals, halal (permissible) meals, and prayer spaces. Many of those accommodations have come from student-led efforts.

“Students do need to be proactive,” said Yasamine Brown Kocaman, a co-president of the Brandeis Muslim Student Association. She grew up in Massachusetts and told me that despite comments like “not even water?”, residents seem more aware of Ramadan than before.

Still, she said, it’s important to speak up and educate those around you. “It really strengthens the voice when it’s a collective going and advocating for the needs.”

In an interview, Branz added: “We don’t understand how, with everything this program has achieved for BPS families and students, we have to fight so hard to keep it. … For all its talk of evidence-based practices, it makes no sense that BPS would be cutting this evidence-based program." The Boston City Council unanimously passed a resolution last week asking the district to preserve funding for the PMP.

A BPS spokesperson said the district is “deeply committed to partnering with organizations that can continue impactful work across the district” but wouldn’t confirm the amount of money that will be dedicated, if any, to any parent mentoring bid opportunity.

Ulana Ainsworth, a kindergarten teacher at the Clap school, has 20 students, half of whom are multilingual learners and many of whom have special education needs. Ainsworth has a parent mentor, Miss Lugo, who is from the Dominican Republic and is crucial to her classroom, she told me in an interview. “This program is helping to change so many people’s lives,” she said.

“Not a lot of other teachers in our building speak Spanish, not as much as I do,” Ainsworth said. “I don’t think we could have survived to the point that we are right now without [Miss Lugo’s] help, there is no way,” especially given the academic demands of kindgergarten. “I would like Mary Skipper to come spend a day and teach in my classroom.”

All students are supposed to leave Ainsworth’s classroom “being able to know how to read and write, count all the way up to 100. Some of these kids have never been to school before, and a lot of my kids aren’t able to learn in a whole group [setting],” she said. For instance, Ainsworth would have Miss Lugo teach phonics in a small group, she said. “Our kids made enormous growth in math and reading,” Ainsworth said.

Here’s another reason why the program is so promising, and why it’s baffling that BPS would want to endanger it: Some parent participants have gone on to become paraprofessionals and others have pursued higher education to become teachers themselves. Branz said that 17 parent mentors are currently enrolled in the Urban College’s Lead Teacher credential program. At a time when BPS needs bilingual teachers, the program has built a pipeline for them.

One of them is Dora Sandoval, an immigrant who used to be a teacher in Mexico, her home country. “It makes me very proud because I never thought I’d be working at the Boston Public Schools, and now the kids in the classroom see me as a teacher,” Sandoval said in an interview.

“It’s only because of the PMP and the ladder of opportunities that it offers us that I was able to enroll” in Urban College, she said.

If BPS is committed to equity, supporting multilingual learners, and strengthening the teacher pipeline, it must do more than talk the talk. Instead of gutting the Parent Mentor Program, the district should be expanding it.

“It always comes back to the consumer,” Lambert said Tuesday, between restocking shelves. “Sometimes you try to split it, you try to figure it in and not raise the prices. If you don’t have to, you don’t raise the prices. Customers are really important to us.”

Across the United States, a large portion of grocery stores’ fruit, vegetables, meat, and seafood comes from Mexico and Canada, so the tariffs pose a direct threat to costs of fresh food. Products like fish, beef, avocados, strawberries, peppers, nuts, cooking oil, and butter are especially likely to rise in price as a result of the tariffs, Quartz reported.

Profit margins for grocery retailers are thin — 1.6 percent, according to the industry trade group Food Marketing Institute — leaving business owners “little choice but to pass on these import taxes to remain in business and continue serving customers,” the organization said in a news release.

Target CEO Brian Cornell warned customers Tuesday that prices in Target stores could go up in coming days. Over the next year, the tariffs could cost the average American household more than $1,200, according to the Washington, D.C.-based Peterson Institute for International Economics.

More expensive groceries could increase the already high portion — 20 percent — of Massachusetts families who struggle with food insecurity, according to the nonprofit Project Bread.

“We are already in an elevated crisis when it comes to people affording food,” said Project Bread CEO Erin McAleer. “We are so scared of any policy that is going to increase the price of food.”

During his address to Congress on Tuesday night, President Trump said his trade policies would be “great for the American farmer” by lessening competition from international farmers.

“Tariffs are about making America rich again and making America great again, and it is happening and it will happen rather quickly,” Trump said. “There will be a little disturbance, but we are OK with that.”

At Lambert’s on Tuesday morning, customers filled their baskets from produce cases that run the length of the store, bursting with an array of fresh, brightly colored fruits and vegetables arranged in neat sections. Others ordered sandwiches from the deli or cuts of fish and meat from the butcher’s counter.

Seafood and meat will likely become more expensive next week, said Neal Asnes, owner of Plaza Fish, the fish and butcher shop located within Lambert’s.

“It’s going to affect everybody, absolutely,” said Asnes. “So much of my fish, so much of my lobster, is from Canada. It’s going to be hard to avoid.”

With warmer weather on the horizon, Lambert said he plans to purchase more US-grown produce, a factor he hopes will lessen some of the tariffs’ impacts for him and his customers.

As Dorchester resident Xianni Brown paid for groceries at Lambert’s, prices were top of mind.

“There are already people struggling to make it, to feed their kids,” said Brown. This particular trip to her usual market wasn’t just for her — Brown said many items in her basket, which contained soups, granola bars, and lettuce, were for a homeless woman outside trying to provide for her family.

Grocery prices have already ballooned so much in recent years amid inflation. Now, shoppers like Brown are worried what the tariffs could do.

“Everything is already up,” said Brown. “Anything more could kill us.”

Some customers wondered if produce options will decrease in the coming weeks, and whether some types of foods will remain within reach.

“We’re going to have to start making those tough choices,” said Ken Holland, a Weymouth resident who stopped by Lambert’s for its plentiful array of affordable fresh fruit and veggies.

As business owners prepare to navigate the impacts of tariffs, Lambert said, it’s difficult to predict what’s ahead, but he will strive to continue serving his community.

“We’re a little blind about it, too,” he said. “We weren’t really filled in on what the problems are going to be on us.”

The Democratic Party is desperate for strong leadership — a voice that can counter the relentless vilification of immigrants. As Republicans in Congress prepare to grill Wu over Boston’s welcoming immigration policies, she has an opportunity — perhaps even an obligation — to demonstrate that leadership.

Boston, where nearly 30 percent of residents are immigrants, is not in chaos. It is not a city in disarray, overrun by dangerous newcomers. It is, by the numbers, the safest major city in America: 24 homicides last year, the lowest in decades.

Those are the facts. And yet one needs more than facts in a fight with Republicans. Wu is walking into a hearing designed for political theater, not truth-seeking. The GOP-led House Oversight Committee will rely on loaded questions, out-of-context statistics, and scare tactics to sell its dystopian vision of liberal cities in collapse — an attack on Democratic governance as much as immigration itself.

Still, Wu’s message could be sharper. She has yet to fully articulate a comprehensive vision on homelessness, which has increasingly intersected with immigration as newly arrived migrants struggle to find stable housing. While she touts Boston’s public safety record, she must acknowledge the anxieties some residents feel about crime, even if the data do not support the GOP’s exaggerated claims. The hearing is an opportunity not just to defend, but to present a vision for long-term solutions.

And for the love of God, set the record straight — don’t call Boston a “sanctuary city.”

Will any of this hurt Wu in Boston? Unlikely. If anything, standing up to the MAGA-led House will only bolster her support among progressive and moderate voters alike. But she must be wary of traps. If she is painted as out of touch with working-class concerns, particularly around housing and city services, it could be weaponized against her in the mayoral race. Republicans may not defeat her in Congress, but they could hand ammunition to her local opponent, mayoral candidate Josh Kraft, who’s eager to frame her as prioritizing ideology over practical governance.

If I were Wu, I’d walk in with a message that’s clear but not oversimplified: Immigrants are not a burden; they are an asset. This is the moment to fight back — not with defensiveness, but with clarity, nuance, and conviction.

By Carine Hajjar

What Wu says all depends on what she’s asked. As mayor she doesn’t have much power when it comes to enforcing immigration detainers, or changing the scope of the state’s right-to-shelter law. If Republicans keep blaming her for crime in shelters, or criminal migrants being released by the police despite ICE detainers, they’ll be met with the unsatisfying answer: I can’t change these things, they’re a matter of state law.

But if the Republicans actually want to get answers that can help Massachusetts, answers that can put pressure on the true levers of power at the state level, they’ll focus less on attacking Wu and more on pushing her to admit that Massachusetts’ Democratic leaders need to course-correct. Here are some questions they might consider:

Do you support any of the various bills in the state Legislature that would allow Massachusetts law enforcement to honor ICE detainers for migrants charged with or convicted of serious crimes?

Why it’s important: Wu and Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox have been Trump administration border czar Tom Homan’s targets for criticism when it comes to the release of migrants with detainers. But per the 2017 Lunn v. Commonwealth decision from the Supreme Judicial Court, it’s up to the state Legislature to determine if law enforcement can cooperate with detainers. Though Wu can’t create a law that allows Boston police to honor detainers, she can still call for that change.

Would you rather ICE be apprehending people in an orderly way at jails, or out on the streets?

Why it’s important: ICE is going to continue to find and deport migrants with criminal records. But in Massachusetts, it’s a question of where. If the state’s law enforcement doesn’t honor immigration detainers, it’s more likely that ICE will continue to go out into the community looking for migrants with criminal charges or convictions.

If the state Legislature passed a law that allowed law enforcement to cooperate with certain ICE detainers, would you support it? And would you push for a corresponding change in the city’s Trust Act, which currently prohibits Boston police from carrying out federal immigration enforcement?

Why it matters: Right now Wu has an easy deflection when she’s attacked for not complying with ICE: She can’t, BPD can’t, because the courts have ruled that law enforcement doesn’t have the jurisdiction to do so. But if state law were to change, would she uphold it?

Are you concerned about the state’s lack of transparency when it comes to the crimes happening in emergency shelters — some of which have been in the Boston area, like the Melnea Cass Recreation Center in Roxbury that briefly served as a migrant shelter?

Why it’s important: This question would put pressure where it really matters – on the governor’s mansion.

By Joan Vennochi

Uh-oh.

Mayor Michelle Wu paid an outside law firm $950 an hour to prep her for testimony she is scheduled to give before the Republican-led US House Oversight Committee?

That sounds familiar, in the worst possible way. Former Harvard president Claudine Gay was also prepped by lawyers before testifying to Congress, and we all know how that ended. When Gay refused to say that calls for the genocide of Jews violated the school’s conduct code, she came across as a too-woke, lawyered-up academic who lacked common sense and a moral compass. Between her testimony and subsequent plagiarism charges, Gay was out as president of Harvard.

Put aside the cost of high-priced lawyers to taxpayers — Republicans would love it if Wu came across as a too-woke, lawyered-up politician who lacks common sense and a moral compass. Not that it really matters what they think. Wu answers to Boston voters, not to House Republicans, or as Gay did, to rich alumni and a spooked board. It gives Wu an opportunity to make a case for immigrants as the historic foundation of this country, despite the best efforts of Republicans to demonize all for the crimes of a few.

All Wu has to do is speak directly, succinctly — and from the heart.

Boston is a city founded by English settlers who — guess what? — were immigrants. Over time, waves of Irish, Italian, and Jewish immigrants arrived, followed by Asian, Caribbean, Haitian, Cape Verdean, and Latino populations. This did not happen without some strife. Despite challenges and pushback, each successive group contributed to a city celebrated as a center for the arts, academia, and innovation. It’s not perfect, but it is still a community strengthened by diversity.

Today, the city operates under the Boston Trust Act, which bars local police from keeping immigrants in custody for possible deportation by federal officials unless a criminal warrant has been issued for the person’s arrest. That’s where Republicans will try to trip Wu up. In a video they released last week, they disparaged so-called sanctuary cities as “lawless” and threatened to cut off federal funding to them.

Wu plans to argue that Boston is a safe city, in part because of immigration policies that encourage people to report crimes. That’s fine, but the broader message is this: We need secure borders and comprehensive immigration reform, but we also need to treat all people with dignity, and that means making sure they get due process.

That is more than a legal argument. It is a common-sense, moral one.

Barry Chin likes to go where the action is.

Two weeks ago, Chin, a Globe photojournalist, posted up behind the basket at the Boston City League boys’ championship game between English High and Holland Tech, two local high schools. Chin was able to snag the vantage point because high school games usually let photographers stake out their own spots to shoot from, as opposed to pro games, where spots are assigned.

The freedom to choose isn’t without risk. “The downside to shooting under the basket is that it can be dangerous,” Chin explains. “Most high school gyms are small, and the area between you and an athlete running at full speed is short, with little room between you and a potentially serious collision.”

But at the English vs. Tech game, held at Madison Park High School, taking a chance paid off. Using a telephoto zoom lens, Chin captured the above image as English’s Darvens Alcime, powered by upward momentum, flipped over Holland’s Ian Piper. Piper’s team ended up winning the game.

Last month, this newsletter published a preview of the Globe’s best photos from January, as chosen by our photo editors. Today, by popular demand, we’re bringing you a few of the paper’s other best images from February.

The cold and snow deepened across New England in February. Erin Clark visited the Ice Castles, a winter attraction in North Woodstock, N.H., that features huge icicle formations hand-sculpted by artisans into slides, tunnels, pathways, and caverns for visitors to explore.

Load muskets and fix bayonets! This year marks the 250th anniversary of the start of the Revolutionary War. The Globe’s John Tlumacki photographed reenactors playing American Colonists and British redcoats as they acted out Leslie’s Retreat, a standoff that took place two months before the seminal battle at Lexington and Concord, on the spot in Salem where it happened.

Hundreds gathered in the Strand Theatre in Dorchester for "Lift Every Voice," a city event for Black History Month. Photographer Pat Greenhouse captured Dana Bonner, left, and Akou Diabakhate greeting each other in the audience.

Love and rain were in the air as the Globe’s David Ryan photographed Valentine’s Day flowers for sale in the misty windows of Brattle Square Florist. The century-old store, slated to close three years ago, has continued under new ownership just steps away from its old storefront in Cambridge.

Craig Walker captured the world’s top snowboarders as they caught air before thousands of spectators for Red Bull Heavy Metal, a one-day street snowboarding competition at Boston’s City Hall Plaza. Before the event, sponsors inundated the plaza with 300 tons of artificial snow.

Warrior pose with a side of weed? At Diaspora, a private marijuana club in Cambridge photographed by Brett Phelps, Bhang Yoga class attendees puffed on joints after a warmup of downward dogs and deep breaths. The state will start letting lounges, cafes, and events apply to serve pot products later this year, which could mean more marijuana-infused activities.

No, this isn’t a rediscovered Monet newly arrived at the MFA. It’s Upper Newbury Street, smudged into an impressionistic blur as freezing rain distorted Globe photographer Stan Grossfeld’s field of view.

Wiley made waves as one of the founders of the then-largest minority-owned law firm in New England, the first Black chairman of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, and a key adviser to myriad elected officials and business leaders. But his long list of accolades was an afterthought Friday afternoon, as several family members, business partners, and community members attested to Wiley’s love for Motown hits, competitive basketball skills, and witty humor.

Kerry Bowie, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology alumnus and the cofounder of Browning the Green Space, a nonprofit that aims to bring more people of color into the clean energy field, said he hoped Friday’s service would celebrate Wiley’s singular legacy, as he extended prayers and sympathy to Wiley’s loved ones.

“We’ve lost an icon here in Boston,” Bowie said. “Flash was, you know, his smile, he was gregarious, he was just a fun guy. But under that fun piece, he was getting stuff done, and we know that he was a champion for people. He was a sponsor for people.”

Shortly before 2 p.m. Friday afternoon, The Temptations’ “I Wish It Would Rain” filled the auditorium as a long line of family, friends, and acquaintances of Wiley headed toward the front of the packed venue.

It went dark as the service began, and through the heavy darkness, Walker said she was sure the crowd’s love for Wiley — and the late attorney’s unique personality — shined through.

A number of Massachusetts political figures attended the service Friday, including US Senator Ed Markey, Representative Ayanna Pressley, Mayor Michelle Wu, Attorney General Andrea Campbell, former mayor Raymond Flynn, former governors Mike Dukakis, Bill Weld, and Deval Patrick, and former representative Joe Kennedy III.

In a written statement, former vice president Kamala Harris celebrated Wiley as a “remarkable leader who left an indelible mark on those around him.”

“His commitment to public service and dedication to uplifting the voices of our community were gifts to all those whose lives he touched,” she said.

City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune described Wiley as an “institution,” who left a big impression on her as a young Black attorney.

“Flash always showed up for us,” Louijeune said. “For all of us college students who were thinking about how we break our own barriers, how we participate in these institutions that we know nothing about.”

Wiley and his family, she continued, are “so important to the Boston fabric, to the fabric of the Boston community, but especially the Black community.”

Pressley said that whenever she’d search for Wiley in a crowd, she would follow the laughter. The congresswoman said she considered Wiley someone she could never tell “no,” recalling one of her last conversations with him, in which he asked, “Are you ready?”

She said “Yes,” although she wasn’t sure what he was referring to.

Did he mean ready to defend Black history amid the Trump administration’s anti-DEI initiatives? Did he mean to tackle the racial wealth gap?

“But if what he really meant was, ‘Are you ready to live in this world without me?’, the answer is no,” Pressley said.

Nevertheless, Pressley continued, “we will summon the strength to carry on his work … with Motown as our soundtrack.”

As Pressley concluded her remarks, one attendee adjusted her glasses to wipe away tears.

Ken Chenault, former CEO of American Express, told the crowd that no one could discuss Wiley without mentioning his abiding love for his wife, Benaree “Bennie” Wiley.

Chenault recalled how Flash Wiley gave him an eight-page, single-spaced “legacy document” about the couple’s love story.

“Flash and Bennie were the original power couple,” Chenault said.

Dean Richlin, Wiley’s former law partner, said his longtime friend was not only a fun, lively attorney, he was also “strategic, highly principled, and fiercely committed.”

As the leader of the region’s largest minority-majority-owned law firm at the time, Richlin said, Wiley took the opportunity seriously.

“He saw the firm as creating the predicate for gaining broad influence in politics and the business world,” Richlin said. “He practiced with skill and determination the art of power and influence.”

Raised in Indianapolis, Wiley made history well before settling in Boston, according to an online biography. He was the first African American from Indiana appointed to a military academy out of high school, and became the United States Air Force Academy’s first Black football player shortly thereafter. After displaying his athletic prowess, Wiley gained the nickname that would stick for the rest of his life: “Flash.”

Another speaker, Janine Sijan-Rozina, said her older brother, Captain Lance P. Sijan, was the one white Air Force cadet who agreed to room with Wiley during the Jim Crow era.

Sijan-Rozina’s brother died as a Vietnam prisoner of war, she said, and Wiley was the only cadet who kept in touch with his family over a lifetime.

“I loved him,” Sijan-Rozina said, voice trembling with emotion. “Before, now, and forever, I love you so much, Flash.”

B.J. Wiley Williams, Flash’s daughter, said instead of being raised like a princess, her dad “wanted her to be like him — a trained warrior.“

”I am truly honored to be considered his twin, and I’m eternally grateful for his warrior training,” Wiley Williams said. “I feel prepared to take on the world.”

Pratt Wiley, Flash’s son, said his father slept as a child in a Murphy bed, squeezed with his mom and grandmother in a studio-size apartment. The fact that his father’s memorial service could fill an auditorium with friends and family from across the globe, he said, was once unimaginable.

“Together, you helped him compete,” he said. “Together, you helped him win in the sport of life.”

The two-hour memorial was punctuated with lighthearted videos of Wiley’s past concerts at Berklee, including a cover of Boyz II Men’s “End of the Road.” Donning a white hoodie and a matching, sideways snapback, Wiley recited the ‘90s hit with intensity.

Some attendees clapped along to the video, and met Wiley’s final performance with thunderous applause.

Over a decade later, the soft-spoken 37-year-old meditates for two hours every day and is an author five times over — and internationally famous. As Yung Pueblo, he is ubiquitous and beloved on the internet for his frank, accessible, and insightful poetry and reflections on life, love, pain, and personal growth, which he shares in his newsletter and across social media platforms, including an Instagram audience of over 3 million (@yung_pueblo). Off-line, the Wesleyan University alum was born in Guayaquil, Ecuador and grew up in Jamaica Plain, where his extended family still lives. He’s also a proud alum of Boston Latin Academy in Roxbury — he was commencement speaker for the class of ‘24.

In “How to Love Better,” out March 11, Perez explores the complexities of connection — how being honest about your own needs, triggers, and shortcomings is pivotal to having healthier relationships. Through short nonfiction essays, poems, and self-help questions, Perez opens up about his life, marriage, and the tools he uses to find resolution — and invites the reader to do the same.

We caught up with him on a Zoom call in advance of the book’s launch and March 10 event with Harvard Book Store.

Q. You’ve lived in New England for most of your life. What was it like for you growing up in Jamaica Plain?

A. I was born in Ecuador and I moved to the United States with my family when I was 4. We settled in JP. It was a very different neighborhood back then, in 1992. Very Latino. Pretty working class, lower middle class community. I spent a lot of time in the Connolly Branch Library, right in the middle of JP, just being a little kid, reading every book possible. I grew up there at the library first and foremost.

Q. And what’s your favorite thing about living out in Western Mass. now?

A. Being in the woods and in nature. I’ve always been in areas where there’s tons of concrete. I used to hike a lot in Blue Hills after I graduated from Wesleyan. Out here there’s rail trails. They’re old rail lines, and it’s these straight walkways that people can walk or run or bike. They go on for miles, through multiple towns. It’s beautiful.

Q. You’ve written a lot about personal growth over the years. How did you decide to focus on relationships for this book?

A. I was surprised about this deep relationship between personal growth and your connections. I went into personal growth originally because I’d developed so many bad habits from not spending time with my own emotions and not processing. Growing up with a lot of poverty created sadness and anxiety inside of me that I needed to address. I had no method for that. When I was in college, I was drinking, partying, abusing my body, and pushing it to the edge constantly. It created a breaking moment. I almost lost my life.

After that wake-up moment, I started paying attention to my emotions and building new habits. As I started meditating, I picked up that ability to see where I was creating trouble in my life. There was an immediate effect on my relationship with my wife, and my parents and my friends. I started seeing that I could be more genuine, be more authentic, tell them how I care, be more present with them.

Q. Yung Pueblo means “young people,” right? Why did you choose that pen name?

A. I chose it to honor my Ecuadorian roots, where it’s used often to mean masses of people. When I started seeing how immature I was and how much growing I had to do, I also started noticing, “Oh, it’s not just me. It’s all of humanity.” I like that constant reminder that we’re in a period of growth, and we’ll see where we go. I’ve been reading and studying history my whole life. My plan, if writing didn’t work out for me, was to become a high school history teacher.

Q. You centralize growth being constant on a personal level — in the book, a “river of time,” where you’re meeting yourself and your partner, again and again.

A. I think personally and professionally, that’s been my biggest point. One of the bigger stances for my personal inner peace is: Just let yourself change. Don’t stick to what works. Let yourself go where you’re creatively inclined.

Q. Were there any parts of the book that were your favorite to work on?

A. In my “Art of Arguing” chapter, it’s changing the framework from arguing with someone that you love, to trying to understand them as opposed to trying to just win. If they are able to give you that same thing in return, you find that the tension pretty automatically fizzles out. Thich Nhat Hanh said that love is understanding. When I can understand my partner well, it changes: “Oh, of course you’re not my enemy.” The mind will trick you into feeling like you’re under threat in an argument, when you’re not. You’re just having a disagreement.

Q. You quoted a loved one as saying “I want to have a lot of arguments with you.” Framing it as “this is a part of a relationship,” rather than something scary.

A. That was a big moment for my wife and I, when we realized that for years we were both trying to win, but we were actually both losing. Even when one of us did make a mistake, apologized for it, it still felt like when we were trying to win, we were seeking dominance or control. And it’s like one person falls flat and the other one stands victor — and that’s just not good energy to move forward.

Q. These are communication practices that for me, and I think for a lot of people, as much as you try to learn them, it’s always a continuous cycle of repeating them again and saying, “OK, I messed that one up.“

Yes, the New England Revolution stadium would go up in the city next door, not Boston. But most soccer fans likely would come through Charlestown’s Sullivan Square on game days, either getting off the highway in cars or exiting the MBTA’s Sullivan Square Station on foot. So the Legislature set parameters for negotiations with officials in Boston, as well as Everett, as part of recently approved economic development legislation that rezones the power plant property to allow for the stadium.

Everett Mayor Carlo DeMaria already has the makings of a community mitigation agreement. He signed an initial one with the Kraft Group in late 2023 in an attempt to resolve environmentalists’ concerns — a laundry list that included $750,000 for Charlestown’s athletic fields.

Wu, in contrast, is just getting started. And the clock is ticking: The new economic development law requires a deal by May 1, or a mediator gets called in to referee. If a deal can’t be reached by Dec. 31, then the matter goes before an arbitration panel to decide. (Josh Kraft, a son of Kraft Group chairman Robert Kraft, is running for mayor this year against Wu and has said he would recuse himself from any negotiations with the family’s business if elected.)

The stakes are high. For both sides.

For the Krafts, the former Mystic power plant could represent the end of a yearslong quest to build a stadium with soccer in mind instead of football, and in the urban core of Greater Boston instead of suburban Foxborough where the Revs share Gillette Stadium with the Patriots. The Kraft Group has said that a final decision hasn’t been made yet on whether to actually go ahead and commit to construction. Maybe that’s a negotiating tactic. But a new stadium wouldn’t be cheap — possibly around $500 million — and the Revs can continue to draw plenty of crowds if they stay in Foxborough.

For Wu and her team, it’s an opportunity to finally bring about a significant fix to Sullivan Square, one of the most disliked rotaries in Greater Boston. (Sure, “K Circle” on the Dorchester-South Boston line and the “Circle of Death” at Newton Corner can be more harrowing, but Sullivan’s traffic tie-ups are the stuff of legend.) There was no mention of Sullivan Square in a December letter from Revs boss Brian Bilello to the city, kicking off negotiations, though he mentioned the money the Krafts already agreed to set aside for athletic fields in Charlestown.

Boston planning director Kairos Shen, in his reply in January, did bring up Sullivan Square as he referenced a deal reached nine years ago that was valued at $68 million between Boston and Wynn Resorts over its Encore Boston Harbor Casino in Everett, also just across the Mystic River from Charlestown. Translation: You can do a lot better for Boston than $750,000.

Traffic in Charlestown was obviously a big issue back when Mayor Marty Walsh inked that deal with Wynn. The total included $25 million for infrastructure improvements at Sullivan Square over 10 years, another $11 million for traffic mitigation in Charlestown, and $250,000 for a regional working group that would recommend long-term fixes to the notorious rotary.

Charlestown residents are still waiting for traffic relief. Sure, there have been improvements, including upgrades to bus connections at the T station and the widening and repairing of several feeder roads. The working group issued a set of recommendations, mostly focused on public transit. However, the back-ups between Sullivan and I-93 persist. Biking through Sullivan is still a contact sport. And developers continue to eye the lots, warehouses, and other underused properties around the rotary and nearby in Everett, bringing the potential for even more congestion.

Ryan, the state representative, says he doesn’t have an ultimate dollar figure in mind. He would like to see city officials assemble a plan that combines mitigation funds from Wynn and the Krafts, along with any other potential funding sources, to create a solution to the Sullivan Square conundrum that lasts for another century. That said, Ryan says any final deal shouldn’t simply be limited to Sullivan and the $750,000 that the Krafts have already offered.

Tim McKenna, a Charlestown Neighborhood Council board member and vice president at the Charlestown Youth Soccer Association, has a specific ask: money for an indoor fieldhouse. Many of the association’s 800 kids head to Winchester in the winter because there’s no place to play soccer indoors in Charlestown; a fieldhouse could be used by other sports as well. With a downpayment of $5 million from the Krafts, McKenna said, the association could borrow the rest to build the facility. If the Revs are serious about fostering homegrown soccer talent, McKenna can’t think of a better way for the team to spend its money.

Another neighborhood council board member, Mary Boucher, said she’s arguing that all new construction be put on a back burner until Sullivan finally gets fixed. She said she’s tired of fighting her way through the traffic jams for her roughly one-mile commute through Sullivan Square. She’s lived in Charlestown all her life — she just turned 61 — and has never seen it this bad. The neighborhood, she said, shouldn’t hand a wish list over to Santa Kraft. Instead, all attention must be paid on the biggest problem at hand — that awful rotary.

Boucher’s plight underscores the fact that most of Charlestown is an island walled off by water or train tracks, with only a handful of ways in and out. And half of those routes go through Sullivan.

Residents have been crying out for a solution for years, if not decades. While they may not find the answers in a pro soccer stadium, it’s hard to blame them for trying.

“If this funding is cut, it will have a severe impact on the operations of our Police Department,” said City Councilor Ed Flynn, one of several councilors who called for a hearing on the Boston Trust Act. “We can’t play politics with the public safety of our residents.”

Governor Maura Healey said separately the Trump administration’s threat to withhold federal funding “will hurt public safety and hurt law enforcement.”

“Cities and towns across Massachusetts rely on federal funding to keep their communities safe,” Healey said in a statement.

At issue is the city’s Trust Act, which has been likened to what are known as “sanctuary city” laws. Boston’s ordinance generally — in accordance with a state Supreme Judicial Court ruling — prohibits police from engaging in deportation efforts, which are a federal and civil matter. Wu and Cox have said city police regularly work with ICE and other federal agents on criminal cases, but they cite the state’s highest court ruling that it would be unconstitutional for city police to detain someone for deportation proceedings if they are not charged with a crime.

Trump administration officials have called on cities such as Boston to do more to assist their efforts for mass deportations, under the threat of federal funding and even criminal and civil charges for public officials who interfere with those efforts.

And following Wu’s testimony on Wednesday, Republicans on the House Oversight Committee released a statement saying that Congress must “not allow taxpayer funds to go to cities and states that prioritize criminal aliens over the American people.”

The vague threat of blocking federal funding to so-called sanctuary jurisdictions is not new — in fact the first Trump administration tried the same thing. Those effort mostly failed, as courts repeatedly blocked them on multiple grounds. In particular, the courts ruled it was unconstitutional for the administration to block all government dollars because of local policies on immigration, as the Constitution requires that such spending decisions be related to the policy at issue.

The one area where the administration had some limited success with the courts, though, was in law enforcement and public safety funding. Two federal appellate courts, including one that oversees Vermont, allowed the administration to place some requirements and incentives on Justice Department grant applications that penalized jurisdictions who failed to cooperate in some ways with federal immigration enforcement.

However, the appeals court that oversees Massachusetts and other New England states ruled that the funding cuts broke the law, leading to split decisions among appeals courts. The matter was never considered by the US Supreme Court because the Biden administration had reversed Trump’s policy.

There are some ways that this Trump administration could get away with restricting funding, said Bill Ong Hing, a law professor at University of San Francisco who studies the issue. The policy could withstand court challenge if Congress deliberately passes legislation that authorizes some restrictions on public safety funding, and if the Justice Department takes the proper steps to modify the grant requirements and give local jurisdictions adequate notice and consideration under the new rules.

“If they can get Congress to OK putting those conditions in and it’s some grant that’s associated with [immigration], I think that some court somewhere might go along with them,” Hing said. “I think that’s a gigantic if.”

Still, he said, the administration nor Congress would likely get away with blocking all funds to sanctuary cities, as that’s widely been found to be unconstitutional.

“That’s not going to work,” Hing said.

And Boston’s policy of not collecting information on people’s immigration status probably keeps them in compliance with a federal law requiring jurisdictions to turn over such information when asked. That law has in the past formed the basis of Trump’s efforts to target sanctuary city funding.

“There’s nothing in the law that says [cities] must ask about immigration status,” Hing said. “If that’s what the law said, then fine, but that’s not what the law says.”

Senator Ed Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat, also said any attempt to withhold federal funding for Boston would be met with a lawsuit that he predicted would be successful. But he told the Globe he wouldn’t be surprised if the Trump administration still tried “to engage in political theatrics.”

“It sounds like something that the crazies in the White House might want to do, but in practice, it becomes very legally questionable,” he said.

Still, the threat of funding cuts has thrown Boston’s Trust Act into public debate, as it did during Wednesday’s Capitol Hill hearing and again for a scheduled City Council meeting on Monday that is meant to “audit the effectiveness” of the act.

While federal grants are a small percentage of the Boston Police Department’s $474 million budget, those funds pay for programs that Cox describes as vital: DNA testing to solve cold murder and rape cases, anti-gang and anti-terrorism intelligence and hardening against nuclear threats, among others.

Last year, the Department of Homeland Security awarded nearly $12 million in Urban Area Security Initiative funds to promote security in Greater Boston, according to the state Office of Grants and Research. About $1 million of that money went to the Boston Police Department and another $1.9 million went to the Boston Regional Intelligence Center, which supports local anti-gang and counterterrorism operations.

“A substantial portion of our analytic capabilities are funded by the federal government through grants that are critical not only to public safety in Boston but to the entire Metro Boston region,” Cox testified about those grants to Congress in 2023.

Federal funding also supports private nonprofits that city leaders have described as key partners in reducing violence. Community Development Block Grants, funded by the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development, support job training programs for youth and recently incarcerated people.

For Stone House, a domestic violence shelter in Roxbury, those block grants pay for financial literacy programs that help survivors live independently of their abusers. Federal dollars support efforts to help clients find jobs, build credit, budget for their households, and locate stable housing, according to Stone House’s interim CEO Kathryn Fagan

“The loss of these funds would be devastating to our [domestic violence] clients and would set their goals of security and financial independence back immeasurably,” Fagan wrote in an email.

Another of those nonprofits is the Dorchester Bay Economic Development Corporation, which uses block grant funds to connect people returning from prison with job training, financial counseling, and stable housing, CEO Kimberly R. Lyle told the Globe.

“If this funding were eliminated, it would directly impact those efforts, making it harder for people to successfully reintegrate into the community,” Lyle wrote in a statement. “The bottom line is that cuts to federal funding wouldn’t just affect DBEDC — they would have ripple effects across Boston, the state, and the nation, limiting economic mobility, job creation, and community stability."

After that, Siddiqui, then mayor of Cambridge, did what she never imagined she would have to do: She called top city administrators and the school superintendent to begin the process of shutting down every school and municipal building in the state’s fourth-largest city.

“We all left that meeting terrified,” she said. “I remember saying, ‘OK, we have to shut things down. We have to stop the spread. I don’t want people to die.‘”

Five years later, Siddiqui is still torn about the implications of that decision. On that same day, Governor Charlie Baker declared a state of emergency in Massachusetts and, within days, suspended in-person learning at public and private schools and banned on-site dining at bars and restaurants across the state.

Knowing what we know now, she wonders, did public officials react appropriately? Did they adequately consider the trade-offs among competing values, including the devastating costs of closing schools, businesses, and places of worship?

Those questions remain as relevant now as they were in the spring of 2020. As a lethal strain of avian influenza (or H5N1) spreads from birds and mammals to people, the specter of another pandemic looms over the United States. Public health officials and epidemiologists are dissecting the dizzying range of responses to the COVID-19 pandemic — including the stay-at-home orders, school closures, and quarantines — to determine what worked and what didn’t.

A growing number of scientific studies have concluded the measures in the United States did little to slow the rampaging pathogen. What’s more, the stifling of public debate about them eroded trust in public health policy and prevented more effective strategies, according to a number of prominent infectious-disease experts.

While the scientific community is still divided over how effective lockdowns were, those who publicly criticized the measures during the pandemic have gained the political upper hand. Dr. Jay Bhattacharya of Stanford University, who co-authored a manifesto against lockdowns, is President Trump’s nominee to lead the National Institutes of Health, the nation’s largest funder of biomedical research with a $48 billion budget. And Trump’s health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has described lockdowns as an attack on the poor and middle class.

“We are long overdue for a reckoning on the lockdowns,” said Stephen Macedo, a political scientist at Princeton University in New Jersey, who co-authored a book due out later this month that calls for a national inquiry into the lockdown measures. “What’s become increasingly clear is that a lot of what we did was irrational and based on fear, and we didn’t think through the profound costs.”

Defenders of lockdown policies have argued that stay-at-home orders were among the few levers in the government’s pandemic toolkit, particularly before mass testing and vaccines were available. And a chorus of studies have found that, early in the pandemic, measures such as shutting schools and banning large gatherings did help suppress the virus’ spread in the short term — saving thousands of lives and preventing many hospitals from being overwhelmed.

“This revisionist history that says, `We could have done without the lockdowns,’ is dangerous,” said Dr. Nahid Bhadelia, founding director of Boston University’s Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases. “You would have faced even more deaths and even more hospitalizations in a shorter period of time, which would have debilitated our health care system.”

But while the impact of lockdown policies is still being studied, new research paints a troubling picture of the immense collateral damage inflicted by them.

The measures increased poverty and wealth disparities, spurred a dramatic rise in adolescent anxiety and depression, contributed to a surge in fatal drug overdoses, and led to devastating learning losses in schoolchildren, who have yet to recover, according to scientific studies. As of last spring, the average American student remained half a grade behind pre-pandemic levels in both math and reading, according to a recent report card on pandemic learning loss.

What’s more, months of unrelenting seclusion caused many people to sever social connections, with lasting consequences to mental and physical health. Both volunteering at nonprofits and church attendance, two measures of social engagement, declined and have not recovered to pre-pandemic levels. In 2023, the nation’s surgeon general warned of an "epidemic of loneliness and isolation" — brought on, in part, by lockdown measures that isolated people.

And that’s not counting the other costs in lost livelihoods, shuttered businesses, and the anguish of seeing relatives die alone without being able to say goodbye.

“The lockdowns were never really effective, and the confusion around them sowed a great deal of public distrust in government,” said Michael Osterholm, an infectious disease expert at the University of Minnesota.

On average, states with Democratic governors had stay-at-home orders that were nearly three times longer than those in red states. Yet many so-called blue states — including California, New York, and New Mexico — had among the highest COVID-19 death rates, measured as a share of their population. And some red states, including Idaho and Utah, had among the lowest, national health data shows, according to an analysis by Macedo and a Princeton colleague, Frances Lee..

Those critical of lockdowns point to sobering data showing that, despite widespread school and business closures, the United States had among the worst mortality rates in the developed world during the pandemic.

To be sure, a wide range of factors — including vaccination rates, population density, air pollution, and the age of the population — can influence differences in COVID-19 mortality rates, researchers note.

Infectious disease experts who are critical of lockdowns point to alternative approaches that would protect public health with less pain should another pandemic arise. These include more stringent testing of workers in nursing homes, more generous sick leave policies for workers, and efforts to expand home care and food deliveries for older people most vulnerable to the virus.

“You couldn’t witness the mass deaths in New York City and Italy and not think that something had to be done,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health. “But tools like shutdowns and school closures are sledgehammers and shouldn’t be part of our toolbox.”

The other problem with lockdowns, say many scientists, is they cannot be sustained indefinitely. And once they are lifted, people start interacting again and infections can spread rapidly. For instance, China’s abrupt decision in December 2022 to end its zero-COVID policy, which included stringent quarantines and lockdowns, led to a massive surge in hospitalizations and deaths in the following two months, according to a 2023 study in the medical journal JAMA.

Osterholm at the University of Minnesota has long recommended what he calls the “snow day approach.” When infections surge, or hospital bed capacity falls to unsafe levels, officials could announce temporary school closures and encourage people to stay home. Then, when the virus subsides, after a few days or weeks, the restrictions would be lifted, he said. People would be more willing to comply, knowing the closures are temporary, he argued.

“In defense of public health [officials], they were trying to manage so many unknowns,” Osterholm said. “It was like trying to perform brain surgery while you’re jumping out of a plane and the parachute wasn’t opening.”

Public officials should also communicate more clearly about the uncertain benefits of any measure during a pandemic, particularly when so much is unknown, public health experts said.

Indeed, in October 2019, the World Health Organization analyzed a range of responses to past pandemics, including the 1918 “Spanish flu,” and recommended against forced quarantines of individuals or populations, saying there was “no obvious rationale” for such measures and they were impractical to implement.

“From the beginning, the evidence to support lockdown policies was very, very poor, and there was a large sentiment within the scientific community that the collateral damage far outweighed the benefits,” Macedo, of Princeton, said.

In the bitterly polarizing climate of 2020, some scientists who spoke out against lockdowns in favor of less-restrictive measures faced a harsh backlash. Some even received death threats.

In one such instance, in October 2020, three medical experts from three renowned universities decided the public discussion about lockdowns had become too one-sided.

The trio — which included Bhattacharya of Stanford, Sunetra Gupta of University of Oxford, and Martin Kulldorff of Harvard Medical School — crafted a short statement opposing the lockdowns, arguing that there was no scientific consensus for school closures and other stringent measures.

“Keeping [lockdown] measures in place until a vaccine is available will cause irreparable damage, with the underprivileged disproportionately harmed,” the trio warned in the statement, which was named the “Great Barrington Declaration,” after the town where it was written in the Berkshires.

Kulldorff said he was not prepared for the visceral response. Within days, he began receiving anonymous death threats via email and accusations that he supported mass murder. Facebook deleted a page set up by the scientists, and Kulldorff’s Twitter account was suspended.

Dr. Francis Collins, the former head of the National Institutes of Health, wrote an email at the time to Dr. Anthony Fauci, then director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, in which he called for a “quick and devastating published take down” of its premises, according to emails obtained by the American Institute for Economic Research, a free market think tank.

Three years later, Collins said in a public forum that lockdowns caused widespread harm to public health and the Great Barrington Declaration could have been a “great opportunity” for a broad scientific debate about lockdowns. Collins, who recently retired from the NIH, declined to be interviewed.

Fauci did not respond to multiple interview requests.

To the dismay of some public health advocates, there has never been a public reckoning over the lockdown measures.

Robert Moffit, a senior research fellow at the conservative Heritage Foundation, said Congress should appoint a bipartisan commission with subpoena power that would investigate the extent of the harm caused and why alternative points of view were silenced.

“We need to know why all these federal health agencies failed to respond to the latest science on lockdowns,” Moffit asked.

Even some who supported the lockdown measures five years ago are now doubtful they were worth the long-term costs.

Nate Dube, 53, of Dorchester, was initially relieved that schools and businesses were closed. Dube has spinal muscular atrophy, a rare muscle-wasting disease, and is more susceptible to respiratory illnesses. He also lives a block away from a now-shuttered facility, Carney Hospital, that in May 2020 became the nation’s first hospital dedicated to treating COVID-19 patients.

Each day, ambulances carrying infected patients rushed by the window of his apartment in Dorchester.

He recalled being so paranoid about getting infected that he washed down his groceries and was afraid to open his mail.

But as the months of seclusion passed, he ached to see friends and began to miss the sounds of children playing outdoors.

“Early on the lockdowns felt like a lifesaver,” Dube said, “but then they just went on too long.”

Siddiqui, now a Cambridge city councilor, said a key lesson from the pandemic is that public leaders be honest about what they don’t know — and not create false hopes. “We made the best decision we could with the information we had at the time,” she said. “But we can’t go on pretending like there wasn’t an impact from the lockdown, even if it’s hard to reflect on it now.”

No one — including the neighbors — is questioning the value of the proposed Neighborhood Birth Center. Birth centers provide prenatal, childbirth, and postpartum care in a more homey setting than a hospital, with midwife-centered care that prioritizes natural birth options and fewer medical interventions. Birth centers have been shown to have positive outcomes for women at a lower cost than hospitals. The Legislature recognized this when it passed a bill last session making it easier for birth centers to open, with better-tailored regulations and a framework to license certified professional midwives.

Today, the state’s only operating birth center is in Western Massachusetts, after centers on the North Shore and in Cambridge closed.

A maternal health clinic that is culturally and racially sensitive could also address disparities in maternal health, with statistics showing that Black women are nearly twice as likely as white women to die during pregnancy or within one year postpartum. Neighborhood Birth Center executive director Nashira Baril said the center expects 50 percent of patients will have Medicaid; staff will be multilingual and reflect community demographics; and the center will commit to training student midwives. Around 300 babies a year would be born at the center, which would serve 1,000 families annually with clinical care and programming.

“This birth center is a life-saving investment in our families, ensuring more individuals in our community can give birth safely, with dignity, in an environment that reflects their values and their culture,” state Senator Liz Miranda, who represents Roxbury, said at a zoning board hearing. Miranda told the editorial board she wants the center in Roxbury so it can serve the people of Roxbury, a low-income community with poor birth outcomes. According to a 2023 Boston Public Health Commission report, Roxbury has high rates of preterm births and low-birth weight births.

The proposed site, at 14 Winthrop St., is in the heart of one of Boston’s predominantly Black neighborhoods, near public transportation, and less than 10 minutes by ambulance to Boston Medical Center if a patient needs an emergency transfer. Project organizers say they prefer a residential environment to a storefront since a birth center should provide a home-like feel.

One factor that adds complexity is the birth center partnered with five other nonprofits to buy the property. Sisters Unchained, Matahari Women Workers’ Center, Center for Economic Democracy, Movement Sustainability Commons, and Resist all plan to colocate there. Baril said the partnership was necessary to make the finances work. While neighbors have legitimate concerns about allowing an office building to replace a residential property, the nonprofits — all of which do work in Boston — have responded by scaling back an earlier proposal. The current proposal is relatively modest: 10,550 square feet across two floors, with green space and 11 parking spots. The first floor would house the birth center, and the five nonprofits are expected to employ about 15 staff, with gathering space for around 35 visitors.

The main argument against the center is the neighbors would prefer housing. The plan calls for demolishing one single-family home and one three-family home. Both were built in the mid-1800s. Both are vacant, one deemed structurally unsound.

“Who wants to live across the street from an office building? We’re a neighborhood,” neighbor Nadine Riggs told the editorial board.

While the parcel is zoned residential, the neighborhood is mixed. There are two schools and four churches within a couple of blocks, and the site is steps away from a laundromat, which is on a commercial street that also has a barber shop, public library, and Boys & Girls Club.

City officials received around 100 letters opposing the project and more than 350 supporting it, with opinions split among immediate neighbors and elected officials. Ultimately, the zoning board split, with four members supporting the project and three opposing it, with five votes needed for approval.

The project is not about gentrification but about providing needed services to the local community, and the nonprofits have shown a willingness to work with neighbors on project size and details. The zoning board should reconsider and approve the project. If it doesn’t, city officials should work closely with the birth center to expeditiously find new land that meets its needs.

The Mayers family thanked the Boston Police Department’s homicide unit in a statement describing Mayers as a “beloved son, brother, uncle, pastor, and community leader.”
