For months, scores of parents and educators have protested the proposal and staged demonstrations outside schools. On Tuesday, dozens marched around district headquarters in Roxbury and demanded the School Committee leave the schools open and preserve the communities — teachers, students, and staff — inside those buildings.

“We ask you and we implore you, do not take the school away from us,” said Zoila Alvarado, a teacher at the Dever school, during Thursday’s meeting.

BPS administrators have said the buildings are not capable of offering a full range of student services, including special education inclusion, and most have too few students for the size of their buildings. They also do not have enough room to provide a high quality student experience, which includes physical spaces that support learning and are accessible to all students, according to the district.

More than a third of students affected by the proposed closures and merger are multilingual learners, according to Delavern Stanislaus, the district’s chief of capital planning.

“Closing these schools will create pathways for students to transition into schools that are more fully enrolled, with more resources, and offering a higher-quality student experience — often closer to home,” Stanislaus said in a memo to the School Committee earlier this month.

During a January School Committee meeting, administrators said they intended to close about one-fifth of the district’s school buildings by 2030, and have the goal of moving their students into larger buildings that can better serve their needs.

The proposed rollback of buildings comes as the district expects enrollment to level off over the rest of the decade after it had dropped for several years. Enrollment in 2030 is expected to be around 47,000 students, which is about 3 percent less than now.

Superintendent Mary Skipper said the closures and merger approved Thursday will save the district about $20 million, which will be reinvested into schools and classrooms.

On Thursday night, the sole vote against the plan was by School Committee member Rafaela Polanco Garcia, who argued that the district should preserve the schools and their communities.

“It is my position today to encourage you — let’s keep fighting, let’s keep working together,” Polanco Garcia said in Spanish through an interpreter.

Several of her fellow board members, including Stephen Alkins, appeared to be grappling with the issue shortly before voting for the school closures and merger. Alkins acknowledged that the decision was tough.

“The data and the research does show that closures negatively impact student outcomes and performance,” Alkins said. “That same research also shows that when you move students to higher quality educational opportunities, you actually see them perform better.”

A few minutes earlier, a few dozen parents and educators addressed the Committee, calling on them to leave the schools alone.

Among them was Yanery Diaz, whose son attends Dever. She praised the work of educators and staff at the school, and the strong communication the school maintains with families.

“The Dever community is a very united community with a lot of humanity,,” Diaz said in Spanish through an interpreter.

Dermot Kiernan, whose children attend the Clap school, said the school’s teachers are committed to their community, and make students and families feel like they belong.

“ We prefer to stay at the Clap,” Kiernan said.

But not all speakers favored keeping the buildings as they are. Nachelle Gordon, the head of Excel High School, said she supported closing the school.

“As long as the district supports the transition of every student, staff, family member, and community partner, I’m at peace with the closing,” Gordon said.

Maria Barbosa, whose child attends the Clap school, said she supported the merger, but hoped the current faculty are included in the transition.

“We we would love to see our faculty move forward with us,” she said.

Stanislaus noted there are other schools in the district that meet the same criteria for closures and mergers, but did not name them.

Skipper told School Committee members in January that announcing proposed school closures too early would have a detrimental effect on those communities. Students and staff wouldn’t choose that school, and cause a “drain down” of that school, she said.

Boston is one of the safest big cities in the country, and today’s numbers are only a fraction of what the city saw in its darkest eras in the early 1990s, when the city counted more than 100 murders a year. But local advocates said today’s citywide statistics, though worth celebrating, can hide a tragic reality: that in Boston, gun violence is deeply local. It occurs block by block, person to person. It often stems from gang rivalries and social media feuds, and then from retaliation when the victims or their loved ones seek revenge.

And it means that neighborhoods such as Meetinghouse Hill, whose largely Cape Verdean community has long been afflicted by gun violence, can feel left behind, even as the city becomes safer overall.

“It’s great that stats are down across the city — but not necessarily for the entire city,” said City Councilor John FitzGerald, who represents the area. “We could be doing a lot more, because hurt people hurt people.”

Fitzgerald pushed for more resources and welcomed a recent increase in police visibility in the neighborhood.

Mayor Michelle Wu, who celebrated the city’s historic decline in murder rates at a press conference at the end of 2024, said she recognizes that some neighborhoods are still suffering.

The city is dedicating personnel and money to violence prevention in Dorchester and Meetinghouse Hill, Wu’s office said in a statement. Those initiatives include direct outreach to previous perpetrators of violence, collaboration with neighborhood associations, grants to neighborhood violence prevention groups, and programs targeting Dorchester’s Cape Verdean community.

“Any incident of violence in our city is one too many and leaves lasting trauma on those impacted, so we will not be satisfied with anything less than ending violence in our neighborhoods,” Wu said in a statement.

Boston ended last year with 24 homicides, its lowest number in 67 years. Wu said the city is not taking a “victory lap,” but that the statistics validate years-long efforts to improve the city’s data collection, police recruitment and retention, youth job programs, and community safety initiatives geared toward young people.

At that December press conference, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said: “In the entire time that I’ve been a police officer, going back since when I came on, the city has never been safer, period, when it comes to crime, particularly violent crime.”

But the climb in murders in Meetinghouse Hill shows that those trends can vary, depending on where you live. Homicides in Dorchester’s C-11 police district, which includes Meetinghouse Hill, increased from five to seven last year. Those increases in homicides occurred even as overall safety in the area improved, according to data provided by Boston police.

Meetinghouse Hill is one of Dorchester’s oldest neighborhoods. Behind the historic First Parish Church sits the Mather School, the oldest public elementary school in North America. It is home to a predominantly Black and mixed-race population, according to census estimates. Immigrants, including many from Cape Verde, the Dominican Republic, and Vietnam, have built communities here, making homes in triple-deckers on one-way streets lined with ash and linden trees. From atop the hill, Ronan Park looks out over Dorchester Bay.

Residents there have also struggled economically. A report from the Dorchester Bay Economic Development Association describes the area as “one of the poorest neighborhoods in Boston.” And residents have seen repeated tragedies.

Last year, there were three fatal shootings within a quarter mile of First Parish, a center of Dorchester’s civic life for 350 years.

On a recent afternoon, Maria Hernandez walked her two young children from school to the Ridgewood Street triple-decker they call home. Next door, two months ago, Kareem DaVeiga Booth, 20, was shot dead. No one has been arrested in the case.

Hernandez didn’t witness that shooting, she said, but she’s heard others.

“I’ve lived here two years, and I hear gunshots on different occasions, but I never know where or what’s going on,” Hernandez said in Spanish. “I stay in my house with my children.”

Clementina Chéry, the founder of the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute, a nonprofit that advocates for peace on Boston’s streets, lost her son to gun violence in the neighborhood three decades ago. She said the persistence of violence and the way it is discussed frustrates her.

There’s a shooting, then press conferences, news articles, and promises to redouble antiviolence efforts. Those initiatives are important but they are not enough, she said.

“Homicides are still happening,” she said. “People are still dying, and it’s not private death, it’s public death. And so for us, even in the midst of our pain, we want to shift that narrative.”

Finding solutions can be difficult. For Chéry, it means creating neighborhoods where violence is not just prevented, but peace is actively created, Chery said. Until that happens, she said, reductions in violence will always be at risk and leave some parts of the city behind.

“We want to celebrate, yet tell a mother whose child was murdered and tell a mother whose child is being arrested by the police that this is a safe community,” Chery said. “When we stop the violence, what do we put in its place? Because the violence is going to come back.”

On a recent Wednesday, a dozen members of the Meetinghouse Hill Civic Association gathered for their monthly meeting at First Parish. They listened as officers from Dorchester’s C-11 district listed recent crimes in their neighborhood, watching for patterns and trends.

The Boston Police Department has deployed officers to the neighborhood in “Community Interaction Teams,” which emphasize walking the beat, public visibility, and talking to community members, Boston police spokesperson Mariellen Burns wrote in a statement.

“For any resident or neighborhood touched by violence, we understand that statistics can’t capture the full picture of what their experience is.” Burns wrote. “We work daily to prevent violence when possible and respond to it when it occurs, and our partnership with the community is a critical part of this work.”

Residents have noticed the increased police presence and appreciate it, said Fitzgerald, the area’s City Council member.

“The response to that has been great,” he said. “The visibility is higher.”

Jones, the civic association president, said she has noticed the added patrols and credited the department with keeping the community informed.

“They’re just not riding by being visible in their vehicles,” she said. “They’re actually stopping, they’re getting out and participating. It makes a big, big difference.”

But, she said, it still doesn’t feel like enough. More foot patrols, perhaps. More police presence.

“I do feel like we’ve been left behind,” Jones said.

The Thursday night series at Long Live Beerworks, running for just over a year, has become a hotbed of jazz in Boston, helping fill a void created by the retrenchment of the area’s top jazz clubs.

The Regattabar and Scullers once packed patrons into their hotel jazz clubs six nights a week. Like everything else, they closed when the pandemic hit, and they’ve never fully returned, hosting shows only two or three nights a week these days. Both clubs showcased local acts early in the week, but no more. Ryles Jazz Club, a popular spot for local jazz musicians, closed in 2018.

That’s not to say jazz has disappeared from Greater Boston. Wally’s Jazz Cafe on Mass. Ave. is going strong after 78 years, providing Berklee College of Music students with a spot to workshop. The Lilypad in Inman Square has a full calendar of local and national jazz musicians. The Mad Monkfish in Central Square and The Beehive downtown showcase local jazz talent.

But something special is happening in Roxbury, and it started because Michael Feldman wanted to see live jazz and bring new life to his neighborhood.

“Roxbury and jazz,” he says, “they just go together.”

Feldman is the CEO of Feldman Geospatial, a company that was founded by his grandfather in 1946 as a land surveyor and has grown into a high-tech construction engineering firm.

In 2016, Feldman Geospatial bought into the former home of the Boston Piano Co., a three-story brick factory in disrepair. Feldman rehabbed the 162-year-old building, moved into the top two floors, and now rents the bottom floor to Long Live Beerworks, a brewery that started in Providence and operates its second taproom here.

Feldman, who grew up listening to the Brazilian and Afro-Cuban records his father played at home, says he dreamed of bringing music into the Hampden Street building and initially thought he would try to recruit Berklee students to perform. But it became apparent he could think bigger.

In January 2024 he began hiring local jazz groups to play on Thursday nights — Feldman’s firm pays the musicians, even though they bring business to the brewery — and started with a trio led by bassist John Lockwood. Three weeks later Lockwood was back with The Fringe, saxophonist George Garzone’s trio that has been playing around Boston since 1971.

“Boston’s in bad shape,” Lockwood says, referring to the jazz scene. “When I first came here, there were all kinds of clubs here — stuff in Boston, stuff in Cambridge. It kind of fizzled out, and when the pandemic hit it got kind of weird.”

The Long Live jazz series has “snowballed,” he says, thanks to the strong lineup, free admission, easy parking, and great beer.

“Boston needs places like this,” says Lockwood, who is a bass professor at Berklee.

Sue Auclair, the longtime Boston jazz publicist, happened to come to one of those first shows. Lockwood introduced her to Feldman, and soon she was marketing and promoting the series.

Feldman and Auclair say they have been pleasantly surprised by how easy it has been to lure musicians here.

“We’re booked for the year already,” says Auclair, who has done publicity over the years for Scullers, the Newport Jazz Festival, Miles Davis, and countless other jazz venues and artists.

Long Live’s 2025 lineup is a who’s who of Boston jazz, with a particular focus on Latin jazz. The next shows feature singer-pianist Zahili Gonzalez Zamora (March 27), Brazilian mandolinist Ian Coury’s quartet (April 3), Israeli pianist Alon Yavnai (April 10), keyboardist Matt Jenson (April 17) and Puerto Rican saxophonist Edmar Colón (April 24). The Fringe has more gigs here, the next one being May 22.

Alex Alvear has three shows booked in May with different lineups, including his Boston-based Latin ensemble Mango Blue. Feldman saw that band years ago, became a fervent fan, and flies Alvear in from Ecuador to perform at Long Live.

“What Mike is doing is exceptional for a city that has lost its way when it comes to appreciation for live music culture,” says Alvear, who came to Boston in 1986 to study at Berklee and spent nearly 30 years here before moving back to Ecuador in 2015.

By organizing and funding the music series at Long Live, Feldman is doing “something absolutely out of this world for the Boston music scene,” Alvear says.

“The scene was really literally dying in Boston,” he says from his home in Ecuador. “I was heartbroken when I found out that all of these really emblematic music venues had been dying and closing. The city, when I arrived in the ‘80s, was full of music. Live music was an essential component of the city’s identity.”

Feldman wants to make it part of Roxbury’s identity. The potential effect on this part of town is as important to him as is the music.

“Kids who live in this neighborhood don’t always feel good about their neighborhood because of the way people talk about Roxbury,” he says. “I really hope that we impact this neighborhood.”

Bailey lives in the neighborhood herself, just a few blocks down the street. She came to Boston from New York in 2000 to teach at Berklee, where she is assistant chair of the guitar department.

She started coming to Long Live on Sundays for the beer and now performs in the room.

“Look at this space,” Bailey says. “It’s a beautiful space. There are cool people who come here, and the beer is great.”

Most of the seats are occupied by the time her quartet launches into “Old and Young Blues,” a medium-tempo bop tune she wrote. It’s an appropriate song: A young couple, clearly on one of their first dates, chat near the back of the room, while an older couple pay strict attention to the musicians. A middle-age woman taps her toes alone to the rhythm, and a group of five professionally dressed women sip beers at a hightop.

For two and a half hours on Thursday evenings, this is in fact a jazz club — a big, jolly room on the ground floor of a building that had sat derelict for years, used as storage for old vehicles and construction equipment, now alive with A-list music and friends.

“It’s just good for our community,” Feldman says. “It’s good for our spirits. It’s something that’s needed.”

When I contracted bronchial pneumonia at age 4, my fever soared so high she dipped me in an ice bath. At 8 years old, I came down with viral pneumonia and she introduced me to breathing exercises with a spirometer. Later that same year, lobar pneumonia struck, so she guided me to the edge of the bed, belly down, allowing postural drainage to flush my lungs.

“You’re my best patient, John,” she told me. After she splurged on a stylish camel-hair coat to keep me warm, I imagined myself her only patient.

The physical and emotional stress and strain of nursing took the best of my mother’s health. Over the years she developed diabetic retinopathy, underwent heart bypass surgery, and suffered a compression fracture in her spine. Through it all, my father, Paul Maddock, remained by her side, until his unexpected passing in 2010. Unable to drive, shop, cook, or organize medications for herself, assistance resulting from my father’s military service was just enough to afford us what many families can’t manage. Single with no children, I left the workforce to be her at-home caregiver.

Before switching to modern devices, we relied on the same tools she’d used with me. She taught me to shake down the mercury in an under-the-tongue thermometer; what to listen for with a stethoscope pressed to her chest, abdomen, and back; how to feel her pulse with two fingers on her wrist while following the second hand on a watch; and when a blood pressure cuff was pumped to exactly the right level.

“Nurses call them vital signs for a reason, John.”

Perhaps she was preparing me for the inevitable when sharing stories about the joy, commitment, and sorrow inherent to her field. On New Year’s Day 1967, her picture appeared in the newspaper for the annual first baby born in Boston: “A TIE,” the caption read, between the St. Margaret’s infant and another newborn at St. Elizabeth’s Hospital. During the Blizzard of ’78, she shuttled to work up the steep climb of Jones Hill in a snowplow truck. And all manner of life-and-death situations nurses everywhere know too well.

Time grew precious when I had to accept the limits of at-home care. The tiniest cut, while on a blood thinner for a congestive heart, hemorrhaged, masking an aggressive UTI. Her temperature plummeted. Renal failure and debilitating dialysis soon followed. After a decade in my care, in the midst of the COVID pandemic, emergency care at the Beth Israel Deaconess Hospital – Milton became the mercy of comfort care at South Shore Hospital. She was 88.

The last time my mother saw home, if given the gift of reprieve, we would have resumed our journey. The sun beckoning and so her vision more favorable, she would have asked me to take her for another “ride down memory lane.” To the house in West Roxbury where she was born; to Roslindale where she was raised, learned to ice skate on Fallon Field, and met my father; along the scenic byways of the South Shore where she had lived.

We would have done so together, anticipating our return, optimistic that we still had some control over the wheel.

Confession time: I wrote this newsletter from a place that is not Boston.

I’ll be there soon, it’s true. But I’ve felt some self-consciousness about writing about a city before actually moving there. Don’t worry: I’m no stranger. Growing up in Maine, I visited Boston often as a kid, and lived there for a year before college. Still, I’m anxious to get to know it better.

So to help me get a jump start, I reached out to elected officials, business and community leaders, university presidents, sports figures, and other influential Bostonians for recommendations. I asked them to tell me something they’ve read, eaten, heard, seen, or visited that helped them get to know the city they inhabit. Today’s newsletter shares their responses.

I often understand a place better when I read about it, and several people I reached out to recommended books.

Gayatri Patnaik, the director of Beacon Press, suggests “Dark Tide,” about a 1919 industrial accident that flooded the North End with millions of gallons of molasses, killing 21 people.

Jessica Tang, who leads American Federation of Teachers Massachusetts, recommends “Chain of Change,” a 1981 book about Boston’s Black communities by Mel King, the late activist and community leader. As WBUR has reported, book clubs across the state still read his book.

If you prefer fiction, Governor Maura Healey admires the novels of Dennis Lehane, a Boston native “whose deep connection to the streets of Boston shines through in his storytelling.”

Tiya Miles, a Harvard historian, recommends “Contending Forces,” a 1900 novel by Pauline Hopkins about Black Bostonians struggling to escape the legacy of slavery. “Walking the streets with Hopkins’s characters brings historical Boston to life and also reveals the existence of a color line,” Miles told me.

Boston is synonymous with American history.

James Rooney, president of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, recommends the Tea Party Museum, where you can walk the decks of full-scale replicas of the ships that helped spark the American Revolution — and even toss crates of tea into the harbor.

Marcelo Suárez-Orozco, the chancellor of UMass Boston, recommends reading the Declaration of Rights in the Massachusetts Constitution, which established fundamental freedoms and was a model for the US Constitution.

But the city didn’t stop making history in the 1700s. Mayor Michelle Wu recommends the City of Boston Archives, which contains documents, photos, blueprints, and maps that offer glimpses of the city over centuries. As Wu wrote, “We may think of history in grand moments captured in books and movies, but there’s also magic in feeling the yellowed pages of real life.” You can browse the archive online or visit the Mary C. Beaudry Community Archaeology Center in West Roxbury to see artifacts in person.

If museums and archives sound too dusty, try getting your history on Instagram instead. Vickie Alani, a senior principal at CBT Architects, recommends streetscapecurator, an account that features commentary about Boston’s many historic buildings.

Boston boasts more than a dozen art museums, but several people pointed me to the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. Even if you’ve already been, as I have, museum director Peggy Fogelman suggests taking another look at an 1888 portrait of Gardner, the collector who started the museum. “Mrs. Gardner’s bare arms and a plunging neckline sparked salacious rumors among her contemporaries,” Fogelman wrote.

The museum, which the eclectic Gardner designed to mimic a Venetian palace, is itself a work of art. In the atrium, “soaring glass ceilings and immaculate, lush gardens reflect the passionate vision of a woman ahead of her time,” Susan Goldberg, the president of GBH, told me. “Sitting in the garden,” says Matthew Teitelbaum, who directs the Museum of Fine Arts, “restores the soul.”

Others suggest going outside. Lee Pelton, who runs The Boston Foundation, recommends The Embrace, a bronze sculpture on Boston Common that honors Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King, who met in Boston. (The foundation helped install it.)

Instead of feasting your eyes, maybe you’re just looking to feast.

Alex Cora, the manager of the Red Sox, praised chef Massimo Tiberi’s award-winning Arya Trattoria in the North End as his favorite go-to spot in the city. Other diners spotted there include Melissa McCarthy and the Rock.

For something lower-key, David Nagahiro of CBT, the architecture firm, recommends Bow Market in Somerville, which features shops and dining around an open-air courtyard.

For an auditory experience, Sally Kornbluth, MIT’s president, recommends the Boston Pops, an orchestra that performs both classical and popular music. “They’re a great mixture of playful and serious — sort of a good microcosm of Boston,” she says. Upcoming shows include a screening of “Jaws” accompanied by a live performance of the iconic score and a sold-out event featuring Cynthia Erivo, the star of “Wicked.”

So yes, the numbers back her up. Compared to other cities of its size, Boston does have a lower incidence of violent crime. But statistics alone don’t capture the full picture of public safety. Crime data is an average, a broad measure that can obscure the vastly different realities people experience across neighborhoods.

Boston may be the safest major city in the nation, but it depends on where in the city you live.

That’s something Megha Vadula, a young professional who moved with her family from Jamaica Plain to Dorchester, has learned firsthand. I initially heard from her a little over a year ago, shortly after she moved. She emailed me in response to a column I wrote about the normalization of crime in certain areas of Boston, including Hyde Park, my own neighborhood.

Vadula agreed; she was struck by the stark differences between JP and Dorchester. “We have heard very close gunshots at least three times since moving,” she said back then. But the way people treated gunfire in Dorchester felt different — no one really batted an eye. What’s shocking isn’t just the violence itself, but how routine it’s become for residents.

I wanted to get Vadula’s take now, especially since the mayor is taking pride in the city’s safety record. She told me her neighborhood still experiences public safety issues, including a couple of shootings near her house in Ashmont Hill in December, which left her and her family stressed.

That’s why Vadula challenges the idea that one set of statistics can accurately reflect the on-the-ground perspective of people across all neighborhoods.

“The statistics cover the entirety of Boston,” she told me this week. “That can be a little disingenuous sometimes. Because from a street corner in Back Bay, it’s really unfair to tell someone who lives in another neighborhood, ‘Hey, you live in the safest city,’ when you know that your data is being averaged with someone else’s.”

In fact, Vadula went on, “data is a way to start a conversation. It’s not a solution.”

Her observations speak to a broader issue of perception and policy. While the city celebrates declining crime numbers, it must also address the disparities in safety that exist from one neighborhood to the next. “Everyone deserves the same sort of level of comfort and safety in their city,” Vadula said. But right now, that sense of security is not evenly distributed across Boston’s communities.

Crucially, Vadula doesn’t feel like Wu is doing anything wrong by touting the mantra of Boston being the safest major city. “I do think that’s an achievement,” she told me. “But there is more to do.”

Nor does she believe the answer is increasing police presence in her neighborhood. Instead, Vadula stressed the need to bring nuance into this conversation. “A lot of times these are crimes of poverty, in some ways,” she said. The problem with crime data being touted without context, Vadula said, is that oftentimes that “paints a picture of certain areas of the city as… ‘that area,’ and that creates its own cycle of disinvestment.”

In other words, when a neighborhood becomes synonymous with crime in the public imagination, it can lead to fewer resources, lower property values, and a reluctance from businesses and institutions to invest in the community. This, in turn, deepens the very conditions — poverty, lack of opportunity, inadequate services — that contribute to crime in the first place.

All the same, the block-by-block safety disparity raises difficult questions. What does it mean to live in the safest major city when your block still feels unsafe or is a hot spot? How do officials ensure that citywide progress doesn’t mask neighborhood-specific challenges? Addressing these questions requires more than policing and crime stats — it requires investments in community engagement, infrastructure, and long-term solutions that make every resident feel as safe as the mayor’s numbers suggest.

Wu’s claim about Boston’s safety is true, but for many, it’s not the whole truth. And until every Bostonian can experience that safety for themselves, the work remains unfinished.

A pair of retired professional dancers brought their ballet — and some valuable lessons — into a Boston neighborhood Sunday.

Families, arts organizations, and locals gathered in Chez Vous Roller Skating Rink in Dorchester for the opportunity to learn choreography from Renee Robinson and Amos Machanic Jr., who formerly performed with the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater.

The two dancers spent the weekend leading community workshops in the city’s neighborhoods of Hyde Park, Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester. At their free public events, Robinson and Machanic taught the choreography for iconic late dancer and choreographer Alvin Ailey’s “Revelations,” his best known ballet.

Accompanied by percussionist Roderick Jackson, Robinson and Machanic patiently took an enthusiastic crowd of children, teens, adults, and seniors through the three soulful acts of “Revelations,” set to passionate spirituals that the performers could sing along to.

As they demonstrated the evocative movements, Robinson and Machanic also shared historical facts about Ailey’s inspirations for “Revelations,” rooted in his experiences growing up in Black churches in Texas. When the afternoon drew to a close, Machanic awarded T-shirts and prizes to participants who could recall some of these facts.

The dance theater and Boston arts nonprofit Celebrity Series have been in partnership for nearly 60 years, but this year is the first to see more than one community educational event, according to Shaumba-Yandje Dibinga, founder of OrigiNation Cultural Arts Center in Boston and program manager for the “Revelations” event.

“We normally do one, but we did four this year,” Dibinga said. “Renee and Amos are legends. They led three back-to-back workshops yesterday and their energy never changed, they’re spectacular.”

The addition of three community events meant that around a thousand people in total were able to attend, Dibinga said.

Machanic said that hosting more events meant fulfilling the vision of Ailey himself, who believed “dance came from the people and that it should always be delivered back to the people.”

Courtney Boston, the event’s emcee, emphasized the importance of hosting these workshops in predominantly Black neighborhoods of greater Boston.

“We didn’t want to have these events in Seaport or anywhere that our people might not have access to,” Boston said. “We’re right here in our neighborhoods and our backyards.”

Boston was pleased by the event’s inclusivity of people from all walks of life, including those with dance backgrounds and those without.

“It was awesome. There’s people being centered in Black culture today, using music and dance and arts to bring people together,” she said. “I’m not a dancer, but they had me moving.”

Now, parents, policy makers, and health providers are holding their breath as Republicans in Congress weigh potentially billions of dollars in cuts to Medicaid. Federal dollars pay for more than half of MassHealth’s $20 billion annual budget.

“MassHealth is a cornerstone for children’s health in Massachusetts,“ said Katherine Howitt, director of the Massachusetts Medicaid Policy Institute, an independent policy analysis program of the Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts Foundation.

The consequences of significant cuts to Medicaid, and the potential for voter outrage, have some doubtful Congress will ultimately cut from the public insurance program.

The information coming out of Washington is too vague to act upon, said Mike Levine, assistant secretary for MassHealth.

“We do not have specific contingency plans around what services we offer kids and what we might do if Congress or CMS takes actions we don’t like,” he said in an interview Monday.

Still, the possibility frightens Bernard. When her daughter, Victoria, was 2, before doctors had figured out what prescriptions and dosages would best control her epilepsy, she routinely had multiple seizures a week, her mother said. The child’s speech is delayed, but with the therapy MassHealth pays for, she is learning to express herself verbally.

“Without MassHealth I don’t know how I would do,” Bernard said. “I’m very concerned about it.”

Congressional Republicans have said they want to balance tax cuts by, in part, eliminating $880 billion in federal spending over 10 years. Leading Republicans, including President Trump, have said that won’t include cuts to Medicaid benefits. US House Speaker Mike Johnson has said his party is seeking only to reduce “fraud, waste, and abuse.”

But experts on health policy say there’s no way Republicans can achieve their budget goals without impacting Medicaid. At more than $600 billion a year, the program is among the federal government’s largest expenses.

“We know that the only way to achieve $880 billion in cuts is through catastrophic cuts to the Medicaid program as we know it,” said Megan Cole Brahim, a Boston University professor and co-director of the school’s Medicaid Policy Lab. “There’s really no way it wouldn’t have harmful implications for children.”

Massachusetts expanded MassHealth in 2006 to include children in households earning up to 300 percent of the federal poverty level, extending coverage to more children than in all but a few states.

As of 2023, only 0.6 percent of Massachusetts children were uninsured, according to a report from the state Center for Health Information and Analysis on insurance coverage in the state.

The state’s post-pandemic review of MassHealth eligibility led to about 363,000 people removed from membership last year, including almost 59,000 children ages 17 and younger, the state reported.

Even if Congress took a hatchet to Medicaid, Cole Brahim said she anticipated Massachusetts would seek to protect children from the brunt of the consequences. Officials could be forced to reduce access to some optional benefits, such as physical therapy, case management, and community health workers, and could reduce the kinds of prescription drugs, or the dosage amounts, covered by MassHealth.

Losing even partial Medicaid reimbursements would be devastating to community health centers and hospitals. On average, the health centers receive about 31 percent of their revenue from MassHealth, according to the Massachusetts League of Community Health Centers. MassHealth paid about 18 percent of all hospital revenue in the state as of 2022, according to the Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts Foundation. Boston Children’s Hospital reported roughly 46 percent of its Massachusetts patients are MassHealth members. Substantial cuts to Medicaid, hospital officials said, would create financial aftershocks that would affect every patient in the hospital.

“The danger for any children’s hospital in the country, [if] you start cutting Medicaid, you’re going to affect care delivery for every patient,” said Joshua Greenberg, Boston Children’s vice president of government relations.

On Monday, Governor Maura Healey and her partner, Joanna Lydgate, toured Children’s to highlight how potential cuts to Medicaid, as well as halts to millions in National Institutes of Health research grants, could affect patients. Kevin B. Churchwell, the hospital’s president and chief executive, said federal funding cuts have already disrupted clinical trials and research, including work with vaccines.

“We have patients in clinical trials who had their treatments stop because of this,” Healey said. “Can you imagine the cruelty of that?”

Among the groups Medicaid supports, including seniors and some people with disabilities, children are a relatively inexpensive clientele. They account for about 16 percent of the state’s total MassHealth expense. The families of some children enrolled also have private insurance but rely on MassHealth as secondary coverage to help with medical-related bills their insurer doesn’t cover.

For many children, MassHealth membership means more than covered doctor visits. The program pays whatever is needed to ensure children with disabilities have the equipment, care, and support they need. It allows children to receive Medicaid-covered services through their school’s health services and pays for behavioral health care in the community or home.

In addition, families on MassHealth get screenings to identify dental, aural, visual, or developmental concerns. Such wide-ranging and widely accessible insurance coverage can benefit children their whole lives. Children with good health care do better in school, a 2021 Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts Foundation report stated, and those with access to Medicaid tend to have fewer hospital stays, emergency room visits, and chronic conditions in adulthood.

Victoria Bernard’s doctor, Laura Livaditis, director of pediatrics at Mattapan Community Health Center, said about 90 percent of the children treated at the center are enrolled in MassHealth. Most of her patients are also from families living at or below the poverty line. MassHealth’s wide-ranging coverage has helped them to avoid evictions, she said. And for immigrants, the program has helped them make connections to ensure they have stable food and housing.

“I’m continuously impressed with the breadth and depth of services MassHealth covers for my patients,” Livaditis said. “I can’t remember the last time I had to fight with [MassHealth] insurance for needed services.”

The recent reports of Columbia University’s capitulation to the Trump administration’s demands in order to secure federal funding should worry everyone who values academic integrity (“Columbia yields to Trump’s demands,” Page A1, March 22). This decision raises questions about the role of elite institutions in the safeguarding of principles of higher education. The Ivies, with their immense resources, alumni networks, and powerful platform, have a responsibility to lead in this moment. Instead of individual acquiescence, these institutions should issue a joint statement reaffirming their unwavering commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion and their unyielding protection of freedom of speech.

If the Ivy League schools fail to stand firm, they risk eroding foundations of academic inquiry, research, and open discourse. Their collective voice would reach far beyond their campuses and would offer cover to smaller, more vulnerable colleges and universities. History will judge the Ivies by their courage to defend the principles of intellectual freedom. A coordinated, inspiring message from these institutions would not only protect their own integrity but also send a powerful signal to the nation that the pursuit of knowledge and the values of inclusion are not negotiable.

Howard owns 617 Defense, a company that offers firearms training throughout Greater Boston. He’s also president of the Massachusetts chapter of the National African American Gun Association, an organization that boasts 45,000 members nationwide, nearly half of them women. And he’s one of several local Black entrepreneurs serving a growing market niche: Black people who feel the need to arm themselves.

Greater Boston is famously safe compared with other US metro areas. But not quite safe enough for Howard — or his students. He warns the students that 911 is not enough, that it generally takes 10 or 15 minutes for the police to arrive.

“You are your own first responder,” Howard said. “No one’s going to save you. You’re going to save yourself.”

Despite a high level of gun violence in many Black communities, Black people are much less likely than white people to own guns. A 2024 study from Pew Research found guns in only 34 percent of Black US households compared with 49 percent of white households.

The ownership gap might be due in part to a history of racist efforts to keep Black people disarmed. After the Civil War, for instance, many Southern states made gun ownership illegal for Black people. And even where it was legal, Black people often faced unjust discrimination and were not allowed to obtain gun permits. When Martin Luther King Jr.’s home was bombed in 1956, he requested a gun permit to defend his family. But authorities in Montgomery, Ala., refused.

But there’s evidence that more Black households are arming up. After the 2020 murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer, the National Shooting Sports Foundation reported a spike in gun purchases by Black people. The organization’s latest survey finds that African Americans comprise 32 percent of people who’ve taken up shooting in the past five years, the biggest increase of any demographic group.

Howard said he’s seen rising attendance at his classes, which he began teaching three years ago. He said he believes the root cause is declining trust in government.

“People are taking control of their own lives and doing what they have to do for protecting themselves and their family members,” Howard said. “They’re making their decisions, instead of waiting on the government to help them out.”

Howard is a vocal opponent of laws limiting gun ownership that were enacted in Massachusetts last year. He keeps a loaded pistol on his hip and said law-abiding people of every race should always be ready to defend themselves.

You’ll hear the same sentiment from Howard’s friend and business competitor Antonio Miles, a Black New Hampshire resident who runs the training companyUrban Shooting Experience. A former car salesman who grew up in Roxbury, he first took up arms out of concern for his family.

“My ‘why’ is my three daughters,” Miles said. “I wanted to be able to defend my family by any means necessary.”

He also sees himself as a role model.

“I wanted to bridge a gap on people who look like me teaching about firearms,” Miles said.

Both Miles and Howard offer gun classes to men and women of all races, but they primarily cater to gun-curious African Americans.

It all makes perfect sense to Nicholas Johnson, a Black man who teaches law at Fordham University in New York.

“I grew up in Black gun culture,” Johnson said. “I grew up in rural West Virginia; everybody had guns.” But as a young faculty member, he felt a chill in the air whenever he discussed the Second Amendment.

“If you were a good liberal and had a good social conscience you were supposed to be anti-gun,” Johnson said. “And I wasn’t.”

Years later, Johnson co-authored what he believes to be the first academic textbook devoted to US firearms law. He’s also written “Negroes and the Gun,” a book about how Black people have a long history of relying on personal firearms for defense against racist mobs and criminals.

Meanwhile, Johnson said, there has historically been “tremendous bias in enforcement” of gun laws in the United States. For instance, in 2018 the US Sentencing Commission found Black people were far more likely than white people to be convicted of illegal gun possession.

“We end up with gun control policy that operates in a kind of perverse intersection of the interests of white liberals and white conservatives,” Johnson said. Conservatives dislike gun laws, Johnson said, but don’t mind them being used to lock up Black men; liberals want fewer Black people in prison but are happy to see brisk enforcement of the gun laws.

But instructors like Howard and Miles might help break the cycle by ensuring that Black gun owners know the rules. Both teach a two-hour basic firearms safety course certified by the National Rifle Association. It’s just the first step in getting a Massachusetts firearms license. Each person must also get a “license to carry” issued by their city police department.

One of Howard’s students, sixty-something and retired, already owns several guns and is now interested in making it legal. Others are first-timers.

“When I was in my early 20s, I was grazed by a gun,” said Jermaine McNeill, 46, of Dorchester, a housing inspector and podcaster. “I had friends of mine who were shot with guns. So I just had a fear of them.”

McNeill had a change of heart after he interviewed Howard for his podcast.

These days he’s convinced that gun ownership makes sense, and not just for himself.

“My daughter is 15 years old,” he said, “and I told her, whether you like it or not, when you get older, you’re gonna learn how to shoot.”

Also in attendance were attorney Rochelle Jones, 34, of Randolph and her 32-year-old schoolteacher brother Marcus Jones of Weymouth. Both are interested in personal protection, but Rochelle Jones said gun ownership is frowned upon by left-leaning people like herself.

“I’m not thinking too much of the stigma,” she said, adding, “It’s there, sure.”

Marcus Jones said he wants to dispel the stereotype of Black men as trigger-happy killers.

“I know going forward that I can be a model to show people that we are responsible about this,” he said, “and it’s not just always the negative stuff you see in the news.”

The training is over in two hours, and not a shot is fired. For that, they’ll have to sign up for the two-day basic handgun course, featuring a trip to a gun range. Howard also teaches rifle, shotgun, and even a course called “Stop The Bleed” that teaches lifesaving measures for people who’ve taken a bullet.

“All the Black instructors I know say some of their students, they had friends who got shot,” Howard said. “They didn’t know how to save their life.”

But for Howard, all his courses are about saving lives. He said crime-ridden Black communities will become a lot safer when a lot more of their law-abiding residents have guns and know how to use them.

“To the average person who lives in the suburbs, it doesn’t seem right to them,” Howard said. “But have them trade places.”

“Mer-cee bo-coop!” he concluded, gamely, for a nice applause.

And then the real campaigning began. Kraft smoothly wound through the narrow gaps between the tables, greeting each of the hundred or so attendees individually, shaking every hand, and dropping to one knee for extended conversations with seated guests, like a man about to propose.

Campaigning for government office is personal, intimate, tactile. But, no one in Kraft’s famous family has opened themselves to scrutiny in quite the way a political campaign demands.

Josh, 57, the third of the four sons of billionaire businessman and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and his late wife, Myra, is the first in his family to run for office.

But Boston politics is one arena that has confounded the Krafts in the past. In a failed attempt to win support for a South Boston football stadium in the late 1990s, for instance, they showed a knack for stepping on rakes and angering the community.

If Josh Kraft can solve that puzzle and become mayor, the amount of local influence concentrated under one family name would be unprecedented.

So unprecedented that it’s fair to ask: Is that too much power for one family?

“When I’m mayor of Boston,” Josh Kraft said, in answer to that question, “my number one priority is going to be the people of Boston.”

It speaks to their incredible influence in Boston that many of those close to the brothers personally or in business declined to talk for this profile of Josh Kraft and his three brothers — even other wealthy and powerful people who are fans of the family. One went to comic lengths to elude an interview. “Totally off the record?” this Kraft associate said. “They’re wonderful people.”

It is not just the Patriots that make the Krafts so influential. Robert Kraft bought the team for about $172 million in 1994, then the highest price ever for an NFL franchise. League revenue has since exploded; what Kraft paid for the team now buys about a three-year contract with a good veteran quarterback. With a current estimated worth of $7.4 billion, the Patriots are the sixth most valuable sports team in the world, according to Forbes.

The eldest Kraft brother, Jonathan, 61, is president of the holding company for the family’s many businesses, employers of 9,500 people in industries such as paper and packaging, sports and entertainment, construction and real estate development, and venture capital investment. He represents the Patriots in NFL league matters and shares the title with his father as investor/operator of the New England Revolution soccer team.

He is also chairman of the board of Massachusetts General Hospital, a top position at one of the state’s most important institutions.

Daniel, 59, the next eldest, is president & CEO of International Forest Products, one of the paper companies that built the family’s wealth, and which has quietly grown into a massive enterprise — the fifth largest exporter in the United States, according to the Journal of Commerce.

Josh’s campaign résumé is built on decades of community work that affected thousands of children. He was hired by a South Boston nonprofit shortly after college to do outreach to prevent kids from dropping out of school. In 1993, he was brought in to build up and run the Chelsea Boys & Girls Club, and then in 2008 became CEO of Boys & Girls Club of Boston, a job he held for 12 years. Until recently he was president of the New England Patriots Foundation.

David, 53, and the youngest, worked for the family business until leaving around 2012, according to news articles of the time. He maintains a minimal public profile, though in a short interview with the Globe, David spoke highly of his brother’s qualifications for mayor.

A fifth brother, Joseph, born between Josh and David, died as an infant shortly after his birth.

Josh Kraft, who is divorced with adult daughters, would say little about his kids for the sake of their privacy. It’s a sharp contrast with his likely opponent, Mayor Michelle Wu, who this month brought along her infant daughter, Mira, when Wu testified before Congress, and whose family story has long been an intimate part of her identity as a candidate.

But few things are more destructive to privacy than a political campaign: Voters want to know a candidate’s origin story, which begins with how they were brought up, and with whom.

To understand how the Krafts grew into a powerhouse, you have to go back 50 years, to Chestnut Hill. Before Josh, the closest anyone in the family came to seeking public office was when Robert Kraft, then in his late 20s, was chairman of the Newton Democratic City Committee. He considered running for Congress in 1970 against incumbent Democrat Philip J. Philbin. But Kraft, who had young kids by then, passed on the race, in part due to the loss of privacy that comes with a run for high office.

He excelled in business. His father-in-law owned a paper company, Rand-Whitney, that Robert Kraft ultimately took over and grew; he also founded International Forest Products, in 1972. It would be another couple decades before he bought the Patriots, a move that launched the family into an era of fame and enormous wealth the sons have enjoyed as adults.

Before that, they were more of a prototypical breed of Boston affluence, a family known for their gaggle of boys who loved sports and excelled in the finest schools, each taking on the type of distinct roles that often mark large clans.

Jonathan and Daniel Kraft declined to be interviewed for this story, either about their childhood or their family now.

As an adult, Jonathan is familiar to Patriots fans for his conspicuous seat next to his father in the owners’ box during games. He is known as acerbic, a keeper of grudges who does not suffer fools easily, and has bawled out reporters on occasion for writing things he didn’t like.

People who know him well praise his intellect, discipline, meticulous preparation, and charitable instincts, which tend toward the realm of health care. “Jonathan is the smartest, most driven person I’ve ever met in my life,” said a powerful friend of the family who knows them personally.

He is most like his father from a business standpoint. “Jonathan worships his father,” said another family friend, who knows them through business. “Worship is not too strong a word for the relationship.”

Married with grown children, Jonathan can speak extemporaneously on a wide array of topics, from finance to rock music; in an interview with a podcast dedicated to the Australian rock band AC/DC, Jonathan named all five band members and recounted a good bit of their history off the top of his head.

From an early age, he gravitated to the world of business. As kids, “I remember playing Monopoly with Jonathan and he’d always crush me,” Josh Kraft recalls. “I had to mortgage everything.”

Jonathan went to high school at Belmont Hill, a private boys-only prep school, where he was president of the student council his senior year. The boy he beat in the election, Robert Ricciardelli, recalls finishing second to Kraft.

“I was well liked and I was running on being a likable person,” Ricciardelli told the Globe recently. “Jonathan was determined to do stuff.

“He was 10 years ahead of everyone else. I think this is because he grew up watching his father do deals in business. He knew the politics of it, understanding what people want.”

Ricciardelli became Kraft’s vice president. The major achievement of their administration was a new school rule exempting seniors who maintained high grades from taking their final exams.

“That was Jonathan’s big push,” Ricciardelli said. “The argument was, if you keep your grades up, you don’t have to take your final exam,” as an incentive to avoid the “senior slump,” when kids already accepted to college tend to slough off.

Ricciardelli, who also knew Daniel and Josh as kids, said that from the outside, the Kraft boys seemed a cohesive bunch.

“The dynamic I saw was that they had no conflict,” he said. “Maybe that’s because Jonathan was expected to be the heir apparent and Danny never had a problem with that. Josh wasn’t interested in [running the business] and went his own way. They each had their own lanes.”

Daniel Kraft, also married and with grown children, followed his big brother to Belmont Hill, and then went to Tufts University, where he played lacrosse, which remains one of his passions. He has promoted the sport in Israel with such zeal that the country’s top players train at the Daniel Kraft Family National Lacrosse Center. He is known as an easy-going person who gives off normal-guy vibes.

“Jonathan is a little intense; Danny is the guy you want to hang out and have a beer with,” said a friend who got to know them as adults.

Dan Kraft was part of a group of business, labor, and government leaders who worked to find the money to dredge Boston Harbor and open the port to greater commercial shipping, said Tom Glynn, former head of the Massachusetts Port Authority. In 2016, the group put Dan’s affable persona to use, when it invited then-US Secretary of Transportation Anthony Foxx to Boston for a briefing on the dredging project, looking to earn some federal grants. As the local team had hoped, Dan Kraft and Secretary Foxx hit it off personally.

“That was fortunate,” Glynn said. “And we got $42 million.”

Foxx, now co-director of Harvard Kennedy School’s Center for Public Leadership, recalls the briefing and meeting Dan Kraft for the first time. The pair got along well and talked sports, as mutual fanatics.

“Somebody like Dan clearly had a great head start in life and sometimes people who do are not relatable,” Foxx said. “But he’s not that way. He’s easy to talk to and has a grip on regular-people stuff.”

If Jonathan and Dan are their father’s kids, attuned to the world of business, Josh and younger brother David are their mother’s, say people who know the family well. Myra Kraft, who died of cancer at 68 in 2011, treated philanthropy as an occupation. “She got up every day wanting to give her money away,” said one friend.

Like most of his brothers, David Kraft was schooled at Belmont Hill, where he was on the varsity wrestling team. He went to Columbia College in New York, as his father did, and then Harvard Business School. A Globe article in the early 2000s said that David worked in media and technology for Kraft Group investments.

But later articles reported that David Kraft left the family business around 2012, apparently after an undisclosed dispute with his father. His public persona largely disappeared. David Kraft, it appeared, was done with life in the Boston spotlight. “He tries to live as anonymously as a person can with the Kraft family name,” said a family friend.

Josh Kraft would say little about David. They stay in touch and “have a good relationship,” he said. Campaign finance reports show that David Kraft in February donated $1,000, the maximum allowed, to his brother’s campaign.

In a short telephone call with the Globe, David wholeheartedly backed Josh’s run for mayor. “He’s been dealing with Boston city politics for many years in his position with the Boys & Girls Club,” he said. “He knows Boston well. He has unique gifts and is a genuinely altruistic person.”

As far back as high school, Josh took a different path from his brothers. He was the only one not to attend Belmont Hill, and instead went to The Rivers School, a private prep school in Weston. It simply felt like a better fit. “I do a lot by feel and intuition,” he said. He went to Williams College, and then spent a year as an intern teacher at a private school. He liked helping kids. “I wanted to keep doing that but I wanted to do it in a different venue,” he said, which led him to community work.

One of the people Josh Kraft helped in his work, Abens Maurice, temporarily moved back to Boston from California when he learned Kraft was running for mayor, to help with the campaign. They first met around 1990, when Maurice was 12 and living in South Boston. Kraft helped him navigate school, relationships, conflicts, racism — Kraft’s influence on his life is almost too great to measure, he said.

“Josh has been my counselor, my big brother, my dad — whatever you want to call him, he’s my man,” said Maurice, now 47.

Josh Kraft, who moved to Boston from Newton in 2023, said he wouldn’t be running without what he learned from Bostonians along the way, and from his brothers. Yet when he announced his campaign, asking the voters to grant him the vast powers of mayor, he pleaded for people not to prejudge him by his influential family name.

Why?

“I read some of the comments — ‘Oh, rich kid … What does he know?’ ” Kraft explained.

He repeated the “rich kid” dig several times, as if it was a slur, seeking to refute it.

“I know I’ve been in a room with a kid breaking down … about seeing his parents shot in front of him. I’ve had experiences like that many times. I think I understand.”

Focus on what he’s done, Kraft asks, not what he came from.

“I guess I was pleading with people: Take the time, ask around about me. Hear about me. Because you’ll hear it.”

Josh Kraft, the longtime nonprofit leader and son of New England Patriots owner Robert, is the first member of his family to seek elected office. If he succeeds in unseating Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, it would concentrate a huge amount of local power in the hands of a single family.

Yet that family remains something of a black box. Josh’s three brothers, billionaire father, and their associates are private and tight-lipped. So my colleague Mark Arsenault decided to spend a few weeks reporting on the family. He interviewed Josh, watched him campaign, and spoke to people in the Krafts’ orbit.

Here are five takeaways from Mark’s story.

People who know the Krafts say that Josh, Robert’s third-born son, philosophically resembles his philanthropic mother, Myra, who died of cancer in 2011. “She got up every day wanting to give her money away,” one friend told Mark.

Josh, 57, spent a year teaching after graduating from Williams College, which cultivated an interest in helping children. He later worked to prevent kids from dropping out of school at a South Boston nonprofit, led the Boys & Girls Club of Boston, and helmed his family’s charitable foundation. “He has unique gifts and is a genuinely altruistic person,” said Josh’s brother David, 53, who left the family business more than a decade ago and has donated to Josh’s mayoral campaign.

Their older brothers, by contrast, gravitated to the family business. Jonathan, 61, is president of the Kraft Group holding company and sits next to his father at Patriots games. Daniel, 59, runs a subsidiary paper company that is now the country’s fifth-largest exporter.

Chief among them are deep pockets and a moneyed network. Robert Kraft’s net worth is nearly $12 billion (although state campaign finance laws regarding immediate family members prevent him from donating to or leading any super PAC supporting his son’s campaign, according to my colleague Shirley Leung). The family’s businesses employ nearly 10,000 people. And Josh’s eldest brother, Jonathan, is chairman of the board of Massachusetts General Hospital, a leading state institution.

Those connections already seem to be helping. A Globe analysis found that Josh’s campaign raised 2.5 times as much money last month as Wu’s did. But most of that came from donors outside Boston, including the owner of the Los Angeles Chargers.

The Kraft family is largely new to electoral politics. It came closest when Robert chaired the Newton Democratic City Committee in his 20s. That inexperience has sometimes been a hindrance. In the 1990s, Robert failed to convince residents — or then-Mayor Tom Menino — to build a 69,000-seat football stadium in South Boston.

Robert also has a decades-long friendship with President Trump, which seems unlikely to endear Josh to most Bostonians. The elder Kraft said last year that the friendship ended after the Jan. 6 Capitol attack. But Trump recently named Robert’s second wife, Dana Blumberg, to the board of the Kennedy Center in Washington.

Josh has also had to rebut suggestions that he’s merely a wealthy dilettante. “I read some of the comments — ‘Oh, rich kid … What does he know?‘” Josh told Mark. He says he advises voters to “take the time, ask around about me. Hear about me.”

He may be a neophyte, but he appears to have a knack for pressing the flesh. Mark describes how Josh navigated the room during a recent campaign stop in Dorchester, shaking hands with each attendee and kneeling for longer conversations with seated guests.

His work has also inspired loyalty. Abens Maurice met Josh more than three decades ago as a 12-year-old Black kid growing up in South Boston. Josh helped him deal with school, relationships, and racism. “Josh has been my counselor, my big brother, my dad,” Maurice, now 47, said. When he heard Josh was running, he moved back to Boston from California to help.

Josh is divorced and won’t talk much about his adult daughters. His elder brothers also declined Mark’s interview requests. They may have inherited an instinct to dodge the public eye. Ensuring his family’s privacy was one reason Robert passed on running for Congress in 1970.

Josh has made a different choice. Yet despite his famous last name, he remains politically unknown to many Boston voters. Trying to fix that could strain his family’s inclination to stay behind the scenes. As Mark writes, “Few things are more destructive to privacy than a political campaign.”

Suffolk Construction’s Pat Lucey has helped to oversee some of the most prominent towers to go up around Boston lately. You name it: Millennium Tower, Winthrop Center, the Encore Boston Harbor casino. He’s been at the helm. His most complex project today? The skyscraper rising above South Station.

But now, after about 20 years with the company, Lucey will have an even broader landscape to oversee. Suffolk chief executive John Fish has promoted Lucey to the position of general manager of the Boston construction company’s Northeast region, an area that includes all of New England and much of upstate New York. While Suffolk has been growing significantly outside of Boston for years, the Northeast region still represents the company’s largest division based on revenue.

Lucey was previously an executive vice president, overseeing certain sectors of work in the Northeast: commercial real estate, public schools, energy, and transportation projects. With this promotion, he adds higher education, life sciences, and health care.

Lucey has essentially grown up in the firm, ever since his days as quarterback for Williams College’s football team. Like Fish, Lucey went to high school at Tabor Academy, a private school in Marion. He began interning at Suffolk while in college, and came to work there full-time after graduating in 2008. Among his early roles: assistant to the CEO, in which he worked closely with Fish and attended high-level meetings at the company.

“Pat’s been like a son to me,” Fish said. “He has sat in just about every seat on the bus. He understands the building business and the construction business from the ground up. What he learned very quickly is, it’s not about building buildings, it’s about building people.”

Fish said Lucey’s promotion followed the relocation of his previous boss Jeff Gouveia, who had been the Northeast GM, to the Southeast market, based in Miami. While Fish has no intention of retiring anytime soon, he said Lucey reflects the next generation of leadership at the company.

Lucey said Suffolk’s culture — a hard-driving one, with a focus on teamwork — is one big reason he has spent his entire career there.

“I’ve had an opportunity to really grow in my career, learn so much,” Lucey said. “What I’m really looking forward to is to continue to work with some amazing people [and] looking to grow our existing client base.”

O’Brien, 61, is expected to be accompanied at his announcement by his wife, Tricia, and several of their children — all of whom were adopted from Colombia, Ecuador, Guatemala, and Ethiopia, according to people briefed on his plans. He has chosen a location in East Boston, a neighborhood that has been dubbed Boston’s Ellis Island for its rich history of welcoming immigrants. He also spent years in the neighborhood building community support for his Suffolk Downs project.

O’Brien has assembled a team of senior advisers and is currently polling Boston residents about issues such as residential property taxes, Boston Public Schools, and fiscal spending.

O’Brien would be Wu’s second notable Democratic challenger in this year’s mayoral race, after Josh Kraft, a longtime nonprofit leader and son of billionaire Patriots owner Robert Kraft, officially tossed his hat in the ring on Feb. 4.

Like Kraft, O’Brien is well known in Boston’s civic and business arenas, though neither has held elected office before. O’Brien grew up in Scituate and Andover and now lives in downtown Boston. His brother, Bill O’Brien, is head football coach at Boston College.

There will be a preliminary round of voting in September, with the two highest vote-getters advancing to a runoff in November.

O’Brien and Kraft both have ties to Boston’s business community and would likely be battling for similar contingents of voters: residents who are dissatisfied with Wu’s leadership of the city and have concerns about slowed housing development, longstanding challenges in Boston Public Schools, and her management of the city’s budget. But O’Brien’s decision to jump into the race could be an indication he senses vulnerabilities in the Kraft campaign.

Wu has been enjoying a groundswell of political support after she defended Boston on the national stage earlier this month. Wu and three other liberal city mayors testified before a Republican-led congressional committee on their cities’ policies related to public safety and cooperation with federal immigration enforcement efforts. Wu’s performance on Capitol Hill drew praise and attention from Boston residents and through national headlines, for her poise in the face of attacks from Republicans and for landing several return shots of her own.

She went on to take a victory lap in her third annual State of the City address last week, and with an appearance on national television, joining host and stand-up comedian Ronny Chieng as a guest on Comedy Central’s “The Daily Show” this week.

But deep frustration with Wu has been building among the city’s powerful real estate industry over her increasing of affordable housing requirements and green housing codes for new buildings, as well as her yearlong battle to temporarily shift more of the city’s property tax burden onto commercial real estate to blunt tax increases for homeowners and residential landlords.

Many in the real estate industry earlier this month expressed surprise O’Brien would consider running against Wu. HYM has active projects before the city right now, and the Wu administration has frequently called on O’Brien to support its policy initiatives that have been unpopular among developers.

HYM, which O’Brien founded, is an influential real estate development firm that has shepherded some of the city’s most high-profile, complex projects through Boston’s oft-bemoaned development review process. HYM partnered with NB Development Group, the real estate arm of footwear giant New Balance, in developing the nearly 2 million-square-foot mixed-use Boston Landing campus on the Allston/Brighton border, and also kicked off the 45-acre former NorthPoint development — now called Cambridge Crossing — in Cambridge, Somerville, and Boston.

As part of a decade-long re-do of the old Government Center Garage, HYM also developed the two skyscrapers just outside Boston City Hall: the new headquarters for State Street Corp. at One Congress and luxury condominium tower The Sudbury, where the O’Briens own a unit.

O’Brien recently was credited with directing affordable housing funding from The Sudbury to the newly opened 3368 Washington St. housing project in Jamaica Plain, a permanent supportive housing community for formerly unhoused people run by the Pine Street Inn. O’Brien sits on the Pine Street Inn board and attended the project’s ribbon-cutting, where Wu spoke; Kraft was also in the audience.

But many HYM projects are in varying states of delay at the moment, amid financing challenges and a difficult building environment. Work at Suffolk Downs, the massive redevelopment of a former horse-racing track on the East Boston-Revere border, has paused. And P3, a long-planned mixed-use project on Tremont Street in Roxbury where HYM and My City At Peace hold development rights, has not yet broken ground.

A youth summer jobs fair run by the mayor’s office was canceled on Saturday after a fight broke out among student attendees, Boston police said.

At 12:55 p.m., Boston police received calls reporting a fight at the Reggie Lewis Track and Athletic Center in Roxbury. Two units responded and requested backup to help disperse the crowd, Officer Mark Marron said in a phone interview. No weapons were found at the scene, and no injuries were reported.

Over a thousand teenagers flooded the area outside the center Saturday afternoon, including many who never made it inside the packed fair. Some students came dressed in suits and ties, many bringing their parents along and protecting printed resumes from the rain, volunteers at the fair said.

Boston City Councilor-at-Large Erin Murphy was at the fair when she saw “large groups of youths congregating without clear direction, leading to multiple fights,” she wrote in an emailed statement to the Globe. An off-duty officer intervened before police arrived.

“Notably, there was an absence of Boston Police details, leaving the venue’s security personnel overwhelmed when altercations erupted,” Murphy wrote, adding that overcrowding was also to blame.

The Youth Summer Jobs and Resource Fair aimed to connect thousands of Boston youth between the ages of 14 and 24 with over 200 employers, according to a press release for the event. The fair was part of Mayor Michelle Wu’s Youth Job Guarantee, which promises a summer job to any eligible Boston Public Schools student who wants one. Last year, a record 10,427 young people were hired, according to the mayor’s website.

A city spokesperson said in an email on Saturday that turnout at this year’s jobs fair broke that record.

“We’re grateful to all the employers and families who participated in the fair and thankful to our community partners and first responders for their presence and immediate response to ensure that everyone was safe. BPS support services will be following up with the students and school communities involved,” the spokesperson wrote.

Said Ahmed, a coach at Boston United Track Club who is campaigning to represent Roxbury on the City Council, had been at the Reggie Lewis Center since 7 a.m. for team practice before working at the track club’s table at the fair. Less than an hour before the fight broke out, he posted to Facebook encouraging young people to come out to the event.

“I thought it was a beautiful thing. A lot of young people, a lot of great staff — staff that have done a lot of organizing, a lot of hard work, a lot of time put into it,” Ahmed, 43, said.

Ahmed left shortly before the fight, but said that more schools and community centers should host job fairs to prevent mixing students who may have ongoing conflicts and make the mayor’s program more accessible to students who live far away from the Reggie Lewis Center.

Jonathan Dykes was at the jobs fair recruiting students for a sports camp at Roxbury’s Tobin Community Center, where he works as a gym director. He returned to the center — just a few blocks down the street from the track — shortly before the fight.

Dykes said the “downfall” of the event was allowing students to wear ski masks. Organizers instructed attendees over the microphone to remove their masks a couple of times to no avail, Dykes said. He estimated that he saw around seven masked students during the two hours he was there.

“Sometimes coming from different areas, these kids don’t know who these kids are, these kids don’t know who these kids are,” Dykes, 38, said. “It shouldn’t matter, everybody should be safe in one building.”

Dykes hopes that the city will reschedule the event, especially for the students left out in the rain. “You can’t judge it off of one little fight,” he said.

Thousands gathered at the Islamic Society of Boston Cultural Center in Roxbury on Sunday for Eid-al-Fitr, celebrated by Muslim’s around the world to mark the end of Ramadan.

Throughout the morning, over 2,000 people circulated the mosque which hosted four prayers starting at 7:00 a.m. They prayed, ate, and greeted one another. After each prayer, the traditional “Eid Mubarak” echoed through the crowd as families and friends exchanged warm wishes.

Abeeda Hussain, 23, came to the mosque with her mother and said the true spirit of Ramadan comes from wanting the best for others, not just oneself. Despite fasting’s challenges, Hussain emphasized the importance of the community experience.

“Fasting is difficult, but we’re here together, and we get through it together,” she said.

For Hozifa Yagoub, 22, a Boston University health science major, the end of Ramadan brings a sense of accomplishment and joy.

“It’s like a reward after the 30 days of fasting,” Yagoub said. “Everyone’s happy that it’s over, but it’s also a celebration of everything we’ve endured together.”

Matenneh Bayour, 34, a nursing student at Quincy College, said Ramadan is not only about fasting but also about building spiritual discipline.

“It’s one of the five pillars of Islam,” said Bayour. “You fast for 30 days, abstaining from everything, and this time is also about sharing moments with family and friends.”

While fasting may be the most visible aspect of Ramadan, many Muslims, like Ammar Elawad, 20, a health science student at Northeastern University, view it as a spiritual test that extends beyond food and drink.

“Fasting is the easiest part,” he said. “The hardest part is abstaining from everything worldwide — maintaining a higher consciousness.”

Elawad said that Ramadan is not only about abstaining from physical needs but also about reflecting deeply on one’s faith.

“It’s about asking yourself, ‘Why do I pray? Why do I believe in God?‘” he said.

Hannan Nur, 16, a student at the John D. O’Bryant School of Mathematics and Science, said the month provides a deeper connection to the struggles of others.

“It gives Muslims the experience of what less fortunate communities feel,” she said. “It’s a time to believe in God, to feed someone, and to reflect on the blessings we have.”

Rukia Nur, 23, who graduated from Northeastern last May, said that Ramadan provides a much-needed pause from the chaos of everyday life.

“Our lives are very hectic, and Ramadan helps us cut down on distractions like social media,” she said. “It’s a time for repentance, for change, and for focusing on our spiritual journey.”
