Methodology: To arrive at this annual list, we relied on the finite — but meaningful — wisdom of supply and demand: Significantly increasing prices in these communities are a signal that many buyers are eager to call them home. We analyzed median home prices from 2019 and 2024 to find the biggest five-year increases across three price tiers for each region. In the Boston suburbs, we looked at single-family data from The Warren Group, excluding communities with fewer than 50 sales in 2024. For Boston and Cambridge neighborhoods, we used median home price data — including both single-family and condo sales — from Redfin. Three journalists with real estate expertise collaborated to select our “May We Suggest” entries, our admittedly subjective picks of communities to consider.

“This contract affirms our shared commitment to strengthening teaching and learning, supporting our educators, and building a bright future for every BPS student,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement released shortly after the committee’s vote.

While the City Council must still approve the agreement, district administrators and union representatives said it would raise the wages of some of the district’s lowest paid workers, like classroom paraprofessionals, and guarantee additional staffing for inclusive classrooms with large numbers of students enrolled in special education.

It would also eliminate a requirement that general education teachers obtain a license so they can work with students with disabilities.

“Our district has dedicated public servants on all sides of the [negotiating] table who care deeply about our students and equally understand the importance of our work,” Superintendent Mary Skipper told School Committee members.

Under the terms of the agreement, Boston Public Schools’ teachers, who earn an average of about $120,000, would receive between a 9 percent to 11.5 percent pay increase over the three-year agreement.

Classroom paraprofessionals, who on average earn about $45,000, could see a dramatic boost in pay of about 30 percent over the period. Staff like health paraprofessionals and family liaisons, who earn an average of about $59,000, would see a 12 percent raise.

Sign language interpreters, who earn an average of $63,000, would get a roughly 9 percent raise.

The new agreement is retroactive to Sept. 1.

Lou Mandarini, a senior adviser for Wu who served as part of the district’s negotiating team, said a key initiative was raising the salaries of the city’s lowest-paid workers.

“Over the decades, [contracts have] just given a straight percentage, whether you make $120,000 a year or you make 40 and frankly, that’s something that we’ve sought to correct,” Mandarini told the School Committee. “And the opportunity to do it in the largest collective bargaining agreement in the city is a major win for us” and school employees.

Under the contract, classes with special education students will have new requirements. Inclusive pre-K classrooms will be limited to 15 students. In kindergarten through Grade 6 classes with large numbers of students with individualized education plans, teachers will have the help of another educator.

Additional special education teachers will be assigned to classes in Grades 7 through 12 that have more than eight students with IEPs.

Caitlin Gaffny, a representative of the Boston Teachers Union, praised the new contract, and said it would stabilize staffing in schools and reduce vacancies. By eliminating the dual license requirement, teachers won’t be overwhelmed doing two jobs at once.

“There will be supports for students with disabilities in general education classrooms,” she said. “There are many other improvements which will increase staff well being and allow for a more sustainable career in Boston Public Schools.”

Under the contract, the total cost of union pay would increase by $181 million over three years. That hike is 28 percent more than the $141 million increase included in the last contract, which was reached in 2022. The district did not provide the total cost of the contract.

However, according to the district, the total cost of union salaries under the new contract’s first year in fiscal 2025 would be $815 million. That figure would grow to $843 million in fiscal 2026, then reach $868 million by fiscal 2027.

The union contract would be a sizable chunk of the district’s budget. Last month, the School Committee approved a $1.6 billion budget for fiscal 2026.

To help fund the contract, the School Committee is seeking supplemental budget appropriations from the City Council, including $33.3 million in fiscal 2025 and $55.9 million for fiscal 2026, according to the district’s chief financial officer, David Bloom.

The council must still vote for that additional funding, a decision that could come in May.

Martha M. Walz, the interim president of the Boston Municipal Research Bureau, has raised concerns about the size of the contract’s cost, and focus on wages rather than student outcomes. It appears to do little for English learners, who make up roughly one-third of Boston’s 48,000 students, she has said.

“As BPS stakeholders consider the contract’s substantial costs, the touchstone must be whether and how the contract will lead to improved academic outcomes for Boston’s students,” Walz said in a statement last week. “It is not clear how the limited changes included in the contract will drive improvements in teaching and learning.”

One part of the book that Lobenstine invented was her character’s job at the Globe. She made up that detail, she says, “because it’s such a Boston story and I’m a huge fan of the Boston Globe.” In reality, she adds, “probably the Barking Puppy is the biggest paper I’ve worked at, besides my fourth-grade newspaper.”

When Lobenstine decided to write a children’s novel about their adventures, the real Sophie, now a student at Emerson, jumped right in. “She’s so creative,” says Lobenstine. “I talked to her a little bit about it, and then we decided to do an artist retreat — some friends of ours own a farm in Vermont and they invited us to come. I was working on the book and she was really into being a filmmaker in high school so she made these two short documentaries. She continues to be this amazingly creative person and I’ve seen her really come into her own.”

“The Barking Puppy” is meant to entertain and delight, like any other middle-grade novel — Lobenstine says she was “just smitten with how fun the story could be” — but the author also hopes it inspires its readers, if not to start their own newspapers, to at least “lean into their passions.”

“I wanted the book to model a lot of different ways to be yourself,” she adds, “and to show how a community can be a place where we have room for each other, where we hold each other up.”

Lori Lobenstine will read at 6 p.m. on Thursday, April 24, at the Frugal Bookstore, 57 Warren St., Roxbury.

And now for some recommendations ...

Lydia Millet is one of our finest fiction writers, a cool chronicler of an overheating planet and a master at melding history in humor in novels like “Oh Pure and Radiant Heart” and “A Children’s Bible.” “Atavists” (Norton) is the latest collection of her short fiction, and a perfect introduction to Millet’s work for those who haven’t yet discovered her laser wit and enormous heart.

Tech-driven visions of the future have always had a high error rate (I am still looking around for the robot housemaid promised to me by “The Jetsons”). But as Silicon Valley grows in political influence, the fantastic plans promulgated by industry leaders have begun to influence policy and government budgets. This isn’t great, as science journalist Adam Becker points out in “More Everything Forever: AI Overlords, Science Empires, and Silicon Valley’s Crusade to Control the Future of Humanity” (Basic), a clear-eyed assessment of today’s pie-eyed prophets.

In “Notes to John” (Knopf) readers are given excruciatingly intimate access to the mind of Joan Didion — these collected “notes” comprise the journal she wrote to her husband, John Gregory Dunne, to convey and explain the conversations she had with her therapist over the first decade of the 21st century. They are extraordinary. Didion’s voice is undiluted, bold, open, and the topics she discusses range from childhood to motherhood, from work to money to fame. And yet reading these entries can feel a little invasive, a bit of an intrusion; much as I adore Didion’s work and have learned from her over the years, I kept asking whether we really need to see into her soul, after her death.

You’ve probably heard that the Trump administration has revoked the visas of hundreds of international students studying in the US, including scores in New England. Immigration agents have also detained and sought to deport several, including a Tufts PhD student and a Columbia student arrested this week in Vermont.

What you may not have heard is that the administration seems to have had help.

A handful of pro-Israel groups are publicly taking credit for some of the government’s recent arrests. One such group is Betar, a century-old Zionist organization whose mantra is “Jews Fight Back.” In recent months, Betar’s US branch has compiled a list of allegedly pro-Palestinian students it believes the administration should deport.

My colleagues on the Globe’s Spotlight team have just published an investigation into Betar’s work. Here are five takeaways.

Betar isn’t new to this. Last fall, it criticized prosecutors in Newton for charging a supporter of Israel who shot a pro-Palestinian man at a rally there, urging businesses to boycott the city. Yet Betar’s influence was limited. The Newton boycott fizzled, and local officials considered the group “very fringe.”

President Trump’s inauguration, however, seems to have given it new reach. An attorney for Rümeysa Öztürk, the Tufts PhD student detained last month, said that Betar and groups like it were once seen as “gadflies.” Now, he and other lawyers for targeted students believe the administration is “more than willing to act on the information” Betar provides.

That information came in the form of a list of dozens of allegedly pro-Palestinian students that Betar says it gave to the Trump administration. According to the group, the students’ offenses include pro-Hamas advocacy, as well as jaywalking and a noise complaint.

So far, the administration has targeted at least seven of the people Betar listed, including Öztürk and Mohsen Mahdawi, the Columbia student immigration officials arrested in Vermont this week.

While Betar wouldn’t give the Globe a copy of its list, my colleagues found a version briefly posted on the group’s website. It featured the names, photos, and descriptions of 77 people.

Some of Betar’s entries, however, appear to be completely wrong. In one case, the group listed the name and photo of a woman wearing a hijab, identifying her as a Nigerian Harvard student who spoke at a pro-Hamas rally. Contacted by the Globe, the woman said she’s never visited the US, attended Harvard, or been to a pro-Hamas rally, calling Betar’s claims “completely false.”

Betar made similar mistakes in describing at least two other students it listed, my colleagues found. “Go to hell,” a Betar spokesperson said in response to their questions. “Who are you to judge us?”

The administration isn’t trumpeting any associations with Betar so far, telling the Globe that State Department staff make decisions about visas. Ross Glick, a former Betar employee who spoke to the Globe, wouldn’t say who in the administration received Betar’s list.

But the group does seem to be well connected. A public relations executive named Ronn Torossian, who founded Betar US last spring, has organized fund-raisers for Mayor Eric Adams of New York and done work for the foundation of Eric Trump, the president’s middle son.

Glick also claims to have made inroads with lawmakers. He has said he met with Senator John Fetterman, a pro-Israel Pennsylvania Democrat, and with aides to two Senate Republicans, Ted Cruz and James Lankford. In statements to the Globe, Fetterman denied “any involvement” with Betar, while Lankford’s aides said they have no evidence that anyone from the group met with the senator or his staff. Cruz’s office didn’t respond to requests for comment.

So far, Betar seems unbothered by those disavowals. Its website says it hopes to establish 25 chapters in the US this year, and it has raised tens of thousands of dollars on GoFundMe.

Betar isn’t alone in highlighting the Trump administration’s supposed ideological foes. Canary Mission, another pro-Israel group, has also compiled names of allegedly anti-Israel students. Turning Point USA, a right-wing campus group, publicly lists professors it claims “discriminate against conservative students and advance leftist propaganda in the classroom.”

Betar isn’t done, either. This week, the group predicted that immigration officials would soon target students at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. As Glick, the former Betar employee, told the Globe, “We want to help our government.”

Around $90 million total was expected to come to Massachusetts from the program to prevent flooding, much of it for stormwater infrastructure upgrades and building coastal protections.

The money will instead be reallocated to the agency or returned to the US Treasury. In its announcement, Trump administration officials called the grant program “wasteful” and “politicized.”

The cuts are the latest setbacks for local climate leaders as they race to implement plans to protect Boston from rapidly rising sea levels by the 2030s, at which point flood risks across the city’s waterfront are expected to increase dramatically.

Despite the cancellation of federal funds, Boston city leaders are promising to push ahead with their plans to protect the 47-mile-long coastline from erosion and flood risks.

“While this is incredibly unfortunate,” said Brian Swett, the city’s chief climate officer, “... this is not delaying anything that the city of Boston has underway [for coastal resilience].”

Still, “it does present a challenge that now we have a bigger wedge to fill in terms of construction [costs],” he said.

City leaders had expected $23 million from Washington to help construct the Moakley Park project, and a state agency had applied for a $12 million federal grant for Tenean Beach. Both applications were for funds from the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities grant program, known as BRIC, a Federal Emergency Management Agency program that had received a big infusion of cash under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act that was passed during the Biden administration.

Beyond Boston, dozens of other Massachusetts communities are also scrambling to figure out what to do without the FEMA funds. Chelsea and Everett, for example, lost out on a $50 million grant they were expecting to use to build storm surge flood barriers and restore salt marsh in a short tributary of the Mystic River.

Time is of the essence for such flood barriers: Already, sea levels in the Boston region have risen by about a foot since the 1920s, primarily due to climate change, as glaciers and sea ice melt and ocean temperatures warm, causing the water to expand.

Boston is likely to see another foot of sea level rise by 2050 compared to 2000. (City officials are planning infrastructure to withstand 40 inches of sea level rise by 2070.)

The roughly $250 million Moakley Park redevelopment will likely include a berm disguised as a walking pathway, a coastal marsh that absorbs water, and more. The loss of the $23 million for constructing such climate resilience portions of the project is a loss, city leaders said, but it will not slow down the project’s timeline. They had intended to use the grant money for construction, which will notbegin for another few years.

Despite the new federal funding cuts, Swett said he is optimistic that the city can find a different source of federal funding for construction on the park.

“We’re going to continue to do everything we can to make sure something comes from Washington,” Swett said. “I don’t think this is the end of the federal story of investment in this project.”

At Tenean Beach, the state plans to elevate a parking lot, part of Conley Street, and a portion of the Harborwalk to protect against rising sea levels. The Department of Conservation and Recreation had sought $12 million from the now-canceled FEMA grant program. State officials said the federal cut will both increase flood risks to communities if alternative funds are not identified and any resulting delays in the projects will increase the cost of the projects.

“It’s really unfortunate that the rug was pulled out from under us,” Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll said in an interview Thursday. “When you lose dollars like this, you just don’t get them back. Nothing is cheaper five or 10 years from now.”

“We need these dollars now,” she said.

The origins of Earth Day go back to 1970 when concerns about industrialization’s effect on environmental and public well-being sparked national protests and demonstrations demanding government protections for the environment.

Fifty-five years later, Earth Day is a worldwide event. In 2025, the official celebration falls on April 22, but throughout the month, organizations, groups, and individuals gather to mobilize and raise awareness about sustainable practices. This year’s global theme, Our Power, Our Planet, aims to emphasize the strength in numbers, encouraging collective strides toward a healthy planet.

But whether you’re celebrating Earth Day by mobilizing or helping protect and grow the city’s natural landscape, Greater Boston will host diverse opportunities for locals to immerse themselves in communal and educational practices that support the cause. From eco-cleanups with fellow community members to vibrant sustainable markets, here’s how to celebrate Earth Day in 2025.

Fellow tree-huggers and good Samaritans can unite for the Hub’s parks, forestry, and rivers by spending this week helping to repopulate forestry or caring for our waterways. Planting trees promotes biodiversity in these areas, improving conditions for inhabiting critters and the air quality of the local community. Our rivers, too, need a helping hand, being vital recreational spaces for city dwellers and the habitat of local wildlife. Here are some local tree-planting and river cleanup initiatives accepting volunteers in honor of Earth Day:

ARBOR DAY TREE PLANTING Volunteers can register for Speak for the Trees Boston’s annual Arbor Week tree planting featuring tall and leafy additions to Mount Hope Cemetery and Roxbury Community College. The local organization will provide tools and guidance for participants, so all they have to bring is their green thumb — and probably some gardening gloves to avoid splinters. Other nature-based events will take place throughout the week, including seedling bagging and giveaways, a “Mural Making with Nature Workshop,” and a tree giveaway in Jamaica Plain. April 23-May 3, times and locations vary. treeboston.org

PLANT TREES WITH MYRWA The Mystic River Watershed Association is organizing various tree-planting events across the Boston area. With supplies and guidance provided by the organization, volunteers will help sustain the tree canopies in local parks by adding to their population of bare-root trees. April 24-29. Locations vary. mycsticriver.org

CHARLES RIVER CLEANUP Though the Charles River is an iconic natural landmark, it remains susceptible to litter and invasive species. Every year, environmental organizations invite volunteers to revitalize the Charles during their Earth Day cleanup. The effort is statewide, spanning two days, 80 miles, and over 1,000 acres with plenty of volunteer opportunities for Massachusetts residents. April 25 and 26. Times and locations vary. charlesrivercleanup.org

NEPONSET RIVER CLEANUP The Neponset River, the slightly less famous Western Massachusetts river, is also being given special care this Earth Day. The annual cleanup, organized by the Neponset River Watershed Organization, brings together hundreds of volunteers to revive the 29-mile waterway. April 26, 9 a.m.-noon. Free. Locations vary. neponset.org

While Earth Day is historically a day of advocacy, it’s also a cause for celebration. Those hoping to enrich their appreciation of the Earth can learn more about sustainable practices in an upbeat, high-energy environment while partying eco-consciously.

PARTY FOR THE PLANET This Earth Day, the Stone Zoo is shining a light on the captivating lives of wildlife with its Party for the Planet celebration. Visitors can attend educator chats given by zookeepers and explore the unique stories of sloths, barn owls, and cougars. Families can bring their kids along for crafting activities, including painting wooden bee-themed ornaments and wooden magnets. April 22, 9 a.m.-1 p.m. Ticket prices vary. zoonewecngland.org

FOUND VINTAGE EARTHFEST If you haven’t heard, shopping secondhand is in. When shoppers see overpriced retail items, now more than ever they react with “I can just thrift this for cheaper.” Celebrating the growing community of thrifters and vintage shoppers, FOUND Vintage Market is organizing a secondhand outdoor market with dozens of local vendors in attendance. A DJ and food trucks will also be available for attendees. April 26, noon-5 p.m. 222 Jacob’s St., Cambridge.

EARTH DAY N NIGHT FESTIVAL Whether it’s day or night, there are no limits when it comes to celebrating the Earth, which is why the Great American Beer Hall will be hosting a 12-hour event to raise funds for the Clean Water Fund. The day will begin with a New England vendor market, putting the region’s art and artisanal goods on display for purchase. Then, the event will transform into an indie music festival with artists spanning genres, from surfer rock to EDM. April 26, 1 p.m.-1 a.m. posh.vip/earth-day-n-night

BOSTON PUBLIC MARKET EARTH DAY The Boston Public Market will host a five-day Earth Day celebration, beginning with Earth-themed cookie decorating and nature puppet stories geared toward the kiddos. Other events include workshops, grounding yoga classes, and organic smoothies. The programming will end on April 25 with a plant pot workshop, where attendees will sculpt their own planter. April 22-26. 100 Hanover St. bostonpublicmarket.org

“We’re doing everything we can to maintain it and take care of it as best we can, but it needs a complete overhaul,” said Michael Turner, executive director of business development and marketing for the Reggie.

And there are stark fiscal realities. The center costs between $3.5 million and $4 million to run annually. It’s operating at an annual average deficit of about $2 million, which is covered by Roxbury Community College’s state appropriation. (The site is managed by the college.) Officials at the Reggie, which is also state-funded, hope the center’s separate state appropriation is increased so that it no longer operates in the red.

As the center now celebrates its 30th anniversary, administrators are hoping to reintroduce the center to the communities it serves.

Jennie McDonald-Brown, RCC’s vice president of institutional advancement and the college’s foundation, put it bluntly: The 123,000-square-foot building is a testament to the notion that Roxbury, historically the heart of Black Boston and a neighborhood that has suffered from systemic racism and disinvestment over the decades, deserves nice things, too. It was a world-class facility when it opened and people like McDonald-Brown want to return it to that status.

“This for us is a springboard to bring it back to that place,” she said of the anniversary.

But she and Turner are forthright about the work that needs to be done. The capital needs are significant, and the state is allotting $22 million for center renovations, which, after state fees, will fund $15.3 million worth of improvements in coming months. Turner expects big upgrades to happen over the next two years: a new roof, a new HVAC system, and a new track.

Central to the Reggie’s mission, said Turner and McDonald-Brown, is reducing the life expectancy gap between Roxbury, where more than 80 percent of residents are people of color, and Back Bay, one of Boston’s wealthier, and whiter, neighborhoods, where residents, on average, live much, much longer.

More exercise and healthy programs can help cut into the public health crisis, which reflects structural racism, they say.

When the center first opened, the Globe marveled at the banked, eight-lane 200-meter high school track. But the center’s construction and opening was also imbued with the spirit of its namesake: a basketball legend for both the Celtics and the Northeastern Huskies who was also known locally for his philanthropic work, which included giving away turkeys to those in need at Thanksgiving. Lewis died of cardiac arrest in 1993 at age 27.

At the center’s 1995 opening ceremony, then-governor William Weld said: “Generations of young athletes will use this facility to make their own dreams come true. The name Reggie Lewis will keep them attuned that the real immortals have more than talent and strength. The ones that we remember forever have the biggest hearts.”

Since its inception, the Reggie has had many faces. It is the home to high school indoor track and field in the state, it’s the home to Roxbury Community College Athletics, and it also serves as host to myriad programming, from senior aerobics to AAU basketball to volleyball camps to youth golf lessons to dance classes to political rallies.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, it was the site of a mass vaccination distribution center. Both Turner and McDonald-Brown want residents to think of the facility as much more than a track.

But in recent years, much of the friction regarding the facility has focused on how the center balances those various identities.

Despite the droves who come to the center each year, Turner considers the facility to be underutilized. That’s because the bulk of the 300,000 people who use the facility — about 250,000 — walk through the doors during indoor track season, which runs roughly from late November to late March. During that period, there are on average two track meets every weekday afternoon, not to mention invitationals on the weekends. But for a good stretch of the year, the facility is simply not as busy.

And in recent years, there has been controversy. City councilors raised concerns about use of the track, pushing for more time for city high school indoor runners who were forced to practice in school hallways instead of on the track and questioning how much time is allotted for high school students from the suburbs.

But Turner said recently that the allotted time for city high school students to use the track for practice has not changed in 30 years.

It is a state facility, funded with state money. And as a state facility, it has obligations to host track meets from high schools throughout Massachusetts,according to the state legislation that enabled the creation of the center. But no one uses the facility more than Boston Public Schools, Turner said. He chalked up the recent political friction to “lack of understanding and communication.”

“We do everything in our power to make sure they have access,” he said of serving the city’s public school students.

Officials behind the Reggie agree that the center can do a better job of promoting itself. Too many residents see school buses parked outside the building from well-heeled suburbs and assume that is what the facility is all about.

“We can do a much better job with storytelling,” McDonald-Brown said.

Concurrently with the center’s planned facelift, the Reggie is amid a push to offer more programming, which officials hope will bring in more residents.

Those behind the Reggie hope to raise more than $5 million in the coming years to achieve that. A partnership with the Boston Athletic Association, the organization that puts on the Marathon, has been successful, allowing the center to hire more fitness instructors, which has increased the number of fitness sessions it can offer from three a week for seniors to more than 20 a week for all ages in recent months.

“We want this to be the place that you go to,” McDonald-Brown said. “We have to have more programming. If you build it they will come.”

She added, “You need money to build it.”

Fernandes Anderson announced last week she plans to step down from her seat on the council, after she signed an agreement to plead guilty to two of the six federal corruption charges against her.

However, she has not yet formally resigned, or said when she will do so. According to the city charter, if a district council seat becomes vacant more than 180 days before the next regular municipal election, the city clerk is required to start the process to schedule a special election. This year, that deadline is May 8.

But Council President Ruthzee Louijeune and Councilor Liz Breadon filed a home rule petition this week to bypass that process if Fernandes Anderson does step down before that deadline, arguing the timeline would be too rushed and would disenfranchise voters in a historically marginalized district.

Secretary of State William F. Galvin also said he opposes the idea of Boston holding a special election on this timeline, speaking to the Globe on Monday. Galvin put the city’s elections department into state receivership earlier this year after his office investigated and confirmed reports of widespread problems during last November’s election, including ballot shortages at numerous polling locations, and significant communication failures.

Galvin said administering a special election on such short notice would compromise the department’s ability to address and fix deeper problems before the regular election in November.

Louijeune and Breadon also reiterated Friday that they filed the home rule petition after hearing feedback from community advocates and residents in the district, who said they believe it would benefit the district’s constituents to have more time to vet candidates.

As the District 7 councilor, Fernandes Anderson represents some of the most historically diverse neighborhoods in Boston, including Roxbury, Dorchester, part of the South End, and the Fenway.

But the legislation prompted Fernandes Anderson to deliver sharp words toward her colleagues during the special, virtual meeting Friday, particularly at Louijeune and Councilor Erin Murphy.

Speaking directly to Louijeune, Fernandes Anderson said she has heard “adamantly” from her constituents that they do not want a special election, and have asked her to resign after the May 8 deadline. She argued that, when asked by Louijeune if she was going to resign, she told Louijeune that she doesn’t know when she will step down, but that she is working on a transition plan and there will not be a need for a special election.

Louijeune emphasized that after hearing from residents and community leaders, she filed the measure because she believes it’s in the best interest of the district and its constituents.

Murphy and Flynn said Friday they opposed the measure because they believe it would disenfranchise Fernandes Anderson’s constituents to leave them without representation until November. No. The only Celtics teams to win consecutive championships were the Bill Russell-led teams of the 1960s.

And they did it a lot.

Put it this way: When I walked into first grade at Groton Elementary School in September 1959, the Boston Celtics were defending NBA champs.

I was a freshman in high school by the time I started classes in a September in which the Celtics were not defending champs.

That’s right, ladies and gents. The Russell-Red Auerbach Celtics won eight consecutive championships from 1959-66. Oh, and for good measure, Russell, Satch Sanders, Sam Jones, John Havlicek, and friends won back-to-back one last time in the springs of 1968 and ’69, when Russ and Sam were on their way out the door.

Repeating as champs was simply a way of life for Boston-area Baby Boomers in the 1960s.

April arrived. In succession, we had the Red Sox usually losing on Opening Day, blooming forsythia, hundreds of folks running from Hopkinton to Boylston Street for a cup of hearty beef stew, and then — before the month was over — the Celtics winning the NBA championship. It was just something that happened every April. Like our parents paying taxes.

Sitting here in 2025, waiting for the Celtics’ first playoff game against the Orlando Magic Sunday at the Garden, we are in Full Repeat Mode, but need to be reminded how hard it is to win back-to-back NBA championships. The 2017-18 Warriors are the last team to turn the trick and it’s staggering to realize that even the Celtics haven’t done it since Russell last roamed the parquet floor.

The Cowens-White-Havlicek teams of the 1970s came close. They won a franchise-record 68 games in 1972-73, only to be thwarted by the mighty Knicks in a seven-game series that we know was lost only because Havlicek (shoulder) was a one-armed player for the second half of the series. Boston won the title the following year, when Cowens (most underrated great player in Celtics history) outplayed Kareem Abdul-Jabbar of the Milwaukee Bucks.

Bird’s teams flirted with repeating three times. After winning in 1981, they were bounced in Game 7 at home by the 76ers (the “Beat LA” game) in ’82. After beating the Lakers in 1984, they won 63 regular-season games and routed the Lakers, 148-114, in Game 1 of the 1985 Finals. But they had no depth (Cedric Maxwell knee surgery) and lost in six. The 1985-86 team — best in the history of the NBA — similarly fizzled in the ’87 Finals against the Lakers. McHale’s broken foot, Bill Walton’s unavailability, and Len Bias’s death crushed their chance to repeat.

The KG-Pierce-Allen champs of 2008 had a great chance to repeat until Garnett hurt his knee and missed the ’09 playoffs.

Notice any theme here?

Injuries. A less-than-healthy roster blocked the Celtics from repeating in the ’70s, ’80s, and again in this century. And it’s the only thing that can stop them now.

Never mind those gaudy records in Cleveland (64-18) and Oklahoma City (68-14). The 61-win Celtics are the deepest and best team in the NBA. The only thing that can stop them are long shelf stretches for Jaylen Brown (knee), Kristaps Porzingis (lower leg), or a new injury to another star.

Strap yourselves in for four playoff rounds over the next eight weeks. It’s looking like the Knicks or Pistons after the Magic, then probably the Cavaliers in the conference finals, followed by a 25th Celtic appearance in the NBA Finals against probably the Thunder, Lakers (heart be still), Warriors, or Nuggets.

See you around the gym.
